topic: Should the US Expand (“pack”) the Supreme Court?
argument: Hello. I think expanding is a bad idea for the supreme court. I think that will make things more complicated when it comes to those things that require it. Decisions will take longer to make also. The political systems is already in shambles this would just make things worse.
rebuttal: Diversity is good no debate there but you can have too many people in power. The balance of power will be spread to thin.
conclusion: There comes a point when politics need to stay out of the courtroom and that is an issue in itself. We do need too balance diversity but expanding instead of being more conscious of it in the beginning seems backwards to me. More politics is not a good thing and that is what will happen.
argumentOpponent: Expanding the Supreme Court is a vital step towards checking the balance of power and ensuring diverse representation, critical principles that lie at the heart of a well-functioning democracy. As Democrats, we believe in equality, justice, and inclusivity, values that can be upheld by adding a broader range of voices on the bench.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's true that expansion might initially seem to complicate matters, in the long run, it ensures a balanced court that mirrors the diversity of the nation, thus making more representative decisions. Moreover, rather than worsening the political system, it strengthens it by preventing the court's politicization and ensuring equality and justice.
conclusionOpponent: Rather than diluting power, court expansion ensures a broader perspective and inclusive discussions, a strength that will inevitably lead to more balanced and representative decisions. The democratization of power is not equal to its dilution but, on the contrary, it strengthens the integrity and legitimacy of the Supreme Court.

topic: Should Transgender People Be Banned From Using Bathrooms Consistent With Their Gender Identity?
argument: People should be allowed to use the bathroom consistent to their identity. It's part of allowing them to freely make their own choices.
rebuttal: You use the word everyone, yet seem to disregard the comfort of transgender individuals. They may not feel comfortable using the restroom that would correspond to them biologically. It's better to just let everyone make their own choices versus trying to choose who to side with.
conclusion: I agree that it's tough to side with individuals, but people who identify with their biological sex are also individuals. Just because transgender people are the minority does not mean they deserve less rights. Thus, it would be best to just allow people to use the restroom they choose freely,
argumentOpponent: Public restrooms should be used in accordance with one's biological sex due to concerns about privacy and safety, and to minimize potential discomfort for users. This stance is not about denying the rights of transgender persons, but about preserving the boundaries and rights of everyone.
rebuttalOpponent: While upholding the freedom to make personal choices is important, it is equally key to acknowledge that public restrooms serve a wider audience with diverse beliefs and comfort levels. Therefore, prioritizing individual choices over collective comfort and safety may not always be the most considerate solution.
conclusionOpponent: While it is unfortunate that transgender individuals might not feel comfortable, creating broadly accommodating public spaces requires considering the comfort of the majority. This is a complex issue that goes beyond individual choice to consider societal norms, and thus requires careful deliberation and possibly alternative solutions, such as gender-neutral restrooms.\n

topic: Are Social Media Making People Stupid?
argument: Yes, Social media is absolutely making people more stupid on the whole. People have learned not to think for themselves. They have learned to get all information on life from the internet and from watching videos, seeing articles on social media etc and assuming that the information they are being presented is true. They don't take the time to fact check themselves or the information that is being given to them and therefore begin to adopt beliefs that are not true and do not actually represent accurate depictions of certain events.
rebuttal: If we were to actually gather data, I don't think it would support the argument that social media has made people smarter. I think we would find out that people all too frequently are taking things they see on social media as the truth and therefore they are being fed misinformation from multiple different angles. People become so engrossed in what they are doing that they are unlikely to be taking the time to actually research what they are being told and find out if the information is truly accurate. They take "influencers" for example and assume that because they have some level of popularity that they must know what they are talking about and are telling people the truth. They themselves start to spread this information to others and wind up making the masses less intelligent on the whole than they were before.
conclusion: I stand by my position that misinformation is being spread rampantly, whether intentionally or just purely through ignorance. Too often people just don't know any better and will spread things they see via social media to others on the assumption that because their friend/family member saw it and posted it, that it must be true. We need people to think for themselves and take the time to go through the information they are being fed and actually did into what is true. Social media is often not the real world and doesn't always give an accurate depiction of what the real world is actually like or what is actually going on. News and information spread easier because of social media, but if what is being spread isn't accurate or useful, you would have a hard time convincing me that people are suddenly smarter because of something they saw from a 12 year old on Tik Tok
argumentOpponent: Social media is not making people more stupid, but allows them to research topics and actually become smarter as they can interact better with those around them. Reasoning to show an example of this is how people who have not taken a traditional college or schooling route are able to make a lot of money without ever entering the working world. The idea of the influencer might seem somewhat disingenuous or vanity filled on the surface, but at the same time, it is a growing profession that can absolutely pay off as we have seen with many people. Social media is something that has taken giant steps and leaps to grow, and it will only do so because of its popularity and ability to focus on intellectual and sophisticated interaction, which then allows people to develop entrepreneurial skills. Therefore, the proof that social media is making people stupid is quite the opposite. It's making them smarter.
rebuttalOpponent: Social media aids in the formal conversation and discussion of varying ideas and topics. Diversity of thought is seen abundantly across social media platforms and because of this, people are learning from one another and are crafting in creating new ideas, innovations, and ways of pursuing wealth and happiness. This could only be done by a group of people who have the ability and the smarts to go against social norms and expectations. In this case, social media has made people smarter because they are willing to challenge the typical ways of communicating and job searching and stand by the millions of dollars they have made as they continue to do so.
conclusionOpponent: In my closing argument, I would certainly like to stress the fact that while what we see on social media might appear alien or abnormal, it is certainly worth noting that it now has become trendy and is taking over as a whole because the lifestyle and glamour that it provides is not out of reach any longer. The walls and odds might be stacked against someone who did not go to school or who does not have wealthy parental figures. With the invention of social media, everyone not only has an equal chance at life and accomplishing their natural talents, but those high walls are now taken down as the playing field is now level and even. Social media is now becoming reality whereas before it was only a small reflection of it.

topic: Is Online Learning a Suitable Replacement for Traditional In-Person Education?
argument: I think that it is better to have online learning due to it being more conveinent for the students. for students to be able top learn at their own home and not having to travel it gives students much more motivation to learn more
rebuttal: i think that not having school in person it can mess up the way that a person conducts themselves due to the decrease of social interaction with students their own age
conclusion: Remote learning offers flexibility and convenience, allowing students to learn from anywhere with an internet connection. It can also provide access to a wider range of educational resources and opportunities. Additionally, some students may find remote learning more comfortable and less stressful than traditional in-person classes. However, each learning mode has its own advantages and disadvantages, and what works best can vary depending on individual preferences and circumstances.
argumentOpponent: While online learning can provide the flexibility and accessibility, it cannot fully replace the interpersonal skills, discipline, and networking opportunities provided by traditional in-person education.
rebuttalOpponent: While convenience is indeed a benefit of online learning, the lack of structure can lead to lack of discipline and reduced motivation for many students. Additionally, the absence of face-to-face interaction deprives students of crucial real-world skills such as networking and teamwork.\n
conclusionOpponent: Indeed, the decrease in social interaction can limit a student's growth regarding social conduct, team dynamics, and networking skills, all key elements of in-person education. The convenience of online learning, though beneficial, does not fully compensate for the holistic development offered by traditional education.

topic: Should the US Have Mandatory National Service?
argument: Should the US have Mandatory National Service? I'm here to tell you why it should not. The US has based it's whole foundation on freedom. What is freedom if not choice? Without choice we're not truly free. You cannot force people to care about things they do not. People who are forced to do something they don't want to leads to lack of effort and therefore would weaken the whole gro
rebuttal: If you have to force people to into things they won't be open to actually learning or growing new skills. People need to do things by their own choice if they are to succeed.  When people are told what to do they push back. I think mandatory national service is unrealistic in regards to humans.
conclusion: Collective effort and group contribution is great but what about people who have their plate full of other work? There would need to be exemptions for people who have disabilities and other  criteria that would prevent them from selecting from the areas of service to hel
argumentOpponent: Mandatory national service, beyond just the military, provides a solution towards bridging socio-economic gaps by forging unity and offering equal chances for individuals to acquire valuable skills and life experiences. It's an investment for a more connected, capable and compassionate nation.
rebuttalOpponent: While freedom is integral, it can also yield greater societal equity and unity under a mandatory civic engagement program, which contrary to forcing interest, offers vast opportunities to choose areas of service different individuals are passionate about. A healthy democracy thrives on collective effort and contribution, not passivity.
conclusionOpponent: Mandatory national service does not eliminate choice, but frames it in a context of commitment towards national responsibility and unity; an opportunity to explore diverse fields and learn sought-after skills, fostering growth on a personal and national level. It is our collective duty to cultivate an environment where individual success is intertwined with the country's progress and prosperity.

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument:
Different countries have different needs and capabilities. It is not fair for all countries to have the same policies as it will effect many countries differently than others.

Some countries have contributed far more to global warming than others, so it is not fair to put the same restrictions on all countries.

International policies infringes upon the right of a country to make decisions for themselves.

Policies will hurt some countries more economically than others, causing them to be at a huge disadvantage.
rebuttal: These international agreements will be political in nature and be more beneficial for some countries than others. Those with the most power will dictate the rules to make the policies advantageous to them and try to use them to hurt their enemies. This will end up causing more problems than solutions and may lead to wars. These policies are unlikely to take into account the differences between countries and their priorities. They also will not likely address the fact that some countries contribute far more to the problem than others.
conclusion: This only sounds good in theory, but in practicality this is not how things will play out. Politics will get involved and governments will try to abuse these policies in order to make money and hurt their political opponents. This will make the divide even larger and we will end up further behind than we already are.  There is simply no trust among nations, and without the trust, these policies serve to do nothing except waste money, time, and resources.
argumentOpponent: International agreements are imperative to enforce global climate change policies, as they provide a united front necessary for global cooperation and an accelerated response to the climate crisis, which respects no borders. By pooling resources and knowledge, we can foster innovation and economies of scale in green technologies, making sustainability the road to economic advancement.
rebuttalOpponent: International agreements wouldn't impose one-size-fits-all policies, instead, they would employ a common but differentiated responsibilities principle. Further, it is about protecting global rights over short-term national interests, and economic transition to sustainable practices only poses an 'initial' disadvantage which can be mitigated by global financial support and technology transfer mechanisms.
conclusionOpponent: While power dynamics in international agreements can be challenging, it doesn’t negate the urgent need for global cooperation. Moreover, with principles of equity such as 'those who pollute more, pay more', and democratic processes, such agreements can ensure fair burden-sharing, addressing both historic and current emissions, whilst promoting a collective trajectory towards a sustainable future.

topic: Should There Be Standardized Testing in Schools?
argument: Testing of students is necessary to ensure their competence. Would you want an engineer who was incompetent to design a bridge that your family were forced to travel?\n\n
rebuttal: We should not reward those who do not perform. People must work to receive rewards. Do not reward freeloaders and slackers. This is fair to everyone.
conclusion: Standardized testing gives a great basis for the intelligence and ability of the participants. Without testing ignorant people will be placed in positions that require intelligence.
argumentOpponent: Standardized testing in schools creates an unhealthy emphasis on test preparation rather than holistic learning, stifling creativity and critical thinking. It also unfairly disadvantages socio-economically challenged students who may lack access to test-prep resources.
rebuttalOpponent: Competence isn't solely measured through standardized testing; skills like problem-solving, creativity, and adaptability are equally important and aren't evaluated in these tests. Also, achieving fairness in education requires us to consider individual learning contexts, not measured by standardized tests.
conclusionOpponent: Success should not be boxed into a uniform test score but should appreciate diverse skills, work ethics, and individual growth. Education should inspire learning and exploration, not spawn fear and anxiety that standardized tests often breed.

topic: Should Every Citizen Receive a Basic Income from the Government?
argument: It may disincentivize work and hinder economic productivity by reducing the motivation for individuals to actively seek employment. I also have concerns about the potential strain on government resources and the risk of creating dependency on a guaranteed income,
rebuttal: I think this approach could lead to a society where people are not better equipped to pursue meaningful work or contribute to innovation, ultimately undermining success in life needs.
conclusion: I believe just giving income for nothing which could lead to long-term economic challenges for the government providing welfare for everyone is also a poor principle to get others to believe in hard work.
argumentOpponent: A Universal Basic Income promises to stimulate economic growth, empowering all citizens with the freedom to invest in skills and businesses, ensuring that hard work equates to greater financial stability rather than just survival.
rebuttalOpponent: Studies have found that basic income does not discourage employment, rather, it provides a safety net that allows people to take calculated risks, fostering entrepreneurship and innovation. As for governmental strain, funding UBI could involve restructuring current welfare systems, resulting in a more efficient use of resources.
conclusionOpponent: Universal Basic Income isn't about undermining success; on the contrary, it's about creating a level playing field that allows everyone, regardless of their present socioeconomic status, to have personal and professional fulfillment, invest in their passions, and in turn, contribute meaningfully to society. By doing so, we can foster a culture of entrepreneurship and innovation, key tenets of successful economies.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: Animals are living things and this should not be used for our own selfish benefit. We should find other ways of obtaining what we need.
rebuttal: All of these reasons sound selfish. There are alternate ways that we can advance science without involving other living things. I think there are just excuses
conclusion: I just dont see a reason in today's science that we cannot explore other ways. We have way too many resources at our disposal to keep doing this.
argumentOpponent: The use of animals in scientific research is crucial to advancing medical knowledge and developing treatments that save human lives, as it provides invaluable and irreplaceable insights into biological systems. While the welfare of animals is important, very strict regulations are in place to ensure their humane treatment.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's true that exploiting animals is ethically concerning, their use in controlled, ethical research is not selfish, but rather a key element in progress for all, animals included, as many veterinary medicines owe their existence to animal research. Furthermore, until viable alternatives with the same level of biological accuracy exist, it is a necessary practice.
conclusionOpponent: While alternatives are being developed and encouraged, they currently cannot yet fully replace animal models due to complexity and variability of living organisms. The goal remains to reduce the necessity of animal testing, but until then, it serves as our most reliable pathway to scientific progress, far from being a mere excuse.

topic: Should Governments Have the Right to Censor the Internet?
argument: I feel that given the rampant spread if misinformation on social media and online in general is getting out of hand and something needs to be done about it. I think the government should work towards censoring hate and misinformation done online. This would cut down on potential huge crimes such as terrorist attacks and mass shootings. But additionally could help produce a more functional society with lies not spreading as much.
rebuttal: An informed society is sometimes worse as some people feel they are informed when in reality they are misinformed due to the rampant spread of misinformation. In the digital age of communication we must have ways of limiting lies from spreading and causing massive real world issues.
conclusion: The issue with leaving it up to the consumer to fact check themselves is that more than likely they read something and believe its true without ever looking to fact check themselves. Most people don't like to be proven wrong and thus simply believe whatever sounds good to them. Due to basic human nature we need a government entity to offer oversight on this matter.
argumentOpponent: Government censorship of the internet curtails freedom of expression and stifles innovation, leading to an uninformed society and a stagnant economy. In an age of digital communication, free flow of information is vital for democratic processes and progress.
rebuttalOpponent: While combating misinformation is essential, government censorship can easily become a tool for political control, suppressing dissent and manipulating public opinion. Moreover, it's more effective to promote media literacy and fact-checking initiatives, rather than resorting to outright censorship.
conclusionOpponent: Indeed, misinformation is a problem, but government censorship isn't the solution - it risks power misuse and the suppression of essential dialogue. Instead, we must strive for a transparent society where critical thinking, fact-checking tools, and robust public debate are fostered to differentiate lies from truth.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
argument: Artificial intelligence is good for society because it can make our lives easier and be more productive than human beings can be. AI could also assist with current jobs and improve the quality of work. There would be less of a need for people to work undesirable jobs that the AI could complete more efficiently.
rebuttal: Automation taking away jobs is important but it could also increase productivity. Something such as a universal minimum income, might be a necessity if automation kills a large number of jobs.
conclusion: Human judgement is critical in certain fields, but in jobs that don't require much critical thinking and could be easily automated, it is possible that the AI has a positive impact on these fields.
argumentOpponent: While AI has potential benefits, it poses considerable risks, such as job displacement due to automation and weakening of privacy due to intrusive AI surveillance, thereby posing a significant threat to society.
rebuttalOpponent: AI may improve efficiency, but this efficiency can lead to widespread job losses; it also raises the ethical issue of AI operability in certain fields where human touch and judgment are critical. The quality of work might improve but at the expense of individual privacy and security, creating an invasive society.
conclusionOpponent: Increased productivity should never compromise human livelihood and dignity; the implementation of a universal minimum income won't address the inequalities and social divisions that might emerge from automation. The cost of privacy and ethical concerns still outweigh the convenience automation and AI surveillance may offer to society.

topic: Should the US Provide Military Aid to Ukraine in its Conflict With Russia?
argument: The US should provide military aid to Ukraine against Russia for a number of reasons.  The first reason is a moral argument.  Russia is the aggressor country and is killing and raping innocent people.  They are targeting infrastructure and grain silos to try to freeze and starve Ukraine to death.  The US also was a signatory to the Buddhapist Accords which says that the US will agree to help Ukraine in it's defense for Ukraine giving up it's nuclear weapons.\n\nThe US has stockpiled tons of weapons during the Cold War in order to defeat Russia should there be a conflict between the two countries.  These weapons are close to being decomissioned which costs a lot of money.  It costs us less money to send these to Ukraine.
rebuttal: Russia is trying to run out the clock so that people lose patience with Ukraine.  If Russia controls Ukraine, the US is going to have much more serious issues to worry about in addition to the one's at home.  For example, Putin will next move into Maldova.  Then it will be on to the Baltics and then to Poland.  The Baltics and Poland are both part of NATO, which will get us in a direct war.\n\nAppeasement never works with dictators.  We tried this with Hitler during WW2 to give him Czechlovakia and he just kept going.  We tried this with Putin in 2014 with Crimea and the Donbass.  Dictators keep going so stop them now before it costs us more in the long run.
conclusion: American's should not fund dictator countries.  America should try to fund the opposition.  That way dictators all over the world will not be emboldened to invade or commit human rights abuses.  Putin's biggest fear is that he will end up like Gadaffi - dead in a ditch, which is how all dictators should end up.  All of our foreign policy problems are due to dictators - China, Russia, North Korea, Venezuela, the Middle East, Cuba.
argumentOpponent: The war has already taken too long and too much of the US's money. The US has plenty of other issues that need dire attention at home first before spreading itself thin in Ukraine. Russia does not seem to be letting go and this war can end up costing America too much.
rebuttalOpponent: If America acted on morals, it would have to save the whole world. Most countries in the world are being lead by dictators, for example, most countries in Africa and Asia. Should America fund them too?
conclusionOpponent: America has done all it can to help Ukraine thus far. The most it can do now is try and bring the countries together for an agreement instead of throwing more money at the war. There are many countries in worse situations than Ukraine, will the US throw money at them too? Many people are working hard to pay taxes in America and they probably would like to see their monies go to better use.

topic: Should the Death Penalty Be Legal?

It serves as justice for the victims and their families and it does provide a sense of closure for them as well. rebuttal: It is a deterrent and there's been numerous academic studies that prove it is effective in deterring crime. It is justice for the family and unless you've ever been in that position as a family member of a victim then a person can't really judge If it's wrong or not.
conclusion: While I do respect the "suggests"  of the FBI uniform crime report I don't think they have been a member of a family to someone who was murdered. And I would have to see some hard statistics And I would like to know what they used for data to draw those answers because that's ludicrous to be honest with you I seriously seriously doubt the States that don't have the death penalty Have been lower in murder rates I would compare the states and the population before I would believe that to be honest.
argumentOpponent: The death penalty not only runs the risk of irrevocable mistakes, but also does not prove to be an effective deterrent against crime, hence failing in delivering justice and public safety.

conclusionOpponent: While there are studies citing the deterrent effect, multiple reputable studies and statistics state otherwise, and choosing justice based on emotions isn't prudent; delivering justice isn't merely about revenge, but also about rehabilitation. topic: Are Social Media Making People Stupid?
argument: I believe that social media is making people less intelligent. I think that as social media has become more prevalent in use, the age of use of social media has gotten lower and lower to the point where social media is now being used by children who should not be using it. Due to this, the children are using social media for large amounts of time. In my opinion, this time could be better spent practicing reading, math, and other skills they should be honing in school. Instead, most children with access to social media are using their devices much more than they should be. This is causing stunts in their development, which is literally contributing to them becoming less intelligent than the last generation. If someone uses their time to practice a skill versus looking at a screen for 30 minutes a day, believe the person practicing the skill would end up being more intelligent, and therefore I believe my argument is proven true.
rebuttal: I agree with you about the fact that they can access information from anywhere. However, we are talking about social media and not the internet in general. On social media, fake information and fake news is now becoming prevalent and if individuals are getting their information strictly from social media, they may not be getting correct information. Gaining knowledge is a good indicator of intelligence, but what if the information is incorrect? If I am learning a ton of math in school, but it is the wrong math with the wrong answers, am I still getting smarter? No would be the answer in that situation. Just because we are able to engage with others does not mean we are getting correct information.
conclusion: I stand firm in my argument. Anyone can impersonate anyone on social media. If I reach out to an "expert" for an answer to something and I receive the incorrect answer, does that mean I am making myself more intelligent? No. That means I am thinking I am gaining knowledge when I am, in fact, not gaining anything. And then I may go on to spread that bad information to others thinking it is true, which is in fact affecting other's intelligence as well. If I am looking to learn something, I absolutely do not go onto social media looking for an answer. I would look to the internet and go after verified and reputable scholarly sources. Do you have any proof of your claim? No.
argumentOpponent: Social media is not making people stupid. Social media provides individuals with more access to information that ever before. It allows them to talk to people all over the world. It allows them the ability to learn about anything they can think of. It gives them experience with different cultures, along with being able to hear different opinions and information. It allows them to engage with others on any topic and hear many different points of view. It provides a vast array of experiences that can make an individual more aware of the world at large.
rebuttalOpponent: Social media is all about how you use it. Anyone can use it to just mess around with nonsense. The people who do this would probably waste their time anyway. Social media is the ultimate access to experiences and information. If you want to learn how to do something you can ask experts. If you want to know about something you can join a group and talk others about it. It is full of different cultures and different people who can offer unique experiences and opinions. It allows you to open your mind to possibilities. You can learn skills using social media, even if that skill is just how to best communicate with others different from yourself.
conclusionOpponent: Yes social media does spread some misinformation but so does the internet in general. It is up to the user to be smart about where they get their information. As long as a user is logical they will be able to wade through the misinformation. Social media more than anything allows you the unique experience to interact with the world at large. It allows you to learn about people from anywhere, and everywhere. It provides you will access to information about anything you want to learn about. It allows human connection so that you can learn more about yourself and about the world. Any hobby you can think of has a fanbase you can join to expand your own understanding and knowledge.

topic: Is Arts Education as Important as Science and Math in Schools?
argument: Arts Education is just as important, if not more important, as Science and Math in school. While math and science give us the skills and tools to understand various life aspects, art goes much deeper. Literary and musical arts, in particular, allow us to comprehend other cultures and think outside the box. It's what allows us to be creative and have emotions. It's what makes us feel unique and important. It gives us purpose.
rebuttal: I agree that science, technology, and math create an obedient and disciplined employee; one that will become one of the many cogs of the machine. However, there's no freedom and choice in these fields. To be creative, you need choice and free thinking. And these are the foundation of innovation and invention. Without them, you will simply follow the demands of others.
conclusion: I can agree that STEM (science, technology, economics, and math) are fundamental to the growing challenges of the world. However, without the study of arts, I don't believe students will be prepared or the many challenges they'll face out in the real world. We couldn't survive without both, if I'm being honest. But I would prefer our next generation of workers to have a better understanding of life than they do of trigonometry.
argumentOpponent: While acknowledging the value of arts, the economic and technological advancements of society primarily hinge upon a strong foundation in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) education. Schools should prioritize the subjects that directly contribute to innovation, productivity, and job security.
rebuttalOpponent: While the value of arts in fostering creativity and emotional awareness is recognized, the fundamental role of STEM in driving the economic machinery cannot be overlooked. It's vital that we focus our resources on equipping the next generation with the necessary skills for navigating our increasingly tech-dominated world.
conclusionOpponent: Reiterating, STEM disciplines don't necessarily limit creativity, but offer tangible mediums for innovative exploration and problem-solving. Given the role of STEM in driving technological advancements and economic growth, educational emphasis on these subjects is indispensable for individual growth and societal progress.

Getting a college degree in itself is a rigorous achievement. Many people do not even get t
conclusion: Many people do not even get to graduate. Graduating is an achievement in itself. Furthermore, giving everyone an opportunity to succeed would better society. People should be as educated as possible for the betterment of society in general. Someone having a bachelor's degree does not diminish the value of another person's degree. They are both graduates and can help be
argumentOpponent: While the idea of tuition-free public college seems compelling, it is not financially sustainable as it shifts an enormous burden onto taxpayers, and potentially devalues a college degree by turning it into a universal expectation rather than a rigorous achievement.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's agreed that the tax burden is a concern, it's crucial to note that not all students attending public schools are lazy or privileged; many are there striving for upward social mobility and the opportunity for better lives. Singling out abuses isn't a justification for denying this opportunity to genuinely hardworking students.
conclusionOpponent: While higher education can lead to better jobs and contribute to the economy, it doesn't guarantee it. topic: Should the US Provide Military Aid to Ukraine in its Conflict With Russia?
argument: I will argue that the U.S. shouldn't be siding with Ukraine in its war with Russia or providing direct military aid. Although it is possible to agree that Ukraine was unfairly attacked by Russia, the U.S. should stay out of interfering with world conflicts directly and focus its efforts at issues at home instead.
rebuttal: The U.S. frequently has to interpret international law to see that it aligns with the actual facts of what happened and gauging whether the act of aggression - if it's determined to have take place - represents a direct threat to either the U.S. as a country or the alliances to which the U.S. belongs. In this case, the aggression has taken place entirely in Europe and represents no threat to our country. Additionally, several European nations interpreted Russia's actions differently, so the decision to support Ukraine isn't uniformly accepted and should be further considered in detail.
conclusion: As I had mentioned before, the U.S. has to balance its commitment to global democratic values with the realities of global politics. International peace could be better served by economic pressures levied against Russia and its allies, as well as better ties to Russia's current silent partners, such as China and India. If we could successfully pressure China to step down its support of Russia, Russian campaign against Ukraine might fall apart without direct U.S. military intervention and international peace will prevail through diplomacy.
argumentOpponent: The U.S. should provide military aid to Ukraine to uphold international law by deterring aggression, and to protect democratic values worldwide, which notably align with American foreign policy.
rebuttalOpponent: While domestic issues are crucial, the U.S. as a global leader cannot disregard breaches of international law; the direct military aid not only aids Ukraine but affirms the U.S. commitment to democratic values and international peace.
conclusionOpponent: Aiding Ukraine goes beyond protecting physical threats to the U.S; it is about preserving the democratic integrity of nations and maintaining a just international order that benefits all—core principles of American foreign policy. Indifference towards aggressive acts could set a frightening global precedent where stronger nations overthrow the weaker without consequences.

topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: The US should ban fossil fuels as individuals' efforts to combat climate change might not be enough (recycling, using public transportation). While banning fossil fuels might not be sufficient for reversing climate change, it can make a difference in reducing the effects of climate change. Climate change needs to be combated on a individual, local, national, and corporate level to see real change. If not, future generations may not have a planet, biodiversity will decrease, and natural resources will continue to be depleted. The US should specifically have a responsibility as Americans tend to be significant emitters because of our lifestyle.
rebuttal: A ban would be something to work towards eventually. This can be done in phases to reach the long-term goal so fossil fuels aren't eradicated cold turkey. By starting these habit changes eventually, we can start relying on other resources to wean ourselves off. Relying too much on one thing alone can be negative as fossil fuels themselves likely have a shorter shelf life than we think. For example, we should increasingly rely on solar energy and clean energy resources.
conclusion: The US has a responsibility to combat climate change as we have more resources than other nations, have a larger spotlight on us on a global scale, and we tend to be bigger emitters because of daily lifestyle choices. Without efforts, our planet has a ticking timer and this needs to be taken seriously. Other countries are more advanced when it comes to adopting solar and wind power. While we have other resources available, we should take advantage as we're not in a position where fossil fuels is the only thing we're relying on and haven't found substitutes.
argumentOpponent: I do not think the US should completely ban Fossil Fuels to combat climate change because a sudden ban would cause trouble for the country, as the alternatives may not provide enough energy for our needs. A ban might be something for us to lean into, but a complete ban would be difficult to achieve.
rebuttalOpponent: It would be very difficult to force individuals to comply with this ban, First we should identify the logistics of the issue, and help those that could use less, achieve their goals.
conclusionOpponent: I think we can agree that a ban would be something to work towards eventually. \nMy original argument, to not force a ban immediately, seems to be the logical conclusion at this point.

argument: I do not think the US should completely ban Fossil Fuels to combat climate change because a sudden ban would cause trouble for the country, as the alternatives may not provide enough energy for our needs. A ban might be something for us to lean into, but a complete ban would be difficult to achieve.
rebuttal: It would be very difficult to force individuals to comply with this ban, First we should identify the logistics of the issue, and help those that could use less, achieve their goals.
conclusion: I think we can agree that a ban would be something to work towards eventually. \nMy original argument, to not force a ban immediately, seems to be the logical conclusion at this point.
argumentOpponent: The US should ban fossil fuels as individuals' efforts to combat climate change might not be enough (recycling, using public transportation). For example, we should increasingly rely on solar energy and clean energy resources.

While we have other resources available, we should take advantage as we're not in a position where fossil fuels is the only thing we're relying on and haven't found substitutes.

topic: Should the Death Penalty Be Legal?
argument: I think the death penalty should be legal because some people do not deserve to just be sentenced to life in jail. If someone kills an infant or goes on a mass shooting spree killing multiple people, they should not be able to continue their lives. I think of it in a biblical sense of an eye for an eye. if you kill with the intent to kill, then you should be killed.
rebuttal: What about the criminals that kill children and go on mass murdering sprees? they have no respect for for human life and dignity. Agreed that it shouldn't be the only option but it is should be an option for very heinous crimes.
conclusion: It may not deter criminals in the sense that it would stop them from committing heinous acts but it does set an example of what will be punished to the most serve degree, of death.
argumentOpponent: The death penalty fails to act as a deterrent to crime, implies a risk of miscarriages of justice, and ultimately contradicts the very notion of respect for life and human dignity. Thus, it should not be legal.
rebuttalOpponent: While the "eye for an eye" perspective may instinctively appeal to our sense of justice, it does not allow for mistakes in judgments, and tampers with the principle that every life, even those who err gravely, has intrinsic value. Furthermore, there is no conclusive evidence that the death penalty actually deters would-be criminals from committing heinous acts.
conclusionOpponent: Heinous crimes are undoubtedly deplorable, yet the state resorting to killing does not uphold human dignity but exacerbates an already violent cycle. Instead, we should focus on effective rehabilitation and prevention, striving not to reduce ourselves to the level of those we judge and condemn.

argument: I think Government Surveillance isn't  Necessary for National Security, it's a violation of our freedoms. It's okay in some places but doing it everywhere isn't right. conclusion: What's next? The government telling us when we can and can't leave our home for safety. That's not my idea of a free America. conclusionOpponent: Although surveillance raises valid privacy concerns, effective regulations can ensure the right boundaries; our security is not merely the sensation but the mitigation of credible threats. Emphasizing on regulation instead of elimination may help in appreciating the critical and strategic interventions surveillance facilitates in securing our nation.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
argument: Is artificial intelligence good for society? The short answer is Yes. Artificial intelligence or AI will bring many changes to the world that will make things better, including medical innovations, improving public health, increasing productivity for ordinary people, and making it easier for governments and officials to detect and respond to longterm trends. Artificial intelligence can also help us to fight climate change which is a global problem. Overall, I see AI as something that should not be marginalized in its advancements if we want to move things forward as a society. Ultimately, it will be embraced across the world in all different countries so rather than considering whether or not it is good for society, we should focus on how to implement AI ethically. With the proper rules and safeguards on AI as agreed upon by world governments, we can make sure that AI is indeed good for society.
rebuttal: AI isn't not the problem when it comes to threats to job security, socio-economic inequalities, and personal privacy risks. In fact, it is the lack of policy in place to defend against and alleviate the harms that AI could potentially cause. It is up to government regulators to make it a matter of policy to ensure that businesses do not use AI in a manner than can harm people. All of these threats are entirely preventable. First, it will start with ensuring that AI is democratized and that this powerful technology is not maliciously implemented by the rich and powerful.
conclusion: The argument that governments will struggle to efficient implement restrictions on AI could be resolved by the government itself monitoring these tools and making sure that companies are not violating people's rights and causing inequality. Furthermore, the government should implement an AI tax, for example, on businesses that earn the majority if not all of their revenue from leveraging AI. If the governments put restrictions in place that do not have loopholes then there would be a better end result.
argumentOpponent: While AI undoubtedly has potential benefits, it significantly threatens job security, amplifies socio-economic inequalities, and poses severe risk to personal privacy.
rebuttalOpponent: AI's potential societal benefits, while promising, are not automatic. They require significant regulatory oversight to avoid job loss, privacy violations, and disproportionate benefit to the already-privileged, which history shows governments often struggle to efficiently implement.
conclusionOpponent: While it's true that government regulation is crucial, we cannot blindly rely on it considering the rapid development of AI outpacing legislation. Therefore, society must acknowledge the inherent risks of AI and strive for balance and control, before irreversible damage is done.

topic: Should Every Citizen Receive a Basic Income from the Government?
argument: I am in favor of the proposition that every citizen should receive a basic income from the government. It's true that we deal with rising costs of living and every person has various skillsets and abilities, in regards to the kind of jobs they can acquire. Receiving a basic income can eliminate the process of applying for jobs and acquiring further education to obtain a higher paying job. Receiving a basic income can ensure that everyone receives the same pay and there would be less cases of discrimination and socioeconomic inequality. There wouldn't be a need to divide society into different classes because everyone's income would be the same. Receiving basic income can reduce poverty, improves mental health, increases purchasing power, especially amongst the poor and it is motivational.
rebuttal: Economic repercussions and fostering dependency on the state is a small matter, compared to the benefits that it can provide. I think a basic income can provide people with the opportunity to grow and the time to take care of themselves. It can encourage people to not be so dependent because they have the resources to do what they feel is best.
conclusion: That argument is conditional on many things. It wouldn't necessarily disincentivize personal growth - it really depends on the disposition of the individual. Furthermore, inflation existed even before the idea of Basic Income came about. I disagree that it would cause inflation. Inflation is caused by money being pumped into the economy. However, I believe a Basic Income can stimulate the economy by increasing purchasing power and encourages people to spend. They also have the freedom to spend it on entrepreneurship opportunities.
argumentOpponent: While the idea of providing everyone with a basic income may seem appealing in theory, it's inherently flawed in practicality as it fails to consider factors such as economic repercussions and fostering dependency on the state.
rebuttalOpponent: While the ambition to eliminate socioeconomic inequality is admirable, a universal basic income doesn't necessarily reduce poverty but rather redistributes it, coupled with the risk of causing inflation. Additionally, it could disincentivize personal growth and striving for better, as the comfort of guaranteed income might lessen the motivation to pursue educational advancement and employment opportunities.
conclusionOpponent: Conceptually, basic income could indeed enable personal growth, but this assumes everyone will use it constructively, overlooking the potential for misuse. As an alternative, a focused approach of refining our current systems to support people in need and facilitate upward mobility might yield better results economically, socially, and personally.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: Animals should certainly be used for scientific research. The benefits of animal research are far-reaching, especially when it comes to searching for cures and treatments for disease. The use of animals gives researchers an ethical way to effectively test various treatments on living mammals that serve as stand-ins for their human counterparts. The results from these experiments are much more reliable than "modeled" research whose results may not be achieved in the real world.\n\nThere are ethical concerns - no animals should be mistreated or abused during the process. There should be no pain infl
rebuttal: Animals can feel pain, and steps should be taken to mitigate any pain infliction. However, animals are not people. Nature is ruthless, and animals taking advantage of other animals (for example, as food) is rampant throughout the animal kingdom. The use of animals for a benevolent purpose is easily enough to counterbalance any ethical concerns about their use in testing.
conclusion: Testing on humans is far more unethical. Humans have relationships that are far more complex, and much stronger, than any bonds animals are capable of forming. Animals have no legal rights in the same vain - after all, we kill them for food, use them for labor, own them as pets, and kill pests when it suits us. They are a lesser form of life, and are far more expendible in this way.
argumentOpponent: Animals are living beings that can feel pain.  They are unable to consent to their bodies being used for scientific research.  Their quality of life may be significantly reduced through being used for scientific research.  It's irrational to set different standards for how we treat people versus how we treat animals, because our souls don't get to choose the species of the Earthly vessels we inhabit.  Animals may be less capable of problem-solving and other types of advanced cognition compared to humans, but this doesn't necessarily mean that their experience of the world is less vivid, or less profound.  All living beings should be treated with respect and dignity, and animals should be included in that.
rebuttalOpponent: You suggest that animals can be used for testing without being mistreated or abused.  If that were the case, then why would they need to be used at all?  Why couldn't humans be used instead?  The implied reason for using animals in scientific research is that any harm which would otherwise be inflicted upon a human, is instead inflicted upon a being which doesn't have the legal right to say no to being experimented upon.
conclusionOpponent: The idea that personhood should not be extended to animals is phrased here in a way that makes it sound like a statement of fact:  "Animals are not people."  However, in the same breath, my opponent states that the animal kingdom is a ruthless place.  This, again, is a statement of opinion.  Animals are altruistic sometimes.  We should hold ourselves to a high standard when treating animals.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: There should be mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions because it is the only reliable way to encourage companies to be more diverse when hiring or promoting employees. Without mandatory quotas companies will be free to lie or manipulate the data in favor of the status quo. Quotas can be set based on population data to make sure the targets do not discriminate against other groups.\n
rebuttal: That argument would be believable if the current system was actually based on a meritocracy. Companies have been given plenty of chances to diversify their hiring practices but have historically passed over women in favor of men with questionable qualifications. If hiring was purely done on a merit basis currently many companies should be doing better than they are.
conclusion: If diversity in hiring causes discomfort in employees then I would make the case that those employees are the problem. Companies can still invest in talent development while ensuring that leadership represents the diversity of society. Reverse discrimination simply does not exist and is often used as an excuse to keep leadership predominantly male.
argumentOpponent: While I understand and respect the intention behind the idea of mandatory quotas for women in leadership, I believe it ultimately undermines meritocracy, potentially placing individuals in roles they may not be the most qualified for. Instead, we should focus on measures that promote equal opportunity without compromising true capability.
rebuttalOpponent: Mandatory quotas, while aiming for diversity, may result in reverse discrimination, causing discomfort among employees rather than unity. Addressing discrepancies in leadership positions more effectively might involve incentivizing companies to invest in talent development and fostering a culture of equality at the grassroots level, rather than enforcing a one-size-fits-all approach.
conclusionOpponent: I agree that there are improvements needed in corporate hiring practices, but the solution shouldn't be a superficial fix like mandatory quotas; they can often bypass potentially better-suited candidates. Instead, let's push for transparency policies in hiring and promotion processes, coupled with initiatives to address the root cause of gender inequality, to ensure fair representation based on merit, not just gender.

topic: Is Government Surveillance Necessary for National Security?
argument: Government surveillance is absolutely necessary for national security. Prior to 2001, the U.S. had a significant national security structure to prevent terrorism and promote national security, but it as the events of September 11th, 2001 showed, it was not enough. Things like the Patriot Act enabled the U.S. government to create a massive digital filter, suctioning up great amounts of data to sift through and prevent any potential terrorist acts from occurring. The greater sharing promoted by the September 11th attacks also served to ensure the intelligence made it to the right places to stop any events before they occurred. Additionally, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act served to promote further digital surveillance of personnel suspected of terrorism related crimes, further empowering the government to proactively prevent these acts before they occur. Government surveillance is critical to the success of our continued national security.
rebuttal: It's not possible to strike a perfect balance, however emphasizing personal privacy promotes the risk of events like 9/11 happening again. Reducing personal privacy a small amount to reduce the chance of over 3,000 people dying over the course of several hours. Counter to your point, reduced privacy has paid off in that it increases security. We have not had a successful large terrorist attack in over twenty years, with the Patriot Act being implemented in October 2001. It's now December 2023, and outside of several small attacks like the Underwear bomber, no terrorist has been successful inside the United States.
conclusion: Privacy and prevention of criminal acts will always be a delicate balancing act. Prior to 2001, the U.S. leaned too far towards the civil liberties argument and prioritized data and privacy prevention. In the aftermath of 9/11, they promoted significant measures to place civil liberties at a more appropriate level while preventing terrorist attacks of that scale from happening again. Measures like the Patriot Act and the FISA Act have not significantly reduced our privacy and yet have worked remarkably well to prevent significant terrorist attacks from happening again. The small reduction in privacy after 9/11 has been well worth the cost to ensure the heinous acts of 9/11 never again occur on American soil.
argumentOpponent: While national security is undoubtedly important, government surveillance infringes on individual privacy rights and fosters an environment of mistrust and fear. The erosion of personal freedom is not a justified trade-off for potential, yet unproven, increases in security.
rebuttalOpponent: While preventing terrorism is vital, the implementation of broad government surveillance measures like the Patriot Act or FISA has led to mass data collection on innocent citizens, violating privacy rights and civil liberties. This suppression of personal freedom, without clear evidence of improved security, makes these measures questionable at best.
conclusionOpponent: Though large-scale attacks have been avoided since 2001, attributing this solely to invasive surveillance is misleading and overlooks the numerous small-scale attacks that have occurred despite this surveillance. Sacrificing privacy for security is a dangerous and slippery slope that leads us toward a surveillance state, jeopardizing the very freedoms we strive to protect in the name of national security.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: Since there is such a disparity between men and women in leadership positions, a quota system could be needed to effectively balance things quicker than simply allowing it to happen organically. It would send the signal that other women could become leaders in the future, through present day examples.
rebuttal: Meritocracy and quotas could be mutually compatible, so this argument is a false dilemma. So long as the special treatment is temporary and addressing structural or historical problems, it doesn't imply that women are essentially inferior.
conclusion: Quotas can help provide career examples for future candidates, open up more possible candidates who may not have considered the roles but a highly qualified, and be combined with a meritocratic system. The stereotype that women can only succeed with special treatment is not as harmful as other problems, so even assuming this would be an issue it would be relatively unimportant.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory quotas for women in leadership roles, though well-intentioned, can inadvertently undermine the principle of meritocracy and devalue the accomplishments of women who rise to leadership on their own. Moreover, it could potentially deepen the societal divide, as it would inaccurately suggest that women need special treatment to succeed, rather than removing the barriers that stand in their way.
rebuttalOpponent: While your premise of balancing gender disparity is commendable, quotas could risk quality of leadership by promoting due to gender rather than capability, and may perpetuate the stereotype that women can only succeed through special measures, not merit. It's vital we focus on changing perceptions and eliminating barriers organically, rather than using mandates which could lead to tokenism.
conclusionOpponent: Mandatory quotas might be a temporary fix, but they don't address the root causes of gender inequality and may inadvertently suggest that women need help to succeed. Instead, cultivating an environment that values diversity across the board, implementing unbiased recruitment procedures, and providing equal opportunities for growth and leadership based on merit will have a more profound and lasting impact.

topic: Should Public College Be Tuition-Free?
argument: I strongly support tuition free admission for public college. In the world today without a college degree people are looked at as less important compared to those with one. It would help balance things out if people had the chance to get a degree without having to pay overpriced tuition for some colleges. I don’t think that all of them especially the more prestigious schools should do this but having options that do will help people advance their education further. It could even lead to them paying for additional education later on.
rebuttal: I don’t think the quality of education would be reduced at all if it is done correctly. I don’t think at all that it would reduce the quality of education because it would just be another opportunity and those that want more can still pay a private. I see the point of the increased burden on taxpayers but I also think this would balance itself out if it is helping more people further their education to earn more money to be able to pay taxes from.
conclusion: I disagree that it would devalue a degree and discourage trade skills. The same degrees already have less value today compare to what they had in the past. I’ve known many people who went to college and paid extreme tuition just to work in jobs that aren’t what they went to school for. As far as trade skills, that is something that never will be discouraged because trade jobs are some of the most reliable ones to find once you finish school. They are in much higher demand. I think it would be acceptable to find somewhere in between.
argumentOpponent: Although free college tuition might seem enticing, its potential drawbacks - like reduced quality of education and an increased burden on taxpayers - outweigh its supposed benefits.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's fair to desire accessible education for everyone, making college tuition-free risks devaluing a degree due to oversaturation and may inadvertently discourage trade skills. Rather, we should strive to diversify educational pathways and make existing tuition more affordable and transparent.
conclusionOpponent: Free tuition may present logistical challenges, such as strained resources and increased class sizes, which can affect educational quality. Furthermore, more graduates doesn't necessarily equate to more jobs; instead, we should focus on aligning education with market needs, and promoting a variety of qualifications beyond just college degrees.\n

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument: I think climate change itself is a waste of time. We have no definitve proof that anything we do will have any significant effect on helping the climate. I think the earth is going through a phase that it always does and what is happening ( or not) is completely normal. We have no way of knowing it is not. My biggest argument against climate change is that anything we try we will not see or know the results in our lifetime so we do not even know if it worked. We will however manage to waste time and resources trying without even knowing the results. I can think of many better ways to spend the time and money such as in cancer research; and other diseases.
rebuttal: Nonsense - how will having an international agreement create and economic stability? China is worried about 1 thing - outperforming and outsmarting the United States. They have tried to kill us many times already with COVID and making inferior products and will continue to do so. Climate change will not change this and they could care less about it. Several other countries such as Russia and North Korea are in the same corner.
conclusion: The catastrophic human loss in the future cannot be measured now and is pure speculation. there is no viable proof to support it. I would not trust any of the major superpowers to create jobs or do anything with the United States. There would be competition alright; but it would be to see who could dominate and prevail in this arena; not a cooperative effort for the benefit of mankind. I do not trust China; Russia; North Korea and several other countries.
argumentOpponent: The need for international agreements to enforce global climate change policies is crucial for economic stability and national security, a global initiative that would capitalize on American innovation and leadership.
rebuttalOpponent: While the feedback loop of climate change is not immediate, numerous studies confirm human activity's damaging effect - not addressing this could lead to catastrophic financial and human loss in the future. An international agreement fosters a global commitment to job creation and industries growth within renewable energy sectors, investing in a competitive, prosperous future where climate stability also supports advancements in health and other social services.
conclusionOpponent: A uniform international agreement on climate policy would hold all nations, including China and Russia, accountable and establish a level playing field, enhancing American global leadership and competitive edge in clean energy. In a world where international relations and economies are intertwined, global climate change policies are indeed a strategic move for national security, economic growth, and overall societal advancement.

topic: Should the Death Penalty Be Legal?
argument: I believe we should keep the death penalty legal. If we allow the people who deserve get this punishment to merely languish in prison we will overfill them even further. Additionally, people who get the death penalty should be punished appropriately for their wrong doing. Further, it provides a deterrent for people who would commit these atrocities.
rebuttal: I disagree with your statement on the fact that these people are often times mass murderers who deserve what they get. Sometimes an innocent is wrongfully given the death penalty but more often than not, they are freed before it takes place and given wrongful damages. I think the benefits far outweigh the cons.
conclusion: I believe we'll have to simply agree to disagree. I would rather have one murderer rethink his plans than allow them to get away scot free with just a little rehabilitation.
argumentOpponent: The death penalty should be illegal as it is cruel, inhumane, and perpetuates a cycle of violence, failing to act as a deterrent to crime while denying the possibility of rehabilitation. Furthermore, the risk of wrongful convictions leading to irreversible loss of innocent lives is too significant to ignore.
rebuttalOpponent: Contrary to the suggestion of prisons overflowing, maintaining the death penalty is more costly due to lengthy trials and appeals, thus increasing financial burden. Also, studies have shown that it fails to deter crime, and 'appropriate punishment' shouldn’t echo the original atrocity, evolving societies should aim for rehabilitation not retribution.
conclusionOpponent: While we must ensure justice is served, death penalty's permanent nature leaves no room for rectifying erroneous judgments - a single wrongful execution is too many. Ending a life, even of a criminal, perpetuates a negative cycle of violence, making us no better than murderers; instead, we should aim for restorative justice that supports rehabilitation.

argumentOpponent: While addressing climate change is crucial, an outright ban on fossil fuels in the US would have significant and immediate economic consequences, and likely result in energy shortages due to our current infrastructure's heavy reliance on these resources.
rebuttalOpponent: While the transition to renewable energy is commendable and necessary, an abrupt ban on fossil fuels would create an energy gap we are currently not equipped to fill, causing significant disruption to industry, homes, and the economy. Furthermore, the infrastructure and technology needed for a complete switch to renewable energy, not to mention the financing for such a transition, are not fully in place.
conclusionOpponent: The suggestion of diverting to other energy sources 'easily' oversimplifies the complexity and costs involved in such a massive energy transition. Therefore, a more feasible approach would be a gradual, sustainable transition towards renewables, instead of an immediate ban, coupled with increased investments in cleaner fossil fuel technologies in the interim.

topic: Should Students Have to Wear School Uniforms?
argument: School uniforms should not be required for students. It adds a financial burden that not all families can overcome. It is thought that uniforms can be a class equalizer, but if a family is financially struggling, ripped, torn, or tattered uniforms will still stand out if a family is struggling. Many families and students are financially constrained, and school uniforms will not be the priority purchase. Another argument against school uniforms is that they are wasteful. They are a clothing item that are not necessary. Additionally, if they are produced cheaply and made affordable, there is a greater chance that they may be produced by exploited, or basically slave, labor.
rebuttal: As a former student of a uniform-requiring school, school uniforms did not lead to a sense of equality and belonging among myself and fellow classmates. Cliques still formed and there were still hierarchies. Even though we all wore the same uniform, it was evident which students had money and which did not. The quality and condition of our uniforms along with shoes and other accessories clearly spelt out class differences. Skilled teachers are more effective at reducing distraction in a classroom than a uniform code. Students may also be more comfortable in their own clothing and that will promote better learning.
conclusion: Eliminating the chance of exploitation in production is not that same as ensuring it. There are unnecessary added layers to a goal (wearing uniforms) that isn't even objectively important. Financial assistance programs still requires costs coming from somewhere. It is never free. Still, the use of school uniforms is wasteful because the clothes serve a limited purpose and aren't used outside of schooling. The idea of uniforms creating a collective identity is overstated in
argumentOpponent: Uniforms foster a sense of equality, belonging, and reduced distraction in the learning environment, thus equipping students for the discipline and organization required in real-world situations.
rebuttalOpponent: Financial assistance programs and affordable uniform options can mitigate the cost implication, while ethical procurement practices can eliminate the chance of exploitation in production. Moreover, the focus should be on what uniforms can achieve: an undistracted focus on academics and fostering collective identity, not on their potential negatives.
conclusionOpponent: While clothing alterations may exist, they are minimized in a uniform system compared to a casual clothes environment where labels and styles significantly widen the gap; bringing focus back to education. Bathroom access is a right and important to dignity and quailty - it's harmful and unjust to deny them otherwise, best I

They are most statistically likely to be victims of violence then anyone else!   There is evidence and have been studies to show  that these policies of inclusiveness do NOT lead to an increase in safety issues!!
conclusion: Respect and privacy is for EVERYONE, including transgender..  separating the bathrooms doesn't fix the issue instead it just. makes trans people more upset and takes away their rights.   Just because somone might feel upset by a trans person, doesn't mean we should take away the trans rights.     It's about. upholding civil liberties and we want a society that respects ALL people and diversity.  This has been done successfully in many places already.   the EVIDENCE shows no harm to anyone
argumentOpponent: The central concern here is safety and privacy, as the unrestricted access to bathrooms based on self-identified gender can cause discomfort and potential risk to other users. This is not an attempt to discriminate, but to protect individual rights and societal norms.
rebuttalOpponent: While I respect the importance of dignity and equality, studies have not conclusively shown that there is no risk in gender-neutral spaces, and the reality stays that their unrestricted access can cause discomfort to many. Ensuring safety and privacy for all bathroom users, not just a specific sector, should be our primary concern.
conclusionOpponent: While understanding the concerns raised, it is still vital to consider that total inclusivity creates a conflict of rights - the right of transgender individuals to self-identify and the right of all to feel safe and comfortable in these private spaces. It's a complex conversation that requires a more nuanced solution than absolute access or denial.

topic: Should Elected or Appointed Government Officials Be Paid the Minimum Wage?
argument: The concept of the minimum wage has always been on the publics mind. Many government officials have strong opinions on this matter, some overwhelmingly against raising the minimum wage. However, if government positions were paid the minimum wage it would not only attract more people who will fight to make change, but it will also make the topic one that can be discussed by people actually experiencing it. For too long government officials have had the chance to make decisions on matters that do not directly impact them and that leads to an overall disconnect between the people and those chosen to serve. By having the officials experience the
rebuttal: My opponent brings up a good point - who will do the job for minimum wage. Yes there are less stressful jobs out there, however this will still be pursued by those passionate about social change. Many people take on lower paying jobs because it's what they are passionate about - not because they are an already wealthy group. This will once again allow people to make decisions that not only impact the masses, but themselves as well as they will be experiencing it too. For these reasons we need to pay our officials the minimum wage to lead to change.
conclusion: It would attract those who want real change because it's what they are passionate about. The kicker is that those in power will finally be able to experience the difficulties of living on minimum wage and the end effect will likely be an increase in the minimum wage. This change would be difficult at first, but once people experience the trials and tribulations of living on an unlivable wage, there is a real chance for change to happen. Not only will people continue to pursue these jobs, but with their passion they can drive real social change.
argumentOpponent: It is difficult to promote paying government officials only minimum wage. One issue is the question of who would actually do the job for minimum wage, There are many other minimum wage jobs out there that are less stress and responsibility. Likely the position would attract people who are already wealthy through some means, and want the power of the position. It also wouldn't help corruption, as people desperate for money are likely going to be susceptible to bribes. The position would attract a very select group of people that don't represent most . The idealistic side of it that our officials should know what it's like to live on minimum wage is great, but the real problems that poses might be insurmountable.
rebuttalOpponent: How can paying minimum wage attract people who want to fight for change? Those people need to live, eat, support their families as well. The only way these people could pursue a minimum wage position with this level of responsibility is if they have someone with enough wealth supporting them. Those who are already wealthy are going to fight to preserve their wealth, not in the best interest of the masses. These positions would attract a select group of people who want power and don't need moneym.
conclusionOpponent: Passion cannot provide a roof over one's head or food on their table. A select few people without access to other wealth can manage this situation - those who are single with very low living expenses, no family to provide for. But the majority of people who have the passion and right ideas to implement changes, simply wouldn't be able to afford taking this position. If they had to work multiple jobs to make it work, I would say that would be a detriment to their ability to think clearly and lead. And if they fell upon any sort of hard time, it would leave them susceptible to bribes.

rebuttal: If the students deserve to be there then a diverse environment will be created within itself. Universities treating race that way makes it seem as if it is a qualification necessary to bypass. It will come at the disadvantage of another student.
conclusion: If there are multiple students who share the same qualifications but the students that get picked only get picked over the others because of their race, it is not a fair admissions process.
argumentOpponent: Colleges should consider race in admissions as it promotes educational diversity, enriches the learning environment and aids in the breakdown of racial biases, ultimately providing students a well-rounded education. Equitable representation in higher education is essential for a democratic society that values inclusivity.
rebuttalOpponent: Implementing race-conscious admission policies isn't about accepting lesser qualified students based on race, it's about creating equal opportunities by considering historical and societal disadvantages. Race in admissions helps counter systemic bias that exists in other "qualifications", providing a more holistic assessment of a student’s potential.
conclusionOpponent: Diversity doesn't just naturally occur without conscious efforts. Race-inclusive policies simply level the playing field, recognizing both the academic potential and the unique perspectives that diverse races bring, thereby enriching the learning experience for all students, and not disadvantaging anyone.
