topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: Climate change is real. Up to 97 percent of the scientists agreed on this phenomenon. Fossil fuels contribute a major chunk of global carbon emissions. It is thus logical that we phase them out quickly. This can only be done via a ban. Since this fall at the national level, we can only enact a ban on fossil fuels in the U.S., which, ironically, is still the biggest per-capita polluter.  Gasoline, coal and other fuels need to be replaced by clean energy, including nuclear. The ban won't come immediately though as we need to give a grace period of five years or so. Other countries can follow the American example and this will have a net positive impact on the global climate.
rebuttal: The gradual transition argument is cogent but lacks cognition of the pressing issue. The transition can continue for decades without any tangible improvement in climate metrics. While an immediate ban is not feasible either, we should ban fossil fuels starting 2030. Any further delay can bring climate disasters, which we are already seeing today.
conclusion: But not doing anything, or using gradual measures, also has a major downside. We are already witnessing climate disasters like unusual flooding, droughts and fires. We need to do this urgently and a set deadline will make us work extra hard to achieve the targets.
argumentOpponent: A complete ban on fossil fuels, while well-intentioned, may cause economic instability and job losses; it would be more pragmatic to gradually transition to renewable energy, simultaneously investing in clean technology and retraining workers for new energy jobs.
rebuttalOpponent: Climate change indeed warrants urgent action, but abruptly banning fossil fuels over a short time will have severe economic repercussions, potentially derailing progress and leading to job losses; a gradual transition, supplemented by carbon capture technologies and increased energy efficiency measures, can lead to substantial emission reductions without drastic societal disruption. It's also important to consider that clean energy infrastructure is not in place for a swift replacement of fossil fuels across all sectors, making a sudden ban impractical.
conclusionOpponent: While immediate action is indeed required, setting a 2030 deadline overlooks the reality of our current energy production and consumption; it risks causing more harm than good, both socio-economically and potentially environmentally, if we replace fossil fuels with less efficient and under-researched clean alternatives. Instead, promoting a balanced energy portfolio that combines cleaner technologies and improving fossil fuel efficiencies, while progressively lessening our reliance on them, will cultivate a more sustainable and resilient energy future.\n

topic: Should Elected or Appointed Government Officials Be Paid the Minimum Wage?
argument: I think being an elected official is a very difficult job to have. As such, I think that they should be rewarded for their efforts. rebuttal: This is a selfless focused job, but they still have to be able to provide for their families and themselves. This isn't an easy job, so they should make more than minimum wage for their required efforts. If we do not offer enough pay for the position, we're likely to get less than qualified people to get the job done.
conclusion: Anyone who makes minimum wage from a job with a family knows how hard it is to make ends meet with low wages. I do not think an elected official should barely make enough money to survive when the job requires such a high skill set from all individuals.
argumentOpponent: Elected or appointed government officials should be paid the minimum wage to promote humility and public service-oriented mindset, and to redirect funds spent on exorbitant salaries towards more important public concerns. Given the enormous responsibility they bear and the trust placed in them, they should be motivated by a selfless drive to improve society, not by financial incentives.
rebuttalOpponent: While acknowledging the difficulty of being a government official, it is essential to remember that these roles are intended for public service, not monetary gain. Minimum wage serves here as a symbolic reminder about wage inequality; the main goal would be to raise minimum wages for all workers to support a decent standard of living, bolstering equality across society.
conclusionOpponent: While the need to provide for families is recognized, public service should draw those who prioritize communal good over personal wealth; an equation of higher salaries with qualified candidates can lead to attracting individuals motivated by self-interest. Instead, investing in raising the public sector's minimum wage along with officials' salary can create a more economically balanced society, driving home the principle of equal work, equal pay.

topic: Should Students Have to Wear School Uniforms?
argument: I agree with the idea of student uniforms, especially from grades 6-12. I believe this is a preparatory item regarding when someone will eventually enter the workforce in the future, and what will be required of them when they work for an employer. It also provides for insight on how someone should behave when under a particular authority at particular times. It should also define how the work versus personal life boundaries are also defined.
rebuttal: There will always be controls in place in life. That is not necessarily a suppression of individuality, it is simply that individuality cannot always be expressed at all times. Freedom still is very much not suppressed, opinions and civil opinion is always available to be shared withing certain contexts.
conclusion: How is when having controls undermining diversity or authenticity? They always exist, but that doesn't mean one can do whatever one wants at any given moment. If everyone can do whatever they want at any moment, then how will anything get actually done in life and work? The end always surmounts to chaos in any society.
argumentOpponent: Mandating school uniforms suppresses individuality and creativity, disregards students' right to freedom of expression, and can place an unfair financial burden on families. In an evolving educational system, self-expression should be nurtured, not controlled.
rebuttalOpponent: While I appreciate the said preparation for work etiquette, it's important to remember that the school years are also a time for self-discovery and individual growth, both of which can be stifled by uniform policies. Equating professionalism with uniformity risks undermining the importance of diversity and personal authenticity in the workplace and society at large.
conclusionOpponent: While acknowledging life's unavoidable controls, we should not allow them to encroach unjustifiably on spaces of learning and development like schools; imposing a dress code in such environment often signals that conformity is more important than individual thought. The cornerstone of a thriving society is the understanding and respect of diversity, which allows for all forms of self-expression, including clothing choices, to be seen, understood, and appreciated.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
argument: AI is taking away work from a wide variety of jobs. It's stealing original work from artists and writers. It's not good for society for art and other creative work to be taken away from humans. AI is also being used to cheat at assignments in school which is a major issue. We need to support human intelligence and creativity. AI is pushing us away from that and it's going to lead to unhappiness. There are also major privacy issues with AI as it currently stands.
rebuttal: Quality of life will plummet when people are put out of work thanks to AI and when AI takes over art and other creative endeavors. Supporting human creativity and intelligence will always lead to better and more innovative ideas. We can't count on AI to solve pressing issues like climate change.
conclusion: We're currently seeing AI taking over creative fields with those jobs being cut. This is the opposite of what should be happening and is lowering quality of life and appreciation of human intelligence and creativity. In education, we should be focusing on supporting teachers and on much needed reform instead of pawning our kids off on AI. It's unlikely that privacy issues will be properly addressed as that is simply not how politics and regulation realistically works. Because of that, it isn't reasonable to plan for an ideal scenario that won't happen.
argumentOpponent: Artificial Intelligence serves as a catalyst for societal growth, enhancing productivity and innovation, while helping address pressing issues ranging from climate change to healthcare, thus significantly improving quality of life.
rebuttalOpponent: While AI does parallel human tasks, it frees up human capacity for deeper, creative problem-solving, and its use in education can enhance personalized learning; regarding privacy, the focus should be on tight regulation, not complete abandonment of a transformative technology.
conclusionOpponent: AI's role in job displacement is real, but it's a transition akin to previous industrial revolutions, with new opportunities arising in its wake; with regards to innovation, AI doesn't replace but complements human intelligence, it's a partnership that can expedite solutions to global problems like climate change.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: Women have been historically, systemically discriminated against in nearly all industries and especially in leadership positions. In many major corporations there are no women at all in any of the top leadership positions. This is morally wrong and it is also a bad way of doing business. A more diverse leadership team allows for different perspectives that can lead to innovation and new ideas. Although many companies claim to have anti-sexism policies, in practice their leadership is still predominantly male, especially in certain industries like technology, government, and medicine. It's not enough to pay lip service to the idea. There need to be mandatory quotes to ensure that sexism ends for good.
rebuttal: Given the dearth of women in leadership positions, it's clear that special measures ARE needed for women to get a fair shot. Many women are qualified for positions but don't get that chance to succeed because of systemic sexism. I absolutely agree that individuals must be qualified to get leadership positions, but I think we have to take a broader view of the context of someone's credentials, experience, and talent. If only men are promoted, then only men will ever be qualified. It's a systemic problem that we must address at all levels.
conclusion: Anti-sexism education and policies are important. But diversity training and lip service is not enough. Many companies do these things and still have no women in leadership (see the tech industry for one good example). Recommendations and gentle nudges are not enough. We have to hold companies to their ideals and make it a mandatory requirement for women to be represented.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions may appear beneficial, however, it undermines the principle of meritocracy, suggesting women need special measures to succeed, and it risks promoting unqualified individuals based solely on their gender.
rebuttalOpponent: While making strides towards diversity is essential, mandatory quotas may breed resentment and could potentially stigmatize women as being appointed on the basis of gender, not competence; better solutions lie in promoting gender equality, education, and policies that empower women to naturally take on leadership roles.
conclusionOpponent: Instead of imposing quotas which artificially skew the representation, focus should be on dismantling systemic barriers and biases, fostering a work culture that genuinely values diversity, and encouraging the natural progression of qualified women into leadership positions by means of education, mentorship, and support.

topic: Should the US Provide Military Aid to Ukraine in its Conflict With Russia?
argument: This is a delicate time in U.S. foreign policy history. In this moment, we must stand up and support Ukraine in any way possible. Not only has Russia encroached upon Ukranian territory previously without any backlash, allowing them to conquer Ukraine would be a major US foreign policy disaster. Appeasement is a strategy that has consistently failed and it is only through helping Ukraine defeat Russia that we can establish order in the international stage.
rebuttal: You assume that these measures are not being taken and they do not have to be mutually exclusive. You can still engage in diplomatic methods even though you are supporting someone with financial and military might backing. Russia would not hesitate to do the same so why should the United States play by Russia's rules?
conclusion: Although a diplomatic option would be ideal, there is little chance of that occurring. To prevent Russia from further taking land away from a sovereign nation, the United States should continue in its support of Ukraine through monetary and military methods. Only by punishing the actions of others will we be able to keep order on an international level.
argumentOpponent: Providing military aid to Ukraine could easily escalate the conflict with Russia, risk a direct war between the US and Russia, and destabilize global peace further. It is more beneficial to invest in diplomatic tools and mediation efforts to solve the dispute.
rebuttalOpponent: While ensuring global order is crucial, escalating the conflict by providing military support could result in a more significant foreign policy disaster, triggering a potential large-scale war. Diplomacy and de-escalation strategies, not appeasement, ensure long-term stability and minimize the overall risk of conflict.
conclusionOpponent: Contrary to merely following Russia's rules, this is about establishing a different diplomatic standard of resolving conflicts without resorting to the escalation of violence. Maintaining peace needs a measured, non-aggressive approach that focuses less on military might and more on international cooperation and dialogue.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: It is simply wrong to purposefully inflict pain and suffering on other living creatures. Science has advanced to the point that experiments on living subjects are not as necessary as they were just a few decades ago. We don't need to hurt animals to see if a treatment or product is effective or safe.  It is not worth the moral cost to get a little gain in science, when it isn't entirely necessary.
rebuttal: Science has advanced to the point that animal trials are not necessary any more. New advances, like the MRNA vaccines you mention, do not need animal trials to determine either efficacy or safety. For every lab that maintains the "strict ethical guidelines" that you mention, there are probably 10 more that don't, and cause horrible suffering.
conclusion: Science has indeed advanced to the point that animal trials are not necessary, and the only regulation we should have is the regulation banning the practice. Cruelty might have been advantageous in the past, but time, and science, have evolved past that point.
argumentOpponent: Using animals for scientific research is necessary for the advancement of medical sciences, as it helps develop innovative treatments and vaccines, like the COVID-19 vaccines, which benefit humans and animals alike. This practice adheres to strict ethical guidelines, ensuring minimal harm and maximal benefit.
rebuttalOpponent: In an ideal world, no pain to any living being would be ideal, yet the scientific value gained through this research has more extensive implications in alleviating suffering in the larger picture. While alternatives are praiseworthy, none have fully replicated the complexity of living organisms, making animal research still a necessary and regulated component in our fight against diseases.
conclusionOpponent: While MRNA vaccines represent significant progress, the initial stages of their development were indeed made possible by animal research—experiments that helped establish the entire field of biotechnology. Addressing the ethical concern, let's not lose sight of the stringent laws in place that regulate these studies and ensure animal welfare, implying that any violations thereof should be treated as exceptions, not norms.

topic: Are Social Media Making People Stupid?
argument: Social Media has made people more stupid than in the past.  People get involved in echo chambers instead of seeing out differing views and opinions.  In fact, social media has given a voice to idiots and fools that is as loud as those of experts, and for some people, it is difficult to discern who is right, especially when they choose who they want to be right, rather than who is actually right.  For example, there are some people now who believe that the earth is flat.  A generation ago, virtually no one believed this, but social media spread this thought and people want to be "in the know" and want to show that they are smarter than the rest of the people, and instead wind up showing they are dumber.  \n\nTo close, social media gives equal time to both morons and experts, and users often don't take the time to differentiate between the two, which leads to more people being led down false pathways by idiots than ever before.
rebuttal: Evidence shows this not to be the case.  In fact, using my example of people believing in all sorts of crazy conspiracy theories these days shows that people hear what they want to hear and don't listen to everything they should listen to.  Social media also reinforces belief systems by using algorithms that make you more likely to hear viewpoints that coincide with your own instead of being challenged by opposing viewpoints.  So it narrows your worldview as opposed to informing you.
conclusion: The fact is that people are not taught how to discern good information from bad.  So they turn to social media not to be informed, but to have their worldview reinforced.  The very fact that we are dealing with issues that have long been settled which now are seemingly open to debate (like flat earth) shows that people are willingly becoming more stupid by their usage of social media.
argumentOpponent: Social media does not make people stupid; instead, it provides platforms for global communication, immediate information, and socio-political mobilization, thereby fostering smart, informed citizens. The issue lies not in the medium itself but the individuals' use and interpretation of it.
rebuttalOpponent: Echo chambers and misinformation existed before social media; the platforms merely democratize the access to information, not the quality of it—people are still responsible for their discernment. Flat earth belief, though amplified by social media, is not indicative of overall intellectual decline but of some individuals' choice to favor controversial views, an issue predating the internet era.
conclusionOpponent: Algorithms' role in narrowing worldviews should be attributed to tech companies' profit-driven motives, not social media as a concept, which when utilized responsibly, can expand perspectives, not contract them. Associating the emergence of conspiracy theories with social media's influence overlooks our responsibility in discerning fact from fiction, and fosters a cognitive bias against this medium, instead of tackling the roots of ignorance and misinformation.\n

topic: Should Felons Regain the Right to Vote?
argument: There are certain instances where felons should morally be given a right to vote. These instances are few and far between, but they definitely are there. Some felons have a change of heart and even convert to faith during their imprisonment. These individuals are then not the same that they were before, and are able to contribute in a meaningful way to community again. There are programs that provide training and counseling in prisons that rehabilitate prisoners to begin a new life that is vastly different than the one that they led before. Finally, there are a very few felons that may have committed a felony for a good reason, (i.e. to protect a family member or to prevent a catastrophe). In those cases, the individual's ability to vote in a beneficial manner has never been violated.
rebuttal: I honestly agree wholeheartedly with you for most felons. It is for the few that do change in prison (i.e. convert to faith and/or learn skills and get counseling to improve) that I argue in favor of. These few deserve a second chance in life, just as we all would hope for. There are also a very few that may have committed a crime for a good reason, for instance to protect a mother or to prevent a crime. These may not have ever become violated in their conscience to begin with and therefore are still able to contribute to society in a meaningful way.
conclusion: All humans mess up from time to time. Some much worse than others. Some are evil to the core, but not all. There are definitely those who have gotten tied up with the wrong crowd, grown up in extenuating circumstances, and never were given a chance in life. I would hope that there would be forgiveness and a second chance for those who have a change of heart and are trying to live a new, good life.
argumentOpponent: Said person committed a crime and even if and when they are released they have lost that right to vote. They did something that sent them to prison and it was something bad enough they lost the right to help decide what should happen in the community and country they live in.
rebuttalOpponent: I do not buy a change of heart and convert of faith to me is a massive copout. I do agree that some might have committed a crime to protect family, if that was true they would have been found not guilty. That point does not hold up to me.
conclusionOpponent: I still do not agree. I believe that once you have does something that bad and are sent to prison for whatever the reason you have lost that right to vote.  Yes, some might change. That is the price that needs to be paid so that we have a just society (if you even want to say we have one now).

topic: Should Students Have to Wear School Uniforms?
argument: Uniforms are simple for every student to wear, are all consistent and no student has to worry about whether or not they have the expensive clothes.  Students also don't have to worry about picking out their clothes for the next day so they are more likely to be on time to school for learning and not rushed out the door.
rebuttal: The schools should have an allotment for uniforms that are provided.  Also, the colors of the uniform don't have to be lighter colored or they can have multiple options for school colors so stains/dirt don't show up as often.  Also, even without uniforms, the parents need to do laundry and take care of that, dirty clothes are not just a uniform issue.  There will be plenty of options for shirts/pants to accommodate different body types, and the school districts can work with local retailers and or fashion companies to make sure these options are available to everyone.
conclusion: Clothes, whether they are uniforms or not need upkeep.  Just like with free lunch programs, if some family can't afford the uniforms, there should be financial help for that.  Students get teased if they don't have Nike, Adidas or other name brand clothes.  Students also take forever picking out their clothes to impress their friends causing them to lose valuable hours a week to focus on home work, study and sleep.
argumentOpponent: Students should not have to wear school uniforms. Although this is a well-intentioned gesture it can also backfire. First of all, there is the expense of the uniforms. There is also the day-to-day upkeep of the uniforms. Parents who are of limited means may find it burdensome to not only have to buy the uniforms but also to have to launder them and otherwise keep them clean and spotless. Also, these days, there is pervasive childhood overweight and obesity, and uniforms may not be flattering for all body types. This is an unfortunate reality. Some students may feel very awkward and uncomfortable in uniforms for this, and for other reasons. This may have a deleterious effect on their concentration and focus on schoolwork. School uniforms may have been beneficial in bygone days, but they may cause more problems than they attempt to solve.
rebuttalOpponent: Uniforms may not be "simple for every student to wear" for the simple reason that not all students' parents will be able to afford the uniforms and the upkeep. These uniforms may not be flattering or suitable for all body types, and students who find themselves in this plight may suffer because they may be teased or bullied. They may also feel self-conscious and not able to focus on school work. Unfortunately, these days, we are not in a one-size-fits-all situation and uniforms are not a solution.
conclusionOpponent: Schools might now have an "allotment," as budging for education is often quite restrictive. Students' parents will already be encumbered with many tasks, not least of which is getting their children to focus on the schoolwork and homework. Trying to cope with buying and upkeep of uniforms adds an additional burden. While it is a well-meaning gesture to have unforms, the problems will outweigh the benefits. And again, I reiterate, the focus needs to be on learning.

topic: Should Elected or Appointed Government Officials Be Paid the Minimum Wage?
argument: No they should not be. They are in positions to help alleviate poverty and should be subjected to the very thing they are trying to eliminate from society. The government by default provides programs to the public many of them without income or who make minimum wages. They thereby know that it's something of inaccuracy. The government would be failing itself internally by paying their elected officials below or in the poverty rates.
rebuttal: It would not significantly shrink the wealth gap as most wealthy people don't work for the government. And many government workers make average salaries. As for elected officials they too have lives and deserve the salaries they make. The issue isn't their salaries, the issues is the real issues on poverty and how the government puts a band aid on it, won't really address it and how it plays out in communities of color particular. This trickles down to crime and more poverty, incarceration, etc. The issue is providing enough great jobs and opportunities for all Americans even those who are in jail.
conclusion: One does not have to know struggle to appreciate the struggle of others. They can literally see it. The goal of society is progress. It's not to struggle for the masses. Struggle leads to crime and crime leads to pain which leads to more crime and struggle; the process repeats itself. Officials should be mandated to go into the communities they serve to see what the people are needing not be shortened of their salaries. There needs to be restructuring of the system and requirements.
argumentOpponent: Paying elected and appointed government officials the minimum wage would shrink the wealth gap and democratize power, mirroring principles progressive or democratic leaning individuals often endorse, in addition to reminding them of the realities ordinary citizens face.
rebuttalOpponent: While it seems counterintuitive, paying our officials minimum wage directly makes them stakeholders in poverty alleviation, thereby motivating action. This hands-on experience with struggling economies adds authenticity to the programs aimed at uplifting the lower-income population, aiding the government, not failing it.
conclusionOpponent: While many wealthy people don't work for the government, this step would symbolically impact the conversation on wealth disparity; moreover, the personal financial stake for government officials could incentivize them to foster more job opportunities and address socio-economic issues head-on. A government anchored in reality can better understand and respond to the lived experiences of its people, especially those who are economically disadvantaged or marginalized.

Limitations may not be great but it prevents illogical beings from further harming their own kind. Also, stifling personal development is solely on the indivi
conclusion: Then it is on the fault of the society's government and culture. You can recognize that it is ideal for individuals to react rationally and positively to hate speech but refuse to see that as an issue when society cannot keep up with something as important as that. Hate-speech comes from lack of knowledge and respect which stems from a human's younger years of development. The system must be changed.
argumentOpponent: Imposing limitations on freedom of speech to prevent hate speech can lead to potential misuse by authorities to suppress dissenting views, thus inhibiting the vibrant marketplace of ideas vital for a healthy democracy. topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: Colleges should consider race as a factor in admission because we need to level the playing field.  Students who have not done well in high school still deserve a chance to go to college and make something of themselves.
rebuttal: While I appreciate that argument we must consider that black and brown skinned students have been treated marginally by their schools and did not have the same path to success as the students who came from households where parents had been to college.
conclusion: All students deserve a college education and it is difficult for minority students to compete with the white and Asian students who are not first generation college students
argumentOpponent: The college admissions process should be focused on merit and academic potential, rather than trying to artificially ensure diversity by appealing to race, which can lead to reverse discrimination. Understanding and valuing diversity is vital, but it can also be encouraged through other, fairer means, such as socio-economic background, geography, or personal experiences.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's important to offer opportunities, the suggestion that underperforming students deserve college admission risks diluting the value of a college education and undermining fairness. Instead, emphasis should be on improving lower-tier education systems to ensure all students have equal chances to perform well acadically from the get-go.
conclusionOpponent: Acknowledging the systemic struggles faced by certain social groups is crucial, but race-based admissions can perpetuate stereotypes and inadvertently create division. Instead, investing heavily in high-quality early education and support systems for all students ensures a level playing field from the start, fostering true equality of opportunity rather than symbolic diversity.

conclusion: The logistics of change are never easy.  There are costs involved in making big changes for sure. Our innovations in recent decades with technology don't only prove our capability but can also be instrumental in helping us on a path to a better future.

topic: Should Abortion Be Legal?
argument: The legal right to abortion guarantees that women have a right to their bodies. Making abortion illegal will be assumed that the government is against body autonomy. People will still get abortions either way, making it legal will guarantee a woman's safety because the process will take place under safe conditions and by professionals.
rebuttal: Unborn children are fetuses and do not have rights since they are not people yet, or not born yet. The pregnant person, however, has the right to choose what to do with their body. That will mean that fetuses can have life insurance policies if they have rights.
conclusion: Like I stated before, fetuses cannot have rights since they are not people. Children after they are born depend on their parents to make decisions for them as well. It is impossible for a fetus to have body autonomy since they are not yet self-aware; they don't have likes of dislikes or know right from wrong. Sex education has proved ineffective.
argumentOpponent: While we can all agree that individual freedom is crucial, I believe that the rights of the unborn, much like the rights of the living, should be protected and respected, making abortion a serious ethical issue. This stance promotes fairness in society by ensuring every life, regardless of its stage, is given equal value and opportunity.
rebuttalOpponent: While I understand the perspective of body autonomy, we must also consider the autonomy and rights of the unborn, who have no say in the decision. Furthermore, legalizing a potentially harmful act doesn't make it ethical or safe - instead, it's essential to focus on preventive strategies like sex education, access to contraception, and a robust social support system.
conclusionOpponent: The debate around when life begins is complex, yet the potential for life in a fetus cannot be overlooked; even if unformed, their latent human potential warrants protection. One's personal rights should not have the power to endanger another's existence, leading us to seek balance between individual freedoms and collective responsibilities.

topic: Is Government Surveillance Necessary for National Security?
argument: The government must have broad surveillance powers in order to defend the country from threats.  Without proper intelligence, it will be unable to deter or prevent large scale tragedy.  This does not imply that large-scale domestic surveillance is required.  There are myriad external threats that justify the use of surveillance powers.  Other countries have sophisticated systems in place that allow them to do with the same.  Without similar powers, our government would be left behind or be left dependent on the shared resources that other countries allow us to access?  This could leave the country vulnerable to any number of political and military threats.
rebuttal: It is true that blanket surveillance, particular without proper oversight, can compromise the very values that government has been established to protect.  However, and as you have acknowledged, national security goals can not be met or established without the tools to do so.  Surveillance, targeted to the proper threats, is imperative in manifesting a
conclusion: Again, you and I seem to agree.  Surveillance is necessary for national security, although it must be supervised and targeted to avoid injustices against those that are properly exercising their rights.  Without any surveillance, national security will be compromised.  Without supervised and cautious surveillance, individual freedom will be compromised.  Thus, even individuals require a patient and empathetic surveillance to remain safe within
argumentOpponent: While indeed national security is fundamentally important, the use of pervasive government surveillance compromises the very liberties and privacy rights that form the foundation of our democracy. Rather than blanket surveillance, a targeted approach based on credible intelligence would be more effective and respectful of our democratic values.
rebuttalOpponent: While I agree on the importance of proper intelligence, broad surveillance powers tend to risk civil liberties and result in mistrust between citizens and the government. Additionally, staying tuned with international standards shouldn't mean compromising our democratic principles; we can indeed tailor a more accurate, intelligence-based surveillance methodology that both protects our national security and preserves individual privacy rights.
conclusionOpponent: Indeed, surveillance is a vital tool for ensuring national security, yet, it should be cautiously framed to prevent any infringement upon citizens' privacy; fair oversight, transparency, and regular auditing can achieve this balance and maintain trust in our institutions. We should never feel obliged to trade our cherished democratic principles for safety when we have the capacity to accomplish both.

topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: College should be completely based on merit, right? Well let's consider what this statement means. Is merit being born into a family that can afford to move to an area with good education? Does merit include being tracked into classes that lead to college admission? Do you consider it merit that one can apply for prestigious colleges only if they have the money to pay for the application fee? There is much more to this train of reasoning than first appears. Deep seeded racial biases, historical and structural racism, and barriers to education lead to the inability to merely use "merit" as a accurate measure for college admissions. The ground is not level from the beginning and if diversity is to be a value in the U.S. and in any college, there must be a consideration of race in the admissions process of higher education.
rebuttal: Diversity of thought is certainly a noble cause, but how much diversity of thought comes from a college system based on this so called "merit"? Consider the factors needed to get into college- a high school degree, technology to apply, extracurricular activities, money to pay for the college. These factors immediately eliminate an entire class and status of people from the college campuses across America. Should this be happening? Of course not. And in a perfect world, complete merit might be an option. But the diversity of thought you talk of is flawed from the beginning.
conclusion: While there are very valid thoughts and concerns with focusing on community programs, financial aid, and scholarships, the reality is that these are not enough to fix the stratification that is already happening. Students attending college should be able to learn from those who are vastly different from them. Right now, the college admissions process produces a cookie cutter student. Diversity in higher education is not just a vague goal but should be an integral part. Every college student learns that we learn the most from those who are different than us, but each student sitting in the class is the same, how is that supposed to play out in the classroom?
argumentOpponent: College admission should be based on merit and ability, not on race, ensuring a fair competitive environment where students work hard to earn their place, inspiring integrity and personal growth. Diversity in thought, not simply race, cultivates a richer educational experience.
rebuttalOpponent: While acknowledging obstacles some students face, it's unrealistic to deem "merit" unachievable due to one's circumstances; financial aid, scholarships, and community programs are designed to empower disadvantaged students. Rather than stratifying students racially, let's focus on providing resources to level the education terrain, maintaining the sanctity of merit-based admission.
conclusionOpponent: A merit-based system doesn't inhibit diversity of thought, as socio-economic barriers are not determinant of individual merit or intellectual diversity. Instead of race-based admissions, let us advocate for accessible resources and fair opportunities for all, thus enabling genuine meritocracy and fostering diverse educational environments.

topic: Should Students Have to Wear School Uniforms?
argument: I believe students should wear school uniforms because it promotes inclusivity and unity in schools.  School uniforms typically go on sale at stores and are fairly affordable.  Most school districts allow parents to donate uniforms so that families who cannot afford them can provide uniforms to their children.  Having students wear school uniforms can also help bridge the socioeconomic gap to where no one is judging one another by how they dress or if someone is wearing a brand name versus a lower priced brand.
rebuttal: I disagree because school uniforms tend to be very affordable and most stores put these items at sale prices for back to school.  On the other hand, regular clothes have become very expensive.  Most students will typically prefer name brand clothing.  Low income families have the option to call their school district and inquire if there are school uniforms that have been donated by other families.  Families also save on time and students don't have to worry about what to wear for school every morning.
conclusion: As I mentioned before, school polos tend to sell for under ten dollars and are available at most stores.  The reality is that there will always be families who need extra help and whether they need to purchase "regular" clothes or school uniforms, something will need to be purchased.  Regular clothes tend to be pricier versus school uniforms.  I don't think there is anything wrong with accepting donations.  Help is always available from what I have seen at several school districts.
argumentOpponent: Mandating school uniforms stifles students' freedom of expression and creativity; a more inclusive environment can be generated by promoting individuality and diversity. Additionally, the financial burden of purchasing uniforms may disproportionately affect lower-income families.
rebuttalOpponent: Inclusivity and unity can be achieved without uniformity; teaching acceptance of diverse personal styles better prepares students for life outside of school. The affordability and availability of uniforms is not universal, and the reliance on donations further underscores the financial burden placed on disadvantaged families.
conclusionOpponent: The mission of education is not to homogenize, but to nurture individualism and autonomy, which inclusive dress code policy supports. Schools should focus on eliminating socioeconomic inequalities in education directly, not merely their superficial symptoms, like clothing choices.

topic: Should Abortion Be Legal?
argument: I don't think abortion should be legal in most cases because it's a human life, and there are many more alternatives that women can choose other than abortion.
rebuttal: What about the autonomy of the innocent human life that's being ended? Also, I've never heard any real evidence that women are using "back-alley" procedures.
conclusion: Again, I've never heard that in most abortion cases, the woman would die if she had the child. Most cases of abortion are simply women not wanting to have the child because it interferes with their lives.
argumentOpponent: Abortion should be legal as it is a matter of personal autonomy over one's body and life, and because banning it does not eliminate abortions but merely consequently forces them into unsafe, backalley procedures.
rebuttalOpponent: While the sanctity of life is a crucial aspect, it is equally important to ensure the quality of life and wellbeing of the woman involved; alternatives are not universally feasible or desirable, and unsafe abortions, more common when legal abortion isn't accessible, also drastically endanger lives.
conclusionOpponent: True autonomy involves having control over one's body and life choices, which inclusively covers the decision to have an abortion; concerning 'back-alley' procedures, evidence abounds globally showing increased instances of unsafe abortions and complications where abortion is inaccessible or illegal.

topic: Is Arts Education as Important as Science and Math in Schools?
argument: Arts are important because they encourage creativity and promote cultural diversity. These traits are important in the development of individuals and society as a whole.
rebuttal: Standardized testing for math and science is impractical because it does not define the intelligence of the individual. These tests are only used to give funding to the schools that test at the highest percentages, whereas the schools that get the lowest scores need the funding the most. It is a false equivalence
conclusion: Creativity is absolutely important. How do you think tech is made? Some creative mind came up with an idea and implemented it in technology. The same is valid for the arts.. Companies rely on arts, especially in graphic design, animation, motion picture, photography, etc.
argumentOpponent: Science and math education equips students with skills that can actually be applied to real world situations. We heavily rely on technology, and science and math is just more practical. These also help with standardized testing much better than more creative education, meaning the student can get set up much better for their future. With how little schools get as far as resources, it just makes more sense to focus on what will help the students get better results.
rebuttalOpponent: While creativity is valuable, it doesn't really help students stay competitive in job markets today. Technical skills are way more important, and often lead to the better paying jobs. You can be creative in your free time if you have more money. Art focused careers unfortunately aren't really rolling in cash, with a few exceptions.
conclusionOpponent: While standardized testing doesn't define intelligence, it doesn't really matter. What matters is the scores. Employers and higher education schools don't care how smart or creative you actually are. All that matters, at the end of the day, is how high that number is on that paper. Higher scores and more funding means more wiggle room for things that aren't as important, like art or sports. You get those higher scores by pushing things that can actually be measured, like math and science.

topic: Should the Death Penalty Be Legal?
argument: Unfortunately, there are some people in this country that commit horrible crimes. More severe that some people are able to bear. Heinous crimes require heinous punishments, especially if there are victims that suffered due to this awful criminal activity. Their loved ones have to live on and knowing that the person who took their family away will never do it to anyone else is sometimes the only thing we can give them. The death penalty is sometimes needed to resolve terrible actions.
rebuttal: In this country "we the people" are the ones who decide how we are governed in these matters. Yes, death surely can come back to you, which is why the death penalty is needed. It's needed so that if someone took a persons life, we can close that loop of evil with the death of the one who committed the original offense. This is the only way the terror can end.
conclusion: We are the judges of our peers and that is how we keep order in this country. We cannot simple wait around for karma and hope justice is served. We have a duty to ensure there are checks and balances to everyone's actions. The death penalty will always be needed if we want to create a better society for ourselves and our children.
argumentOpponent: It should not be legal because only God should determine who lives and who dies and not another human. Also there could be severe consequences for anyone that carries out the execution. Death can come right back to you. So, people need to think twice before they choose to end someone's life.
rebuttalOpponent: I do understand that the actions caused by some individuals can really affect the victims. But I think that we should let God be the judge. It might not be today or tomorrow, but those criminals will get a taste of karma. It will come right back to them. So let God be the judge. I know humans are very emotional, but I think this is the time to let our creator handle things.
conclusionOpponent: It is not up to a human to decide whether another lives or not. It is not up to you to decide.  Death penalty is not needed.

topic: Should the Rich Pay More Taxes?
argument: It would make sense that they should pay more in taxes due to the fact that the taxes would not necessarily be as much of a burden on them as they would be on others with lower incomes.
rebuttal: It might also aid economic growth by freeing up money for people with lower income to either spend or invest. Tax evasion could be avoided by better scrutinizing such avenues.
conclusion: It would make more sense to have these taxes paid by those who could most afford it, or perhaps by lowering taxes for all. The burden should be shared.
argumentOpponent: Forcing the rich to pay more taxes does not invite prosperity, but hinders economic growth, as it discourages entrepreneurship and the productivity they bring into society. Higher taxes can also encourage tax evasion and capital flight, further impacting the country's economic stability.
rebuttalOpponent: While on the surface it seems equitable, making the wealthy pay more can disincentivize earning beyond certain tax brackets, potentially stifling innovation and growth. Furthermore, it presumes that wealth is a static pool when it’s often the result of constant reinvestment and risk, elements crucial to economic vitality.
conclusionOpponent: However, tax hikes on the rich tend to lead to reduced investment and fewer job opportunities, elements critical to economic growth and stability; lower income individuals fare better when jobs are plentiful. The focus on tax evasion tends to distract from the actual solution: simplifying tax codes to promote compliance.

topic: Should There Be Standardized Testing in Schools?
argument: I think that having standerdized testing can pressure teachers to teach according to what the test has. This means a teacher will not be able to give students that personal on one teaching experience and create more of a limited teaching atmosphere. I also think that the tests don't really relate to real world skills and can impact not only teachers but students as well in a negative manner. The focus on teaching would not have a big variety and will just be focused on the main subjects the test will have. These tests don't give you feedback on what you did wrong either.  They don't really allow you to be creative like you should be in the real world. These tests are made for students that are higher up on the social ladder
rebuttal: Standerdized testing in schools lacks a proper way to measure a student's progress because it puts the students in a stressful environment where they can't really give their all. They don't give any value to  what the real world will be like after school ends for these students and that's why I feel like they aren't an objective measure. They don't provide feedback on how to perform better, so you can't say that they're fair.
conclusion: I agree that teaching the test can be a valid strategy, but only if it reflects the real world. Standardized testing doesn't really prepare you for the real world, I'd say its more relatable to a prison where you can't get up and move around. It just creates stress, which doesn't allow the student to perform to the best of their ability. They reduce the human experience and replace it with numbers.
argumentOpponent: Standardized testing in schools provides a consistent and objective measure of student understanding and progress, making educational quality and fairness more achievable across socioeconomic boundaries. Moreover, it gives us the data to hold educational institutions accountable and guide governmental funding and policy decisions, key aspects for a fair society.
rebuttalOpponent: While your concern about education's creativity and breadth is valid, it doesn't negate the need for standard measures to ensure educational equality and quality. Teaching to the test can be a valid strategy if we ensure the test is comprehensive and well-rounded, reflecting the diverse skillset needed in real-world situations.
conclusionOpponent: Standardized tests do pose challenges, but they also provide an essential, quantifiable standard that allows us to identify gaps in education, ensure equity and mobilize resources effectively. If improved with constructive feedback and better representation of real-world skills, this can be a powerful tool in shaping fair and competent future citizens.

topic: Should the US Expand (“pack”) the Supreme Court?
argument: I believe the US should not expand the Supreme Court. The Court has remained the same for a reason. We have tenured judges who are practiced and aware of the laws and situations. The system is party balanced and voted upon. It is the grounds for our society, to expand it, may be to unbalance and uproot its core structure. The structure has been time proven and should remain.
rebuttal: Circumventing political stalemates, sounds like one party will hold power and its opinions will overrule its counterparts.  The system can move slowly, however this is intended in order for due diligence to take place.  The system must remained balanced and pure.
conclusion: Tradition is what America has relied upon for centuries, it ensures all beliefs are heard and equality reins true. The systems in place have been upheld and enforced in success.  Why alter something that is proven to be effective.
argumentOpponent: Expanding the Supreme Court creates a more nuanced view of justice by including varying perspectives, paralleling the diversity and complexity of our nation; this results in fairer rulings that better reflect the values and principles of all Americans. Additionally, circumventing political stalemates enhances the Court's ability to promptly address urgent matters, which bolsters overall governance efficiency.
rebuttalOpponent: While the tradition has its merits, our society evolves and so should our institutions; we're not expanding the Court to disturb its balance, but to embrace a more representative viewpoint, ensuring it evolves with our dynamic society. The assurance of prompt decisions in a politically polarized environment is a compelling reason to explore court reform, enhancing not only the representation but the court's overall functioning as well.
conclusionOpponent: Empowering diverse viewpoints via expansion does not equate to domination by one party; instead, it ensures broader representation, making the Supreme Court more resilient to political polarization. Slow progress in the face of urgent matters is not due diligence; enhancing Court capacity could thus improve both the speed and quality of justice delivered.

topic: Should Abortion Be Legal?
argument: I think abortion should be legal because a woman should always have bodily autonomy. No one else is obliged to use her body without her permission. Oftentimes, pro life arguments will be in accordance to someone's religious beliefs, however in The Bible it says life begins at first breath. That means life does not begin until the baby is actually born. However, late term abortions should only be performed if there is risk to the mother or the baby is not viable. Otherwise abortions in the first trimester should be legal.
rebuttal: A fetus is not a child. In the first few weeks of development, it is a clump of cells smaller than that of a housefly. The "heartbeat" is a pulsating vein which is not a fully formed heart. A woman has the right to end a pregnancy if it interferes with her bodily autonomy and life does not begin until first breath as a fetus it not a child.
conclusion: A person is not obliged to give their body to someone else. Just as we have to have permission beforehand from a deceased person to donate their organs, a woman's body should be required to have permission to use it. Nor is a woman required to use her body to breastfeed after a baby has been born as it is her body.
argumentOpponent:
The wording is odd. As I understand it I'm arguing that abortion should NOT be legal.

I have a strong moral belief - it is integral to my well-being to maintain it - that abortion is the murder of an innocent child. Regardless of the reason, a life has been created. It is against all we hold good and right that nobody has the right to end someone else's life. Once sperm meets egg, someone else has been created and that person has a life. Nobody has the right to take that away.

This life may not be aware of its surroundings, perhaps cannot perceive anything or feel emotion, but that doesn't matter. It's alive, and that life belongs to it, not you.

Since I believe it's murder, the killing of an unborn person, I don't think you can persuade me by describing the wants and needs of other people, parents or not. You can't kill innocent people, and you can't convince me this isn't an alive person.
rebuttalOpponent:
The unborn child has a body, even if that body is just a couple of cells, and that unborn child should have bodily autonomy as well, not just the pregnant person. No one else is obliged to use their body without their permission, either. Stalemate.

The bible says life begins at first breath, the bible describes how to do an abortion, the bible says not to wear clothing of mixed fibers, that drowning everyone on earth was a good idea. The bible says a lot of things and none should be at play here.

You're killing an unborn child whether it's the first, second, or third trimester, whether or not there are complications in the pregnancy, regardless of any of that. N
conclusionOpponent:
You can declare a fetus not to be a child and I can declare a fetus to be a life. Where's that get us? How does the size of a clump of cells matter? I contend that this is the life of an innocent we're talking about here, regardless of the development of a body.

The "heartbeat" is a *different* thing that indicates life, not this pulsing vein that also indicates life, those are different? 

A woman, or anyone else, has the rights that we decide they have. The alive person inside that woman has the rights we decide they have.

"Life does not begin until first breath" is just a statement, not any kind of scientific fact. You don't get to choose when life begins.

topic: Is Government Surveillance Necessary for National Security?
argument: Taking into account the pros and cons, I believe that monitoring people foresees and prevents many scenarios that endanger the integrity of people. The downside doesn't outweigh that.\n
rebuttal: An unlikely potential scenario is not more important than a scenario that is being fought at all times. It is known that there are organizations that are against American ideals and want to see us defeated. That's why I think sacrificing some privacy is something we can do to keep ourselves protected as a nation.\n
conclusion: I believe that there would be many more attacks without surveillance, furthermore, those scenarios that you want to point out are gradual scenarios that can be acted upon and faced together. We will not be able to face the scenarios that can arise due to poor and lack of Surveillance in time or effectively.\n
argumentOpponent: While safeguarding national security is a priority, mass government surveillance infringes upon our constitutional rights, leading to potential misuse and diminishing our cherished values of individual privacy and liberty.
rebuttalOpponent: While prevention of threats is crucial, mass surveillance has not proven to be universally effective and justifiable; with the risk of creating a 'big brother' state, individual liberty and privacy are compromised, which goes against the principles of a free and democratic society. Moreover, it opens up a dangerous path to potential misuse and abuse of power, which could be far more detrimental than any intended benefits.
conclusionOpponent: While it's true that threats loom, the erosion of personal liberties in the name of security is a defeat in itself; it undermines the very principles that define us as a nation of freedom. Balancing security and individual rights is critical, and it's possible with targeted, evidence-based surveillance that respects citizens' rights, instead of unchecked mass surveillance that breeds mistrust and fear.

topic: Should Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico Be Granted US Statehood?
argument: I'm in favor of this proposition because Washington, DC and Puerto Rico are apart of the United States: it's actually within or near the country. Especially Puerto Rico, if you 'own' the land or territory then why not just integrate it into the US states? They are US citizens who deserve all the same rights that Americans within the 50 states do. Puerto Rico is practically the 51st state, if that is not established or implemented than citizens should at least get the same rights we do and be granted statehood.
rebuttal: Granting statehood to Washington and Puerto Rico doesn't upset the 'established' balance, as it is already struggling and in disarray. Granting statehood to a country that is considered US 'territory' shouldn't be an issue, as it is essentially part of the US already. Incurring substantial federal costs is unlikely, as the US already covers a variety of costs that are worth much more that what would go to Puerto Rican citizens. And every person has differring view, doesn't mean they cant live together in harmony.
conclusion: In conclusion, granting Puerto Rico and Washington, DC, isn't going to cost the US much financially or socially. Making a US 'territory' a state gives the citizens the respect and rights they deserve and would strengthen our country in a variety of positive ways. Equal rights equals statehood
argumentOpponent: Granting statehood to Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico could upset the established balance of political power in the U.S. and incur substantial federal costs. Plus, it disregards the opposition and concerns of many citizens within these territories.
rebuttalOpponent: While Puerto Rico and DC populations are indeed substantial, granting statehood isn't about geographical proximity or population size but rather democratic consensus from the inhabitants and feasibility. Additionally, equal rights don't require statehood, hence steps can be taken to improve their scenarios without necessarily going down the statehood route.
conclusionOpponent: Statehood requires more than just territorial ties; true consensus and readiness among the people is essential. To enforce this on regions where mixed views exist isn't democratic, and could prove immensely costly, not just financially, but also in terms of social harmony and political balance.

topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: I think AA is necessary to combat discrimination and in equality that still exists in the US.  Black Americans have less access to quality education.  Therefore they should not be held to the same standard as white and asian americans who have had the benefit of a good quality education as children.  AA gives black americans an equal chance to get a higher education and a chance to succeed in life.
rebuttal: There are differences in the experiences of people as the grow up.  Black americans often get a substandard education and therefore have less access to higher education and better jobs.  AA aims to correct this problem and give Blacks a better chance at higher education and jobs

topic: Should Governments Have the Right to Censor the Internet?
argument: I strongly believe people should be able to freely speak their minds and disagree with others and openly discuss things but I also think the government has a duty to protect its citizens against hate speech and threats on the internet just like they would in real life.
rebuttal: Just like committing any other crime against people, I believe the government has a right to remove dangerous and hateful content.  This doesn't mean that people are only allowed to express views that the government agrees with but that users can expect to be protected when online from hate speech, stalkers, threats against them.
conclusion: If there are many laws that are already in place that protect people from these type of verbal threats then how is that not censorship? argumentOpponent: I think that governments should not have the right to censor the internet because it takes away valuable perspectives and insights from the public forum. I think that government censorship would actually make it more difficult for people making threats to be caught because it would be blocked/removed entirely without as much of a trace being left behind for the victim to report.

topic: Should Public College Be Tuition-Free?
argument: Making public college tuition-free may sound great, but it comes with some downsides. First off, it's expensive, and that bill usually lands on taxpayers, which isn't fair to those who didn't attend college or already paid off their loans. Plus, it might lead to overcrowded classrooms and a dip in the quality of education. Critics say it doesn't fix the real issues causing high education costs and might not help those who need financial aid the most. So, while the idea seems generous, it's not as simple as it sounds and could have some unintended consequences.\n
rebuttal: While it sounds great to make public college free, it's like saying, "Let's have a massive party, and someone else will pick up the tab!" The truth is, making college free is super expensive, and that usually means taxpayers foot the bill. It might also lead to too many people wanting to join the party, making classes crowded and possibly lowering the quality of education. Instead of a one-size-fits-all free tuition, it makes more sense to figure out why college costs so much and help out those who really need the financial help, rather than making everyone pay for a free-for-all.\n
conclusion: While the idea of tuition-free public college may seem like an investment in our nation's future, the reality is that such a move poses significant financial challenges. Funding education on a massive scale requires a substantial amount of resources, and expecting taxpayers to foot the bill raises questions of fairness, particularly for those who may not have attended college or have already paid off their student loans. Moreover, the potential surge in demand for higher education could strain resources, compromising the quality of education that students currently enjoy. Instead of a blanket approach to free tuition, we should focus on addressing the root causes of rising education costs and ensuring that resources are targeted efficiently to support those who truly need financial assistance, rather than burdening everyone with the costs of universal free education.
argumentOpponent: Making public college tuition-free is an investment in our nation's future, increasing access to higher education and leveling the educational playing field, while boosting our economy by producing a more educated workforce. So yes, public colleges should be free.
rebuttalOpponent: Making college tuition-free can be viewed as an investment, not a cost; it helps make education accessible for all, leading to a skilled workforce that spurs economic growth which outweighs the initial costs. As for quality, strategic planning and resources allocation can mitigate potential overcrowding without compromising educational standards.
conclusionOpponent: Guaranteeing tuition-free public college should not be a "party", it's an absolute necessity for societal evolution. We are investing in our people, opening doors for opportunity, and driving economic growth - thus mitigating socioeconomic disparities and fostering a progressive society.

topic: Should the US Enact More Regulations to Ensure Fair Elections?
argument: I'll be honest, I am not very familiar with this topic. I worry about more regulations making it more difficult for people to vote. I imagine more regulations would make it more difficult for marginalized people to vote, such of people of color and those living in low-income zip codes. Their votes are important and voting should be as easy as possible. Voter turnout is already low to begin with. If this question assumes federal regulations, then that impedes state and local procedures which may be conflicting with how local elections are already run. Each state may have its own way of running things smoothly that won't work in other states.
rebuttal: I'm not sure how more regulation leads to diverse experiences and backgrounds being accounted for, I think more regulation can put up more barriers for marginalized people to get out and vote. Powerful people and corporations always seem to find a way to escape power imbalances. It seems that any entity with a lot of money can override regulations.
conclusion: I see, the word "regulation" is loaded and can mean a lot of different things, so it is hard to give a general overview without knowing what the regulation is. The effect would really depend on what the regulation is then. It seems that people in power often don't care about the voices of the marginalized so why would they go through efforts to make voting easier for those communities? How can uniformity allow for local adaptations? Overall, this is a complicated topic but we could all agree that we want elections to be fair and
argumentOpponent: Greater election regulation leads to fairer processes, acknowledging the diverse experiences, backgrounds, and needs of citizens, thus enhancing the democratic essence of our country. As observed in today’s landscape, unchecked political power can lead to imbalances, which proper regulation can rectify while maintaining the vigor of an independent political stance.
rebuttalOpponent: Election regulation does not necessarily mean limiting voter access; it can also emphasize equal access and means to simplify voting processes tailored to particular communities. Also, federal regulation can ensure best practices for fair elections, fostering uniformity across states while still allowing for local adaptations.
conclusionOpponent: Regulations can indeed be a tool to safeguard the rights of marginalized communities as well as to control undue influences of wealthy entities, provided they are designed and implemented with justice in mind, therefore, they're not inherently detrimental but have the potential to correct systemic imbalances. Ultimately, the goal is to reinforce the democratic principle that every vote should hold equal value, strengthening rather than inhibiting citizens' voices.

topic: Should the Death Penalty Be Legal?
argument: Sentencing one to death is wrong because the person might be innocent of the crime that they were convicted of. Also, "an eye for an eye" is ancient and barbaric, an advanced society should be able to have someone pay for their transgressions humanely. Prejudices are also of concern, certain people will always be sentenced to death while others are not.
rebuttal: What if the convicted is innocent and put to death? You can't bring them back to life after having taken it. Also, all crimes are different, so how can there be a blanket punishment "death?" Putting someone to death seems like the easy way to a complex issue. It is an escape of society to kill others, but then call itself advanced and civilized.
conclusion: I disagree because of the possibility of human error. I disagree with this as well, the death penalty is not a deterrent to heinous crimes, if it were, there would be no such crimes committed. There is no such thing as a fair trial, those who have been wrongly convicted are proof of that.
argumentOpponent: The death penalty should be legal as it serves as a strong deterrent to prevent grievous crimes and ensures justice for the victims, maintaining a balanced society where legal retribution fits the gravity of the crime. Imprisonment fails to drive this strong message of accountability, thus inviting chaos and lawlessness in society.
rebuttalOpponent: While the risk of error exists, improvements in modern forensics significantly reduce this risk, ensuring that only those truly deserving face the death penalty. Concerning the humane aspect, by imposing a strong enough penalty, we ensure the security and safety of the society, which is ultimately, the most humane act. As for prejudices, they exist in every part of life but should be eradicated within legal systems, not by abolishing the death penalty but by implementing fair trial standards universally.
conclusionOpponent: While it is undeniable that taking a life is a grave matter, the risk of wrongful execution can be mitigated through rigorous legal and forensic procedures, keeping the death penalty as a deterrent for heinous crimes. Rather than seeing it as an escape or a blanket punishment, it should be viewed as a significant measure to safeguard societal peace, a crucial aspect of being a civilized society.

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument:
There should be international agreements to enforce climate change. 
As we all know, climate change is a global issue affecting all countries.
Therefore, there have to be some agreements about changes that have to be met to reduce climate change. 
There should be a shared responsibility by all countries and regions of the world, as one or two regions can't do everything.
If someone doesn't follow the agreements, then they are benefiting from the work and money that other countries have put in. 
Countries should be held accountable for their actions.
This will all lead to collective action and change.
There are always going to be countries that may not be able to meet the targets and unfortunately, it may mean that bigger countries may have to lift more.
rebuttal:
It's true that different nations have different economic capabilities.
Some of these smaller countries are actually part of bigger countries that have more money to deal with climate change. 
There should be some leeway given to smaller countries that have far more pressing priorities.
However, if it's a bigger country, and they do have the capability and decide not to do their fair share, then they should face repercussions, as happens with various other issues.
We shouldn't let the smaller country argument stop an agreement from happening as if these smaller countries aren't part of bigger countries or allied with a bigger country in some way.
conclusion:
The opponent keeps on sticking with the smaller country red herring.
Again, not all countries have the capability, but they often part of or allied with a bigger country.
For example: the US and UK are big countries and have numerous countries and territories that they are affiliated with.
The US and the UK can take that burden for example. 
This is for countries like the US and UK that can clearly handle the economic burden, but parts of it may not decide to.
argumentOpponent: International agreements on global climate change policies fundamentally infrive on the sovereignty of nations, who best understand their specific environmental needs and economic capacities. Moreover, they tend to disadvantage developing countries, restricting their growth potential by imposing stringent, often unattainable, environmental targets.
rebuttalOpponent: While climate change is indeed global, uniform solutions often overlook regional distinctions and unique challenges; therefore, national strategies may be more effective. Also, assigning 'shared responsibility' risks penalizing developing countries trying to grow, since larger nations often dictate these standards.
conclusionOpponent: The argument that smaller countries are part of larger entities oversimplifies geopolitical realities; each nation has autonomy and unique needs. Imposing international standards could backfire, leading to non-compliance or burdening economies, and instead we must empower nations to develop tailored, sustainable solutions.\n
