topic: Is Arts Education as Important as Science and Math in Schools?
argument: I don't believe that the arts are as important as math and science in schools. The way that the future is going, math and science are very important to the future of our society as a whole. Technology such as ChatGPT and other artificial intelligence tools have rendered the arts nearly obsolete, as these tools can generate documents, artworks, and other artistic mediums. They can also correct grammar. However, technology is consistently evolving, and students need to be prepared for what the future holds.
rebuttal: It's important to understand that creativity and innovative thinking, while they could be fostered, are not universally understood. You could even make the argument that creativity either exists within a person or it doesn't. I think that it's important to teach objective science and math over these subjective abstract-based subjects. You could also teach about diversity without the need for unnecessary material.
conclusion: Human creativity is not something that is easily understood and is not exclusive to the arts. This means that it could easily be encouraged in a more pragmatic environment. Also, it's well-understood that you can't teach creativity, it either exists within a person or it doesn't. Furthermore, a balanced education is not necessarily a good thing. Schools should be focusing on students' strengths based on what is in demand, not making them casually good at a variety of subjects irrespective of the job market.
argumentOpponent: Arts education is as critical as science and math in schools given that it encourages creative thinking, fostering not just artists but also innovative engineers, designers, and problem solvers, which are all pivotal to our nation's progress and growth. It also ensures a balanced curriculum, nurturing emotional intelligence and diverse perspectives, essential qualities that our increasingly interconnected global society needs.
rebuttalOpponent: While advancements in technology, primarily in math and science, are indeed crucial, they cannot replicate human creativity, emotion, and perspective inherent in the arts, which aids in broadening our horizons and understanding of the world. Furthermore, many of the innovative technologies we use daily were devised by individuals well-versed in both technology and arts, indicating a balanced education is pivotal in preparing students for the future.
conclusionOpponent: While creativity might not be universally measurable, we need to remember that not all intelligence is quantifiable; a well-rounded education, featuring both the arts and sciences, cultivates critical thinking, empathy, and innovation, essential skills in our diverse world. Moreover, arts education provides a unique, enriching perspective on diversity and human emotions, allowing a deeper, comprehensive understanding that simple instruction about diversity might not achieve.

topic: Should the US Enact More Regulations to Ensure Fair Elections?
argument:
There should be more regulations on elections to ensure fairness. The reasoning for that relates to election interference via poll workers, potential issues with hacking election computers, and a lack of voting opportunities for some communities. 

Not all poll workers can be trusted, and regulations on who can work the polls would ensure a more fair election. Opposing countries to the United States could also meddle with polling via computer hacking. There needs to be stronger regulation on how ballots are counted to hopefully avoid that issue entirely.

Lastly, certain places don't have access to polling like other places do. This can lead to unfair election outcomes simply by access means.
rebuttal: You simply cannot trust that elections are fair as they are. Nothing would be taken away from the election process if more regulations were enacted. More regulations would only ensure every eligible vote gets counted and anything ineligible would not get counted. The history of recent elections shows that some regulation of elections is needed.
conclusion: Not all states have mail in ballots. Some locations even have polling places which are inaccessible to people without access to reliable transportation. Polling places are not accessible to everyone.\n\nOn top of that, poll workers in the past have been untrustworthy in their conduct. There needs to be more regulations on who can become a poll worker because of that.
argumentOpponent: The US does not need to include any more regulations for the election process. Voting is a part of the American citizen experience and any further regulations could prevent citizens from using their voice to partake in elections. There is no reason to enforce any more regulations that could take away from the election process and skew election results. As long as you are registered to vote, you are part of the democratic process that is elections.
rebuttalOpponent: Poll workers are a part of helping elections run smoothly in the country and should not be demonized. There are already balances in check to ensure voting fairness. \n\nThere are multiple ways to cast a ballot, including by mail. Therefore, voting is already accessible to all places and people in the US.
conclusionOpponent: If more regulations were enacted, there would be even more opportunity for the election to be skewed by the fact that there would be more people meddling in the election results. Evidence of election results being tampered with is slim.

topic: Should There Be Standardized Testing in Schools?
argument: As a current teacher standardized tests will ensure you have equal representation of test scores. It will make it easier to streamline results. It could serve as a starting point for student a etc. to see what they know. And develop lessons based on those scores. Also if a family moves, they have a starting point. They have the scores that can be used in any state. Every student is tested over the same kinds of information. SO it creates cohesion and unity. Its not different from state to the next. Makes the whole school system flow a lot easier this way.
rebuttal: I get where you are coming from. However, how do you fairly measure what they know across the board then? Do you have individualized instruction for each student then? This seems like from a logical standpoint hard to replicate. During tests there are different learning styles that are offered. Those with hard of hearing are read the tests. Those with slow reading are read the tests. There are accommodations for all kinds of students. Standerized tests serve as a starting point. It allows teachers to know what they know and what they need to teach.
conclusion: Students should be taught about identifying their own strengths and weaknesses. We should teach about self esteem. Having a nation wide class that is mandatory that talks about mental health. Having tests like this set them up for the real world. Its a dog eat dog world and we have to be used to competition. Having the same questions across the board allows for test scores to looked at evenly. If you give different kinds of tests then you cannot look at them with a balanced approach.
argumentOpponent: Standardized testing can do much more harm than good, and here are some ways: it can set an unfair standard for students who learn slower or are a bit more behind than the other students. This can cause unnecessary anxiety and depression. The tests have no natural way to measure progress; those with better memories can do better than those who learn at a slower pace. They also need to consider different learning styles that students may have and, in this way, DO NOT measure academic proficiency. Finally, many of the questions on the test have no relevance to the material taught by the teacher and are random questions the student may have never seen before.
rebuttalOpponent: You need to take into account the different ways students learn, the subjects they like the most, and the further processing abilities of each student. Having all the same questions doesn't measure a student's ability to the utmost respect; different students with diverse learning abilities may be better at other sections than others. They should not be shamed for this. These tests cause unnecessary stress and anxiety to an already vulnerable youth and create space for depression when the student believes they cannot live up to the other scores.
conclusionOpponent: Okay, but many of the questions on these tests will NEVER be taught by the teacher or put into the curriculum. So much of the information clog up the memory or will never be addressed again, and failing a student for not knowing something they DON'T need to know is entirely unfair. Different learning styles don't mean 'hard of hearing'; we're talking about kids with varying learning abilities or disorders. What about kids who have autism or something along those spectrums? Should they be included in the same testing as other kids? Tests don't always measure a kids ability, stress can produce poor test results while the kid excels in homework and every other part of school.

topic: Should Felons Regain the Right to Vote?
argument: I think if you are not responsible enough to stay out of trouble and obey the law, then you might not be responsible enough to vote. Voting is a right but only people who contribute positively to society should be able to vote. If you are breaking the law and being a bad person i do not know if you should have a say in important matters that shape our country.
rebuttal: People who get in trouble and go to prison don't really seem to care about democracy. If you can not follow a democracies laws do you really deserve to have a voice in shaping that democracy? I think it should be pretty simple. If you are a contributing member to your country then you have the right to vote. If you are a troublemaker who can not obey the rules, then you have lost the right to vote.
conclusion: You make good points but i still say it should be a privilege for people who are good to and contribute positively to the country. People who do not contribute positively and show a lack of respect to the democracy should not have a voice in what goes on.
argumentOpponent: Fairness and equality are fundamental principles of democracy; thus, stripping a citizen of their right to vote, even if they have served time for a felony, fundamentally undermines the democratic process. Being able to vote aids in the reintegration of the individual into society, fostering responsibility and a sense of civic engagement.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's critical to uphold law and order, judging someone's voting rights based on their past mistakes can create a slippery slope of excluding citizens from the democratic process. Remember, a felon's capacity to change and contribute positively after serving their time is equally important in shaping our society.
conclusionOpponent: Democracy thrives when it's inclusive of all voices, even those who've erred; their voting rights affirm our commitment to rehabilitation and transformation rather than eternal condemnation. A society that focuses on punishment without the capacity for redemption and societal input remains stagnant, lacking the growth that embodies a true democracy.

topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: When concerning admissions, colleges should only ever consider a student's academic prowess and their personality. A student's race should never be acknowledged as it suggests ideals that historical icons have tried so hard to dismantle.
rebuttal: Considering race to promote diversity in admissions is a flawed thought and actually works differently in practice. The non-diverse counterparts begin to feel a grudge and the diverse students become ostracized. It also makes the diverse students feel that they are some sort of token for the school.
conclusion: Considering race in admissions does nothing but help the board try to look good. The systemic barriers that are in place will not even be a discussion if race is never considered to begin, white or otherwise. The admission paper should have the students name, their background and thats it. Their race, pronouns, and identity do not matter because none of that will pinpoint whether they will be a good student or not.
argumentOpponent: College admissions should consider race as a factor to promote diversity, thus creating an inclusive learning environment that mirrors the multicultural world we live in. This averts racial bias, promotes varying perspectives, and prepares students for a diverse workforce.
rebuttalOpponent: While academic prowess is crucial, omitting race overlooks the systemic barriers some racial groups face in education, thus inhibiting true fairness. Considering race does not dismantle historical ideals but acknowledges and addresses societal disparity, ensuring equal opportunities.
conclusionOpponent: While potential negative reactions exist, they can be mitigated by comprehensive inclusion policies. Furthermore, any discomfort is outweighed by the necessity to confront systemic racial disparities and to create a diverse, culturally enriched learning environment that mirrors our society.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: With a shorter life cycle than humans, animal models can be studied throughout their whole life span and across several generations, a critical element in understanding how a disease processes and how it interacts with a whole, living biological system. However animals can be used for scientific research.
rebuttal: Virtually everyone alive today has benefited from the medical advances made possible through animal research. Polio, smallpox, diphtheria, cholera and measles are no longer major threats to public health in the United States. Sophisticated diagnostic tests mean early treatment of cancer and heart disease. If using animals for research is unethical, kindly give a specific alternative to this opposition you're making.
conclusion: Numerous vaccines and medications throughout human history became what they are today from animal testing. Everything from cholera to polio had animals leading the charge to save millions of human lives. It is not just vaccines and medications — they also advanced surgical procedures, like organ transplants and other body part replacements. Biomedical research would not be the same without it.
argumentOpponent: Using animals for scientific research exhibits an unethical disregard for sentient beings' welfare, and it often fails to provide accurate data applicable to human health due to substantial biological differences. We must prioritize exploring more accurate and ethical alternatives like advanced in vitro models and computer simulations.
rebuttalOpponent: While studying diseases in whole, living biological systems is crucial, it's misleading to assume that an animal's response will mirror a human's due to significant biological variances, thus detrimental to science advancement. We should prioritize long-term benefits of ethical alternatives which offer accurate human data without causing harm to animals.
conclusionOpponent: Yes, past medical advances were significantly supported by animal testing, but technology and science have evolved. Utilizing innovative alternatives like organ-on-a-chip, stem cell-based models, and computational models can provide more accurate results on human biology, eliminating the ethical issues associated with animal testing.

topic: Should the US Expand (“pack”) the Supreme Court?
argument: While expanding the Supreme Court may seem like a good idea to some, there are a multitude of reasons as to why it should never happen. The U.S. government is meant to exist on a system of checks and balances, where the supreme court is to function as a largely impartial entity. Packing the supreme court sets a dangerous precedent in which outside forces would be allowed to interfere with this impartiality.
rebuttal: While it is true that court packing may ensure a balanced justice system, it seems unnecessary given the fact that, historically, the court is able to balance itself. Moreover, it makes more sense that a court free from outside interference would be more impartial than one influenced by other government forces.
conclusion: The Court has had a long history of having nine judges. Changing long-held traditions now may lead to more strife between political parties, shaking the boat for a change that is not necessary to upholding democracy.
argumentOpponent: Expanding the Supreme Court is crucial to ensure a balanced, impartial justice system, reflecting our diverse society, preventing ideological monopolization, and ensuring that crucial decisions such as healthcare, LGBTQ+ rights, and climate change are not skewed by a partisan outfit. A larger Court encourages a broader dialogue and engagement within the judiciary, promoting societal progress and the advancement of democracy.
rebuttalOpponent: While maintaining checks and balances is essential, current advocacy has shifted the Court's perceived neutrality, making expansion necessary to restore impartiality. Packing the Court doesn't equate to interference but rather rebalancing, ensuring a Court representative of broad societal perspectives, making it more resilient to partisan politics.\n
conclusionOpponent: While self-balance may have been possible historically, the rapid polarization of recent years has disrupted this equilibrium, necessitating intervention for a balanced judiciary. Expanding the Court isn’t an outside interference but a legal, constitutional remedy to ensure our Court reflects and protects the vast array of diverse voices within our democracy.

topic: Are Social Media Making People Stupid?
argument: Arguing in favor of the proposition, I assert that social media's design and content structure contribute to a decline in critical thinking skills and intellectual depth.
rebuttal: Disputing the CON side's view, I emphasize the detrimental effects of social media's addictive design, superficial connectivity, and its impact on critical thinking skills and depth.
conclusion: The inherent challenges posed by algorithmic biases, the prevalence of echo chambers, and the risk of misinformation outweigh these potential benefits. The addictive nature of social media, coupled with the platform's design aimed at maximizing engagement, often leads to passive content consumption rather than active curation.
argumentOpponent: While there exists criticism around the influence of social media on people's intellectual capabilities, it's rather a tool that can enhance learning, stimulate creativity, and improve connectivity, given its judicious use.
rebuttalOpponent: The design and content structure of social media platforms, contrary to supporting cognitive decline, can actually catalyze critical thinking and intellectual growth by exposing users to a diverse range of perspectives and opportunities for knowledge acquisition. This potential for personal enrichment is enabled by users' ability to filter and curate their online content, which empowers them to optimize their online experiences according to their intellectual needs and interests.
conclusionOpponent: While acknowledging social media's potential for misuse, the key lies in responsible usage and digital literacy education; its utility as a platform for knowledge-dissemination, creative expression, and maintaining ties should not be overlooked. By encouraging discerning usage, we can realize social media's potential to foster intellectual capacity rather than erode it.

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument: There's enough bickering and interference between countries as it is. We don't need to add to the list. Do you want your neighbor telling you how to run your household? Probably not, and it's the same with countries. Let countries have the right to decide their own climate policies. And how difficult is it going to be to establish policy that many countries agree on? Nigh impossible, I contend. All the energy and money and time spent on the endeavor will prove futile and a waste.
rebuttal: If you and your country feel that particular issue is more important than the wellbeing of the populace, crime, defense, and so many others, then I say you and your country are entitled to act upon that belief. But for you to impose that belief onto another country and its citizens, for you to tell them what should be most important to them, is immoral.
conclusion: It may be sad, but the times we're living in... climate change just isn't as important to a country and its citizens as other issues. And on so many of those other issues, global disagreement is more common than not. Collaboration on the scale required to effect environmental results just isn't realistic today, this year, this decade.
argumentOpponent: Strong international agreements are essential to enforce global climate change policies, ensuring a safe, sustainable world for future generations and protecting jobs in industries like renewable energy and green technology.
rebuttalOpponent: While national autonomy is important, climate change is a global issue requiring cooperative action; without consistent policies, efforts by one country can be undermined by another's inaction. Establishing policy isn't easy, but the effort, paralleled with international collaboration, can bolster job opportunities and economic growth in the sustainable sector rather than wasting resources.
conclusionOpponent: Tackling climate change doesn't detract from a country's well-being but enhances it, by creating jobs, improving public health, and ensuring long-term sustainability. International collaboration isn't about forcing beliefs but about mutual respect, ensuring that all nations play their part in protecting our shared planet.

topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument:
As an advocate for considering race in college admissions to ensure diversity, I firmly believe in the value of a diverse educational environment. From my perspective, when colleges include race as one of the factors in their admissions process, it's not just about numbers or meeting quotas; it’s about enriching the educational experience for everyone.

I've seen firsthand how diverse classrooms lead to more dynamic and comprehensive discussions. In an increasingly globalized world, being exposed to a variety of perspectives and backgrounds is essential. It prepares us not just academically, but also socially, for the real world where we will interact with people from all walks of life.

Moreover, it's important to acknowledge the historical context. For decades, certain racial and ethnic groups have been underrepresented in higher education due to systemic barriers and inequalities. By considering race in admissions, colleges can play a role in leveling the playing field and offering opportunities to those who have been historically marginalized.

This isn't just about benefiting minority students; it's about benefiting all students. When we interact with people who are different from us, we learn tolerance, empathy, and gain a broader understanding of the world. It prepares us to be better leaders, innovators, and citizens.

Finally, the legal framework in many places, including the U.S. Supreme Court, has recognized the importance of diversity in education and upheld the limited use of race as a factor in admissions. This is a testament to the value our society places on diversity as a crucial component of education.
rebuttal:
Comprehensive View of Merit: Firstly, it's important to clarify that considering race in college admissions doesn't mean neglecting merit or individual achievements. It's about broadening our understanding of what 'merit' encompasses. topic: Should Transgender People Be Banned From Using Bathrooms Consistent With Their Gender Identity?
argument: I agree that transgender people should be banned from using bathrooms consistent with their gender identity. They should use the bathroom that is consistent with their gender of birth. It is unethical for a man to use a women's restroom, and a woman to use a man's restroom. Imagine your young child using a bathroom with a member of the opposite sex inside the next stall. rebuttal: Again, imagine a female child of 12 using the restroom and comes out of the stall to wash her hands. A transgender man comes out of the next stall and frightens the young girl. My point stands that transgender people should be banned from using bathrooms consistent with their gender identity.
conclusion: People are free to be who they choose to be in this lifetime, however the line must be drawn when it comes to safety and proper restroom protocols. argumentOpponent: Banning transgender people from using bathrooms consistent with their gender identity infringes upon their basic human rights and supports discrimination, standing antithetical to the principles of freedom and equality our society prides itself on. rebuttalOpponent: Targeting transgender individuals doesn't increase safety but perpetuates stereotypes and spawns fear. It's important we focus on educating society for understanding and acceptance, creating safe spaces for all rather than segregating and alienating a group based on their gender identity.
conclusionOpponent: Reality is diverse and children should be taught respect for all genders, fostering understanding rather than fear. Banning transgender individuals from using bathrooms matching their identity won't prevent fear or confusion, but building a society that respects and understands diversity will.

topic: Should the Penny Stay in Circulation?
argument: The penny should not stay in circulation because it is wasteful.  Many people throw away their extra pennies meaning they can wind up in a landfill.  Removing the penny from circulation would cut down on excess waste.
rebuttal: The penny does not accurately calculate the "precise cent."  If that were the case then fractions of a cent would never need to be used.
conclusion: People won't follow the recommendations for proper disposal because most of them are too lazy.  They will still wind up in landfills.  Pennies need to just be removed from circulation.
argumentOpponent: The penny should stay in circulation as it helps maintain affordable pricing and ensures that all transactions can be accurately calculated to the precise cent, preventing any shift of economic burden onto consumers.
rebuttalOpponent: While some pennies might end up as waste, their removal could lead to rounding-off purchase totals, disproportionately affecting low-income consumers. Furthermore, a re-education on the value and proper disposal of pennies can help curb the alleged wastage problem.
conclusionOpponent: While fractions of a cent can be part of calculations, in real-world transactions, pennies do provide the most precise payment option for customers, protecting them from potential round-up policies. Furthermore, the penny's history and cultural significance attests to its value beyond its monetary worth.

topic: Are Social Media Making People Stupid?
argument: Some people argue that social media is making people more stupid, but in actuality social media has been improving peoples' intelligence in many areas. For example, they now have access to different peoples' perspectives about life from a wide variety of cultures without even needing to leave their current location. Being exposed to a wider variety of cultures, etc gives people a broader understanding of life, and thus makes them wiser. Many people also share life skills or hacks that many aren't taught in skills, and people are instead able to learn from people teaching on social media. So in a wide variety of ways, social media is making people smarter.
rebuttal: I would argue that social media is actually doing the opposite. People have been aware of all the misinformation that is out there, and so many are learning from this that they need to use their critical thinking skills to determine if certain posts are true or not. There are some comments on posts where people have gone and done research, and then come back to the post to add intelligent comments or new perspectives to the post. It also exposes people to a wider variety of cultures and views, which I think actually gives people broader perspectives of complex issues.
conclusion: Echo chambers can happen, but people are also very aware that this happens now. Thus many social media posts bring awareness to issues, and then people will often go and do their own research outside of social media to try and learn in a more unbiased way. Same with posts about life skills, etc. People are brought awareness to these skills, and then it's a jumping board for them to do more research on their own and learn more.
argumentOpponent: Over-reliance on social media dampens critical thought, promotes the spread of misinformation, and fosters an oversimplified perspective of complex issues.
rebuttalOpponent: While exposure to diverse perspectives is a potential benefit of social media, the echo chambers created through algorithms often limit this potential, instead fostering confirmation bias. Moreover, the credibility of shared 'life skills or hacks' can be questionable due to the lack of vetting, which can lead to misinformation.
conclusionOpponent: Despite some using social media to exercise their critical thinking, the prevalence of misleading content and the manipulation of these platforms to spread such content is an alarming concern. Importantly, true cultural understanding and grasp of complex issues necessitate serious study and contemplation beyond what the typically short and simplified social media posts can provide.

argument: Although there are aspects that could negatively impact society, if the tools are regulated properly and applied in a way that is thought--through, just like any other tool, AI could benefit society greatly. Some of the examples could include assisting writing to people who have hard time writing due to health or mental issues. IT could apply to any other tasks where AI could be used as a tool. Also, it could benefit production and manufacturing, making products more eleborate and helpful for society. rebuttal: Once the door of opportunities is opened, most productions and companies would prefer having AI in place for jobs that could be completely replaced with AI. It would save them money and increase their profits. IT would be very hard to control the application of AI even if the government would like to regulate it. Regular workers wil lsuffer while companies will gain.
conclusion: It is true, but just like wit DNA altercations and the prohibition of cloning practices in most countries,  there are ways the government could put together very strict regulations.
argumentOpponent: While AI shows promise in improving various sectors, it presents serious risks such as increased unemployment and heightened inequality, as well as threats to privacy and cybersecurity that could result in societal damage.
rebuttalOpponent: Regulation of AI is a good idea theoretically, but in practice, it is nearly impossible due to the pace of technological change and the international complexity of its development. Moreover, while quality control jobs sound appealing, they won't replace the massive job losses in sectors like manufacturing and could further increase income inequality.
conclusionOpponent: The profit-driven incorporation of AI, as you mentioned, highlights the heart of my argument; our society stands to suffer as societal cohesion could be destabilized through increased inequality and job losses, even as companies record gains. With proper regulation proving to be a complex task, it underscores that AI poses significant challenges that far outweigh its potential benefits.

topic: Should Governments Have the Right to Censor the Internet?
argument:
The government should not have the right to censor the internet.  The public should have free and open access to the internet, with no censorship.  

For example, communist countries often censor what their public can and can't see online, and it not only encourages, but makes it a reality that the public will continue to be a giant bubble.
rebuttal: If the government is the one making the rules, and enforcing censorship, how does that imply that only unlawful content would be censored?  The problem with censorship is not that some content online is maybe best not spread, but that by censoring the content at all, you are imparting bias.  The public has the right to all information, and content and to make their own decisions and choices based on that information.  If the government censors the internet, we are encouraging a dumber population, who has not had access to multiple sides of an argument and/or issue.
conclusion: If the government is censoring the internet, who is stop them from generating their own 'fake news'?  No human is truly unbiased and able to be completely neutral.  Therefore, it is important that the public can determine for themselves what aligns with them and what doesn't.
argumentOpponent: Government censorship of the internet is vital for the protection of citizens, as it safeguards against the spread of unlawful content and helps to maintain a safer online environment for everyone.
rebuttalOpponent: While I completely agree about the importance of public transparency, recent developments, such as the proliferation of fake news and harmful content, necessitate a degree of government oversight. This is not about creating a bubble but fostering a safer, more reliable information space.
conclusionOpponent: Instead of fostering a "dumber" population, careful regulation can create a more aware and educated public by minimizing the risk of exposure to harmful narratives and misinformation. The goal is to ensure a balanced, fair, and safer virtual environment without suppressing valid viewpoints, a task well within the capability of a democratic government functioning with checks and balances.

topic: Should the US Keep Using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections?
argument: I advocate for the US's continual use of the Electoral College because it allows representation from every quarter of society.  Without the Electoral College, a few states such as New York and California alone will determine the outcome of the presidential election but the Electoral college helps balance representations from all states.
rebuttal: Without the Electoral College, smaller States would have no real representation and sit at the table of governance of the country. The Big states would have total control and the smaller States would have no say
conclusion: In a nutshell, for the country to be properly represented and every state to have an equal seat at the table, The Electoral College System is necessary to balance and create equal representation.
argumentOpponent: The Electoral College creates a system that allows smaller, less populous states to overrule the majority vote of the nation, often conflicting with the principle of one person, one vote. Considering our shared belief in democratic principles, the fairness and inclusivity of our electoral process should always reflect the will of the populace.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's true that the Electoral College ensures nationwide representation, it also disrupts the democratic principle of equal representation by giving disproportionate weight to votes in smaller states. In a truly inclusive society, every citizen's vote, regardless of their geographic location, must have equal power.
conclusionOpponent: While highlighting the voices of smaller states is a noble cause, it should not be achieved at the expense of marginalizing the voices from populous states. Abandoning the Electoral College in favor of a direct vote system would ensure every citizen enjoys equal representation, making it genuinely democratic and integrative.

topic: Should the Penny Stay in Circulation?
argument: Pennies should be removed from circulation because people don’t really care about them. Often times people just donate the pennies they receive as change into donation stations at establishments or tell cashiers to keep the change. If pennies disappeared today most people probably would not care very much. In this day and age more and more people pay with credit and debit cards or other digital methods. Pennies are also a nuisance most of the time since it takes 100 of them to add up to a dollar. People are much more likely to pick up a quarter or a dime if they drop it than a penny.
rebuttal: The reality is that removing the penny would only cause a very negligible difference in the price of items. Most consumers would not be deterred from buying a product just because the price was rounded up a few cents. The argument that pennies are culturally significant is also not a strong point because most people have no idea about the actually origins of the penny or any other information pertaining to it other than its value.
conclusion: The reality is that regardless most people would not care or be impacted by the removal of the penny. It has very little value and most people do not rely on them when purchasing things. They are lacking in significance.
argumentOpponent: Historically and culturally significant, the penny plays a crucial role in our economy by allowing precise pricing and preventing rounding up transactions to the detriment of consumers.
rebuttalOpponent: While the rise of digital transactions decreases the use of pennies, they still provide a value for lower-income households who rely on exact change, therefore, removing pennies from circulation could disproportionately impact that segment. Also, penny donation stations you've mentioned, support numerous charitable causes, emphasizing the worthwhile purpose of the seemingly insignificant coin.
conclusionOpponent: While few cents rounding might seem negligible, when applied to all transactions across an entire economy it amounts to significant net change, potentially exacerbating economic inequality; the penny is more than just its monetary value, it's a tangible part of our country's history, symbolizing our continuous journey towards economic evolution. Plus, it's the accessibility and unequivocal acceptance of pennies that make them valuable for lower-income communities.\n

topic: Should the US Have Mandatory National Service?
argument: Forced conscription is against everything the United States was founded on. Taxation is as well, but that is another matter. In times of peace it should not be the policy. In the case of a war on United Sates territory it may be required. If required in times of war both male, female, and other sexuality citizens of appropriate age should be forcibly conscripted.
rebuttal: Good points, but it remains a forced conscription. Your argument is about the benefits of service, these benefits may be true, but it is a forced conscription nevertheless. In a free society that is wrong.
conclusion: Per my statement, I said it should be allowed only during times of war that is occurring on United States soil. No overseas wars. Many of your arguments sound similar to the communist values of the last century
argumentOpponent: Mandatory national service in the US would foster unity, instill a sense of responsibility in citizens, and allow for extensive support in different sectors without burdening the government's finances. rebuttalOpponent: Mandatory national service is not forced conscription, rather it's an avenue for developing civic responsibility and rapport among citizens; "forced" connotes violation of rights, but this aims at balanced societal contribution. conclusionOpponent: Even within a free society, certain obligations - like taxes - exist for societal welfare; similarly, mandatory national service can serve as a democratic obligation that fosters shared experiences, mutual understanding and bridges socio-economic divides without infringing upon personal freedom in a substantial way. topic: Is Arts Education as Important as Science and Math in Schools?
argument: I think that art education is as important as science and math in schools because art fosters creativity and imagination. These things allow us to be independent thinkers and help foster growth in ways we cannot see. For example, by learning the arts we grow a deeper appreciation for things we wouldn't otherwise. I believe children who are taught various arts are just learning more broadly and this will help them become more creative thinkers. This in turn will help them in other areas, including science and math. So I don't think science and math  need to be separated from arts; rather they can work together.
rebuttal: It may be crucial, but it can also be argued that the creativity and imagination and ability to think outside the box are also crucial aspects of many careers and in solving real-world problems. For example, in my various jobs I have used almost nothing I learned in my math classes beyond basic addition, subtraction and multiplication. But I have countless times needed to think outside the box, be creative in coming up with ideas, etc. Very few jobs require more than basic math skills.
conclusion: I think this counterargument is saying almost the exact same thing that the previous statement said. So I conclude with saying again that math and science are not needed for many careers beyond just the basics. topic: Should the Penny Stay in Circulation?
argument: The penny is well-integrated into the fabric of this country. It's a part of its history as well as the economy. Taking it away will make it easier for business to charge more for products, leaving many people in a worse and worse financial situation. The process of switching to a penniless society will also be an enormous drain for businesses large and small, both financially and with time expenditure. There will be little positive return for the enormous upheaval for such change. It simply isn't worth it.
rebuttal: Though it might, conceivably, be easier on that side of the glass, getting to that point will be no small feat. It will take many years to get to that place and large corporations may be able to handle this switch more readily than smaller business who lack the money to make such a change (pun intended
conclusion: It's easy to say that the country is increasingly more reliant on cards and online payments. However, that's more the case for those who are better off. And the change to a penniless society will affect the prices paid with cards and online payments as well, necessarily.
argumentOpponent: The penny, the one cent coin, is unnecessary in today's day and age. First of all, recent years have showed a drastic change from an all cash life style to one that focuses mostly on paying with cards and digitally. This shows how actual physical money is less necessary. Due to this lesser necessity, we should be limiting the amount of different coins we have, starting with the one of the lowest value. This can also be more convenient and beneficial for those that spend cash and coins, as well as those who receive it. One of the most irritating parts of spending cash is looking through your wallet and trying to find each individual coin so you have the exact right amount of cents. If we eliminated the penny, we could start to move all prices with ending with 5s and 0s, which would increase convenience when paying for items, which will also make things easier for cashiers.
rebuttalOpponent: While I appreciate the points you are bringing up, I believe that there is no real proof of the negative effects on the economy. While businesses would have to adjust prices, it could also lead to a decrease in prices in order to adjust to the lack of pennies in circulation, which would help individuals deal with rising prices in general. In addition, given how there has already been a large switch to online money and people every day are dealing less and less with cash and coins in particular, now would be the time to make this change. This change would not cause a great deal of time due to the changing society we are already in, in regards to the less reliance on cash.
conclusionOpponent: I understand your argument, but I would say that as long as the government passes laws in consistent ways, and if the American people stay patient in regards to this change, it will eventually go smoothly. Small businesses will see the way that big businesses handle these changes and use them as examples to make their own changes. In the end, all businesses large and small will eventually realize that this change benefits them in the long term, as well as benefits the convenience of its customers.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: Animals should continue to be used for scientific research. There is a long standing ethical agreement that using animals for research is morally correct. The use of animals has allowed for many scientific breakthroughs that have not only made the lives of people better, but have also lessened the suffering for animals. If you are religious you probably believe that animals are here for our use. If this is true, then god intended for us to use animals in this way to solve our problems and make life better. With modern technology, the suffering of animals can be minimised
rebuttal: While it is true that we can now use other methods to research, the use of animals can not be eliminated from the process. After treatments are developed, they should be tested in animals before they are used in human trials. We value human life of that of animals, so this is actually an easy decision. The debate on this has already occurred. Humans decided long ago that it was ethical and morally correct to use animals for this purpose.
conclusion: These are not dark age argument's as you claim. This is an established truth. Most people agree that we should continue to use animals in this way.
argumentOpponent: The use of animals in scientific research is unnecessary, as we now have sophisticated alternatives such as in vitro, computer modeling and human-based studies, thus it's about time we advance and prioritize ethical considerations along with our scientific progress.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's true that animals have been used in the past, societal ethics evolve and we shouldn't rely on dark-age arguments such as divine providence, rather factoring in sentient beings' rights. Even with technology minimizing suffering, not causing it in the first place trumps mitigation, especially when alternative methods are available and advancing fast.
conclusionOpponent: Rather than arguing the ethics of using animals based on historical norms or perceived worth of life, we should establish current standards recognizing animals' capacity for suffering and the advancements in alternatives; as every human trial demands informed consent, animals used for testing are denied this basic right. While we shouldn't undermine strides made through animal research, it's also imperative we evolve alongside the tools science provides us with.

topic: Should the Rich Pay More Taxes?
argument: The rich have a higher income. Everyone is expected to pull their own weight, but it would be impossible for someone who makes 1000 a year to pay the same amount towards better things as someone who earns 400000000 a year. If we don't tax the rich more, things that are supported by taxes won't be able to continue.
rebuttal: There is nothing fair about 1 percent of the world holding 90 percent of the money. These wealthy individuals have found ways to hide money and avoid paying their fair share of taxes, resulting in a deficit of what should already be in the tax fund.
conclusion: When based on a percentage of earnings, it is fair. Someone earning 100 a year paying 10 percent only pays 10 dollars, while someone earning 1000000000 paying ten percent pays their fair share. They are paying more taxes but it's the fairest way to ensure its level.
argumentOpponent: While it seems intuitive to demand the rich to pay more taxes for the sake of income redistribution and social justice, this approach may inadvertently stifle economic growth and hinder opportunities for those climbing the socioeconomic ladder. Consideration of a more measured and incentivizing tax system may better propel our shared goal of a fair, prosperous society.
rebuttalOpponent: While high earners should indeed contribute to society, an excessive tax burden runs the risk of inhibiting entrepreneurship and stifling economic expansion, which ultimately create jobs and opportunities for all. Increasing funding for public services should perhaps be viewed with a lens broader than just higher taxes on the rich, focusing more on efficient budget allocations and combating tax evasion across all income brackets.
conclusionOpponent: The issue isn't taxing the rich more, but rather ensuring everyone pays their just due - dealing with tax evasion and loopholes is vital, so those who have gained wealth aren't able to avoid contributing their fair share. A progressive tax system facilitates this, but over-taxation could discourage the very enterprise and investment that fuels our economy and creates jobs, underpinning social mobility and an equitable distribution of wealth.

topic: Should Every Citizen Receive a Basic Income from the Government?
argument: The question posed asks whether or not citizens should receive universal basic income (UBI) from the government. UBI is a process wherein the government provides citizens with a monthly baseline stipend as default due to their citizenship. This is in addition to any monthly income that they may be currently accruing. Universal basic income is often quoted as a necessity as the economy of the worlds countries continues to increase often without consideration for the everyday citizen. However, proponents of UBI often do not consider the impacts of implementing such a policy. Largely, the introduction of UBI would lead to an increase in taxes across the population. A severe increases in taxes due to the introduction of this policy would heavily burden and likely harm the lowest income classes in a population, placing undue stress upon them that may not be offset by the supplem
rebuttal: While there is an assumption that a guaranteed basic income would ensure economic security, there is no consideration for the economic impact that an increase in taxes, as would be necessary to implement this program would have on the working class. As guaranteed basic income necessities this increase, there is no clear evidence that the net profit gain from the worker would be offset by the loss in the increase of taxes. Similarly, the impact on welfare while a reasonable assumption is not guaranteed. The government would need to enact sweeping policy touching on all sectors for
conclusion: The crux of the argument lies in whether or not the costs of increased taxes would be offset by the safety net provided via the implementation of a universal basic income. This implementation would need to handled broadly - that is not merely by a single policy but various ones that would increase welfare across the board, that is sweeping changes to any non socialized systems (such as healthcare in the US, for example). A simple UBI policy without evidence of any offset costs after the initial tax increases is likely due to fail, as it my end up merely producing a net zero increase in income from the general population. Similarly, the pricing of goods and services may ultimately fluctuate as the general income of the population on average increases slightly, once again offsetting the purpose of the policy.
argumentOpponent: A guaranteed basic income would ensure economic security for all citizens, reducing poverty and income inequality, while empowering individuals to pursue opportunities without the fear of financial instability. It would also simplify welfare systems, creating more efficiency and cost savings in the long-term.
rebuttalOpponent: While UBI might necessitate an initial tax increase, this cost could be offset by reducing current welfare programs and decreasing administrative costs, ultimately leading to overall savings for the public. Importantly, the basic income would directly benefit the lower income classes by providing a safety net thereby reducing the impacts of poverty.
conclusionOpponent: UBI would provide a direct, unconditional income support, lifting the working class and reducing the wealth gap, the additional tax impact being offset by the guaranteed income. Also, UBI would drastically reduce bureaucratic costs involved in welfare programs, and provide a level of essential stability that current piecemeal solutions fail to offer.

topic: Is Space Exploration a Worthwhile Investment for Humanity?
argument: When we think of the term 'worthwhile', we should consider worthwhile to whom, and in what context? Space exploration is worthwhile to humanity because of the individual desires of people who wish to understand the greater universe and all its mysteries. For decades, people have been interested in exploring the unknown, which is why becoming an astronaut is one of the hardest and most competitive career paths. It was a big hot button topic during the Cold War, culminating in one of the most famous events in American history.
rebuttal: This argument posits that it is a mutually exclusive situation, where one can do one of the two but not both. Yes, while it is true that it would be a costly endeavor, previous federal budgets continue to balloon. There is money to go around, and there should be plenty of room in the budget for both initiatives. In terms of the environmental cost, it would be a much more fruitful argument if every human and company's impact on the environment were already perfect. It would be much more impactful to discuss the negative effects of our actions here on Earth, which we can do plenty about regardless of space exploration.
conclusion: Once again, the opposing argument is based on the premise that there can only be one focus at a time. Governments and states should be well equipped to devote resources to multiple things at once. Environmental preservation and education is important, perhaps equally as important as space exploration. There is no reason to pit these two against each other. Space exploration is deserving of its own resources as the pursuit of knowledge of the universe is worthy in its own right.
argumentOpponent: While space exploration sparks curiosity and innovation, the exorbitant costs and the potential of exacerbating environmental issues necessitate a careful re-evaluation of its value to humanity. In contrast, allocating these substantial funds towards solving market failure and improving socioeconomic conditions is a more worthwhile effort.
rebuttalOpponent: While understanding the universe remains a significant human aspiration, prioritizing our planet and addressing immediate global issues, like climate change and socio-economic disparities, should be paramount. The daunting resources for space exploration could be better invested into innovative technologies for environmental preservation and education, fostering a more sustainable future here on earth.
conclusionOpponent: The notion of a ballooning federal budget doesn't justify indiscriminate spending; rather it's a call for greater fiscal responsibility focusing on areas like education, healthcare, and environmental protection that benefit society as a whole. It's not about achieving perfection but striving for improvements where we can - and addressing our terrestrial issues head-on, rather than viewing space exploration as a solution or escape, instantly makes a more substantive impact.

topic: Should the US Keep Using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections?
argument: The US should keep using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections because it's a tradition that's been around for a long time. When foreigners see change occur in such a tradition, it signals a flaw in the US government. This isn't a good thing for the people or the leaders of the United States, especially when you have other countries seeking to be the ruling country of the world.
rebuttal: I disagree with the idea of getting rid of the Electorate College because it's no longer necessary. It's still necessary because it's a tradition that's played a key role in deciding both minor and major elections and if other countries see a switch take place, they will be encouraged to undermine the government of the US.
conclusion: At such a time in history where so many threats against the US have increased, both domestic and foreign, it's more important to maintain structure and show that the US is sure and firm. It's not just about tradition. I might agree with your argument if the threat against US society wasn't so prevalent. But that's not the case. There are many players on the world stage awaiting any chance to take down the US and this would be a weakness they would take advantage of.
argumentOpponent: The electoral college was  created as a way to counter what the founding fathers thought of as an unknowing electorate.  It was designed in a time where there were states with little population.  This is no longer necessary.  We've had decades where presidents have been installed who did not receive the majority of votes.  The Electoral college has made our system less democratic as it ignores the will of millions.
rebuttalOpponent: Traditions are wonderful; they bring emotions and a sense of nostalgia.  Traditions are unbending and we live in a world that is changing.  We need to build the structure that will support the way we live and how we work.  The electoral college takes away the voices of many.  This isn't supposed to be minority rules.   The college needs to be eliminated so that we can grow.
conclusionOpponent: Traditions are great, but we are a nation of laws.  We can make a new tradition of representing all our voters and not rely on an outdated system that was established by a lack of trust in the people.  Installing candidates that represent the minority is not a symbol of democracy and it makes us weaker in the view of other democracies.

topic: Should Elected or Appointed Government Officials Be Paid the Minimum Wage?

For example, Ceo's and high company officials make more because they have more knowledge of the subject and therefore are more valuable. Being so makes them more valuable and that costs more and is shown by higher wages.
rebuttal: People with the most important jobs don't always make the most money. Just because someone is elected to office doesn't mean they are smarter than others. Just look at Donald Trump! The people that should be making the most are not, like teachers and fireman and police officers. Typically its sports figures that make the most.
conclusion: In the end, I don't think that it's smart to give our officials the least amount of money like minimum wage because it will produce people that are less qualified. Minimum wage is mainly reserved for less responsible type jobs only.
argumentOpponent: Elected or appointed government officials should be paid minimum wage as it will directly align their personal financial experience with the constituents they represent, promoting empathy, better labor laws, and genuine efforts to raise living standards. topic: Should Public College Be Tuition-Free?
argument: Public college should be tuition-free in a functioning society. It is the duty of a healthy government and society to provide free education to children and, in our modern era, it should also be considered a duty to provide education to young adults. A college degree is necessary to perform many well-paying jobs in today's climate, and it is beneficial if the most people possible can be trained with the necessary skills. In addition, a well-educated population will make better choices when it comes to voting and for their own life decisions (i.e., finance, relationships, health). All in all, it would benefit everyone to have tuition-free college.
rebuttal: Resources can be reallocated, so it is not simply that resources are limited - for example, a fraction of military funding could be redirected to paying for college tuition, or taxes could be raised by a marginal amount. Offering tuition-free college does not mean that the quality of the education would decrease. In addition, offering scholarships drastically limits the opportunities to only a select handful of students, when all young people deserve to receive an advanced education if they so wish.
conclusion: Why should degrees be devalued by more people receiving them? More knowledge in the population is better for every person and there should be no gatekeeping to artificially increase the value of knowledge. It is a false argument to state that success hinges on quality when providing tuition-free college does not have to result in a decrease in quality at all (in fact, its quality might increase as it would be held to more universal standards). In addition, vocational training and apprenticeships are also not cost-free, and providing free public college does not necessarily limit those routes being overlooked (particularly if they are also made to be cost-free).
argumentOpponent: While I appreciate the sentiment behind free public college, economics and limited resources compel us to question its feasibility and efficacy; focusing on improving the quality of public education and increasing access to scholarships may prove a more productive route.
rebuttalOpponent: While tuition-free college may seem like an appealing solution, it risks devaluing degrees, burdening taxpayers, and diverting funds from more urgent public needs; moreover, educational success hinges not just on accessibility but also on quality, and effort might be better spent enhancing primary and secondary education to prepare students for the demands of college and beyond. On the social level, societal progress does not exclusively stem from academic education, also requiring vocational training and apprenticeships, which risk being overlooked if higher education becomes entirely cost-free.
conclusionOpponent: Redirecting funds and raising taxes for free college might solve one problem whilst creating others, such as hampering defense capabilities or increasing the fiscal burden on citizens; thus, a sustainable approach requires looking beyond mere cost. A holistic, nuanced education policy that caters to all students, not just those who want to attend college, would balance accessibility, quality, and cost-effectiveness, with focus on primary and secondary education improvement, expanded scholarships, and support for vocational training.

topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: The most equitable solution for ensuring that college admissions candidates receive admission to the college of their choice should be based on skills, GPA, test scores, extracurricular activities, and aptitudes. Unfortunately, in our society, we sometimes overlook the most qualified candidates to create a more diverse demographic of students. Higher education institutions must pick the most qualified range of students for admissions, despite students' racial backgrounds. What we should instead, to ensure that colleges do have a diverse student population, is to make sure that public and private K-12 education is funded equitably throughout the nation so that all students have access to the same opportunities for college educations, if desired.
rebuttal: Colleges do not necessarily benefit from having a more racially diverse student body. Education is based on the quality of the institution, resources, professors, and curriculum that is provided - not racial diversity amongst students. Furthermore, anyone of any race can build an environment of inclusivity and increased cultural perspectives. Colleges should instead focus on admitting the most qualified candidates amongst many other factors to ensure the success of thei
conclusion: As a public school educator, I can understand that merit-based admissions are a component of institutional and structural racism that exists. What I think we should focus on, rather than enabling colleges to pick a diverse population of students regardless of their academic merit, is to ensure that all learners in America's K-12 education system have equitable opportunities throughout their schooling. This way, there would inevitably be a more diverse population of students at colleges because a diverse range of students would be highly qualified. Let's fund public schools and public education nationally so that we can alleviate the racial and economic disparities that exist nationwide. High quality public education will ENSURE that colleges do not need to look at race, because students across demographics will ALL be highly qualified candidates.
argumentOpponent: To build an environment of inclusivity and increased cultural perspectives, colleges need to consider race as one of many factors in admissions, thereby promoting diversity which is a critical aspect of a comprehensive education. Without it, we risk maintaining a narrow and homogeneous educational experience.
rebuttalOpponent: While merit-based admissions are crucial, they unfortunately are often unequal due to long-standing educational disparities rooted in economic and racial inequalities. Implementing diversity considerations in college admissions is a pragmatic approach that not only enriches the college experience for all students but also serves as a temporary measure until our K-12 system achieves real equity.
conclusionOpponent: Diversity in higher education isn't just about representation but also about creating a vibrant intellectual community - diverse perspectives foster innovative thinking, better problem-solving skills, and a well-rounded education. Considering race as a factor in admissions is not about compromising merit but ensuring all students gain exposure to a wide range of experiences and viewpoints contributing to their academic success.

topic: Are Social Media Making People Stupid?
argument: Social media is in use by a lot of people in our world. People that use social media are usually very engrossed in it and thereby focus on it a lot. This could lead to assimilating information that could be wrong. From my daily use of social media, I have been influenced to try a lot of ideas I got from social media. As humans therefore, we are prone to believe the things we see, hear and experience. Hence, the possibility of becoming stupid from using social media is on the high side.
rebuttal: I agree that social media provides vast amount of information but what is the assurance that the information it provides is factual. Social media users need to be careful of the information they digest so they do not end up doing things that are wrong. A lot of ideas that float around on social media are just people's ideas that have not been verified even by them. Doing these make people stupid therefore social media makes people stupid.
conclusion: As much as it is on us validate information and check sources, not many people do that. Social media influencers, for example, are believed by their followers and whatever they promote on their pages are accepted by their followers without even fact-checking if they are true. Therefore, a lot of people do not fact-check what they take in on social media and what they take in might actually make them stupid when they implement it.
argumentOpponent: Social media, rather than making people stupid, actually leverages human intellect by providing a platform for enlightened discourse, stimulating creative expression and facilitating access to vast amounts of information. This digital era does challenge us to adapt new ways of critical thinking and decision making.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's true that social media can expose us to misinformation, it's our responsibility, not social media's, to think critically and discern fact from fiction. Our intelligence grows when we validate information, check sources, and engage in in-depth conversations, all of which are plentifully facilitated by social media platforms.
conclusionOpponent: The capacity of social media to inform or misinform isn't an inherent feature but depends largely on how we use it; asserting that it makes people stupid disregards individual agency in media consumption. Thus, while social media can disseminate unverified ideas, it also encourages critical engagement, creative thinking, and broadened horizons, all hallmarks of intellect and wisdom.

topic: Should Elected or Appointed Government Officials Be Paid the Minimum Wage?
argument: Politicians often have multiple sources of income so it’s not a stretch to suggest that they should make minimum wage as they will have other sources of money. While some of it may be unethical maybe it will call attention to more corrupt practices. The president often forfeits his salary. So it isn’t by any means a stretch.
rebuttal: Politicians should focus on public service rather than on exchanging their work for public tax funds. So much of the time they behave as if they’ve won something by being elected. They should be focusing on sacrifice for the greater good
conclusion: Lower class backgrounds don’t specify higher diversity rates so it should follow that lower classes shouldn’t have less incentive to for go higher salaries when their motivation should be to improve opportunities for the masses and
argumentOpponent: While it's tempting to think levelying the pay of elected or appointed government officials to the minimum wage could foster empathy and accountability, it realistically risks attracting only those with alternate income sources, thus compromising the diversity and representative nature of government bodies.
rebuttalOpponent: The president's voluntary salary forfeiture is not a standard and implying all politicians are corrupt disenfranchises potential, ethical candidates who might rely on a livable wage. Reducing their salary to minimum wage could discourage diverse, middle and lower class backgrounds, thus limiting the socio-economic representation in our government.
conclusionOpponent: While dedication to public service is crucial, it is vital to acknowledge that officials' work requires remuneration to attract diverse talent and ensure independent financial security, thereby reducing susceptibility to corruption. The idea of sacrifice must not compromise the attractiveness of public service roles to people from varied socio-economic backgrounds, potentially enriching policy-making with diverse experiences and perspectives.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
argument: Artificial Intelligence is good for society. Once properly trained, AI can be more reliable than a human taking away the risk of "human error." AI can be used to automate certain activities, which frees up time and resources which we can then devote to other endeavors. AI is the future and will assist us in advanced even further. AI can assist us with little tasks like helping us to write a text message to large tasks like driving us to the airport. In that little task, they are helping us to do something better. In the large task they are saving us time and making the task less risky.
rebuttal: Artificial Intelligence is bad for society. Everything is becoming automated with AI and we are losing the human touch. If you look at resumes today, compared to ten years ago, you'll find a large majority of them are written (or improved) with AI. That takes away the personality and invividuality of the person whose resume it is. AI is getting involved in all sorts of things, like driving and customer service jobs, that are causing humans to lose out on those positions. We are becoming less engaged in what we are doing, and with others, because of AI.
conclusion: AI is asisting us. It is not for me to judge what others do with the extra time provided by AI completing tasks. AI is a great and useful tool and to not use it seems foolish. It is the future and it needs to fully utilized and to assist us in making life and the world better.
argumentOpponent: I believe that artificial intelligence is bad for society. I find that the most consistent effect of artificial intelligence on human society is that it robs people of the ability to think for and be efficient in themselves. Artificial intelligence continues to provide for people much more quickly then the human body and mind can but as a consequence people begin to take the easy route and rely on artificial intelligence more. This means that the natural human proclivity towards challenging and improving oneself becomes less common as people just use this technology as a shortcut. Employers no longer train people to do what artificial intelligence can do which takes away peoples jobs and does not improve their station. In the end people are both ostracized by technology and increasingly reliant upon it to function which is truly terrifying. Society thus becomes more atomized and vulnerable with each passing year.
rebuttalOpponent: AI can take away the "risk" of human error but this also takes away the opportunity for self-improvement within the human being. AI automating activities does not guarantee that time and resources that are freed up will be used in such a way as to improve the average person's life nor that they will be the one to benefit resource wise in our capitalist society. AI being the future is something that should trouble everyone. The fact that AI invades human activity on both a small and large scale such as text messages versus driving us to the airport suggest that it is invasive in all aspects of life and we cannot escape it even if we wish to. If AI takes away our jobs, our art and our science than what is there left for us to do better at exactly? They are not saving us, artificial intelligence is rendering human life as irrelevant.
conclusionOpponent: Even if we are losing the human touch we have the opportunity to develop new technologies and new techniques through our integration with AI. AI writing resumes means that the resumes will be more concise and uniform which will make it easier for people who aren't skilled at writing resumes. The personality and individuality of resumes can be a bad thing for many individuals. Humans who lose out on these positions will acquire new ones as a matter of course or they will advocate for government reforms so that they are supported in any case. We will have more opportunities to engage with one another because we will work less and expend less energy due to the aid of artificial intelligence.
