topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: I think colleges should strive to be a place where students of every background want to study. It doesn't look good if a school has to impose certain racial quotas in order to have a diverse student body. It also isn't necessary to have a perfectly diverse student body - the student body often just reflects the makeup of the town/city/state. If colleges work on the quality of their education, students from all backgrounds will want to join.
rebuttal: If our society is naturally diverse, it doesn't need colleges to create diverse learning environments. It's also not the role of colleges to counterbalance socioeconomic discrepancies between racial groups - they aren't going to be very effective at doing that because most of the people from the disadvantaged social groups don't attend the colleges that do this sort of thing (usually very elite colleges).
conclusion: Colleges don't really change the racial diversity of the world - they can only attract people from different racial groups. You can't credit colleges that consider race in their admissions process for fostering a diverse learning environment. They should be doing that regardless of whether they consider race when admitting a student or not. Race is also not the only aspect that makes a group of students diverse or pluralistic. It's certainly not a crucial aspect.
argumentOpponent: Colleges should consider race in admissions to foster learning environments reflective of our diverse society and to counterbalance historic and socio-economic disadvantages that certain racial groups have encountered. A diverse student body initiates a breadth of perspectives, fostering critical thinking and challenging biases.
rebuttalOpponent: While educational quality is crucial, it shouldn't outshine the need for a varied student body, as diverse perspectives enrich learning experiences and prepare students for a pluralistic world. Also, reflecting the local demographic can reinforce existing inequalities, hence race-conscious admissions serve as a tool to challenge these systemic barriers.
conclusionOpponent: Colleges have an explicit role in shaping society and can address diversity issues by considering race in admission processes. Ensuring representation at all levels, not merely elite institutions, contributes to a more equitable system, allowing for broader and richer academic discourse, and fostering leaders from varied backgrounds.

topic: Should the Death Penalty Be Legal?
argument: The death penalty should not be legal because we are humans, not animals. The death penalty could be extremely cruel, as methods such as the electric chair still exist and are used. For crimes such as murder, jail for life is just about as worst of a punishment as you can get.
rebuttal: The death penalty should be legal because for people who have commited vicious crimes, such as serial murder, there is no point in keeping them in a jail-like setting just taking up food and space. These people will be in jail for life regardless.
conclusion: In conclusion, the death penalty should be illegal because it is inhumane. Sure, it might ensure justice where it's needed, but so will life in jail.
argumentOpponent: The death penalty serves as an effective deterrent against severe crimes, protecting society by permanently removing the most dangerous individuals who threaten public safety and peace. Moreover, it guarantees that the worst perpetrators of atrocities cannot re-offend, providing justice for victims' families and ensuring the ultimate punishment for the gravest actions.
rebuttalOpponent: While the methods of execution merit careful reconsideration, the fundamental principle of the death penalty is not simply about cruelty, but about ensuring justice where it's most needed. Life imprisonment, though severe, lacks the finality and retributive value that the death penalty offers for the most egregious crimes, hence fails to fully satisfy the thirst for justice and closure among traumatized victims' families.
conclusionOpponent: Indeed, apart from being a just retribution for heinous crimes, the death penalty also alleviates the economic burden of lifetime incarceration, freeing up resources for other important areas like education or healthcare. Ultimately, it's about delivering the most appropriate justice, proportionate to the monstrosity of the crime committed, reaffirming society's disapproval of such acts, and preventing repeat offenders.

topic: Should the Rich Pay More Taxes?
argument: The rich should pay more taxes because they are able to afford losing more of their income without a substantial impact on their lifestyle. Currently, there are billionaires who pay less taxes than the average citizen, which is very unjust. The wealth in this country is broken down so that the top 1% population own the majority of wealth. With higher taxes, this gross disproportion will be more fairly distributed. All the while, the ultra-wealthy will still be able to enjoy the same lifestyle. This logically makes much more sense than applying higher taxes to the average person, who may be just scrapping by to pay their loans, even though they are working very hard. A successful government is one that can make things equitable, and this is the start of that.
rebuttal: Economic growth an innovation will always be driven by hunger for more success and wealth. Increasing taxes by a small percentage will not cause any significant impact to those who are ultra wealthy; and they will not give up their drive and motivation towards success just because they are taxed a few percent more than usual. Additionally, tax evasion is conducted by all classes. There are many examples, such as Jeff Bezos who pays less tax than the average American. Other examples include those ultra wealthy individuals who store their funds off shore to evade taxes.
conclusion: History has shown that when companies have funds, they will use the majority of those funds for their own benefit rather to invest in job creation. A great example of this is in the healthcare system. While many hospital CEOS make tens of millions of dollars, the hospital system itself struggles as there are not enough staff such as nurses. This is why many jobs can created a union. Ultimately, we should not rely on companies to determine how wealth should be distributed because they will only drop pennies. That is why the rich should be taxed slightly more.
argumentOpponent: Elevating tax rates for the wealthy doesn't guarantee fair distribution of wealth, but rather jeopardizes economic growth and innovation by disincentivizing success. Instead, improving the efficiency of existing tax systems should be prioritized to reduce evasion, ensuring everyone is paying their fair share.
rebuttalOpponent: Higher taxation on the rich may reduce their incentive to innovate and invest, which drives job creation and economic stimulation; it's not about affording taxes but the impact on the economic environment. The focus should be on improving tax code efficiency to ensure fair contribution, not a disproportionate burden on the wealthy.
conclusionOpponent: Taxation should encourage wealth creation, not penalize it; higher taxes potentially reduce drive for success, impact job creation and economic health. Rather than increasingly taxing the rich, let's focus on reforms to eliminate tax loop-holes and offshore banking practices, ensuring that everyone, irrespective of their wealth, contributes fairly to society.

topic: Should the US Keep Using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections?
argument:
One of the hallmarks of a democracy is that all individuals have an even vote, and the majority wins. However, with the electoral college, there is the opportunity for the minority candidate to get elected, whereby the candidate who actually received the most votes, or the majority, actually loses the contest.  This should not be what the U.S. 'democracy' allows.

This possibility actually depresses voter turnout. If a red voter resides in a predominantly blue state, he/she may feel that there is no need for his/her vote as the outcome will already be decided. 

One man (woman)/ one vote is upon what our society should be based.
rebuttal: This concept, like many others, is an outdated ideology. The concept of 'tyranny of the majority' may have worked 1789, but certainly is not applicable today. \n\nThe only way to achieve a true 'fair and representative democracy' is to allow the whole population to be equally represented in all votes, with a true majority prevailing.
conclusion: Federalism is the division and sharing of power between the national and state governments. That system allows both the federal and state governments the ability to determine, apply, and enforce their own rules of law.\n\nThat concept stops, however, at voting rights. If the U.S. wants to claim itself to be a true democracy, then the 'one person, one vote' principle must be equally applied to all votes, elections, and citizens. The true majority must always prevail.
argumentOpponent: The Electoral College system, as established by the Founders, balances representation, prevents tyranny of the majority, and supports our federalist structure, fostering a fair and representative democracy.
rebuttalOpponent: While the 'one person, one vote' principle is critical, the Electoral College ensures all states, regardless of size or population, have a say in national elections, thereby upholding federalism. Furthermore, it encourages coalition building and national campaigns, strengthening our unity as a nation.
conclusionOpponent: While 'tyranny of the majority' may seem outdated, it serves as a safeguard against dominant urban areas dictating the outcome for the entire nation. By giving all states, large and small, a balanced voice, the Electoral College upholds the principles of federalism and fosters balanced national policies.

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument: Have you ever seen Game of Thrones? If you haven't, there's basically 500 internal family arguments and battles going on as well as 1000 battles between other families that own different parts of the country. However, at some point during all these battles, monsters start walking down from very north of the country. And all the families need to pause all their battles so they can defeat these monsters. Or else the world will end and there will be no more battles to even be had.\n\nThis is how I see climate change. If the entire world does not get on board with figuring this out, any problem that may seem bigger or more dire will be null. Since there will be no more world left. So unless international agreements to enforce global climate change policies occur, then any other problem that seems more important literally will not matter. Simply due to the fact that the world as we know it will be changed immensely or just simply cease to exist. Let's stop our battles and fight this monster together. Then, we can go back to our interfamilial issues. Maybe see therapy at that point..?
rebuttal: This is not a voluntary issue. This is an issue of either we all get on the same page and change our bad habits or the world as we know it will be gone. If even one county decides to "opt-out," that could be the difference between our oceans rising above Miami or the glaciers in Antarctica melting. This is not optional. This is life or death. This is the difference between our grandkids having a home like we had.
conclusion: Climate change is dire. As a world, we needed to be on the same page yesterday. This is not an optional issue. Climate change is not the same as choosing if you want ketchup on your hot dog or not. There will be no geopolitical tension in a world where are forests are burning, glaciers are melting, and sea levels are rising above our coastal cities. Furthermore, why are we protecting the top 1% of the 1% of the 1% in stopping harmful emissions and pollution from occurring? Those people are greedy and only have it out for themselves. As a society, world, as literally just people on Earth--we need to act now. We need all countries to get in a room and figure out something that works. I am not saying it will be easy, but I am saying it needs to happen.
argumentOpponent: International agreements on climate change impede national sovereignty and may impose economic burdens on developing countries striving for growth. It's more effective to promote voluntary individual nation efforts rather than impose a one-size-fits-all global policy.
rebuttalOpponent: While climate change is indeed a crucial issue, involuntary international agreements are not akin to uniting against a common enemy; they can lead to geopolitical tension and exacerbate economic disparities. We should advocate for self-governed environmental responsibility, promoting technology and education rather than enforcing global mandates.
conclusionOpponent: While it's true that timely action is needed, imposing climate policies through international agreements may result in uncooperative nations and consequent strife; instead, an international push towards sustainable technology and model adaptation strategies would encourage nations to imbibe changes willingly. After all, true change is voluntary, not enforced.

rebuttalOpponent: While understanding our place in the universe is intriguing, this knowledge isn't as critical or urgent as addressing our earthly challenges. conclusionOpponent: While space studies have given insights such as ozone layer depletion, we can monitor these from Earth or with satellites, not requiring as costly explorations. I believe that imposing further regulations could discourage voters from participating in the election process, leading to a loss of trust in the system. There are already systems put in place to ensure fair elections.
rebuttal: Creating further regulations to ensure fair elections will only cause harm, leading voters to doubt the system and lose faith in the government. There are rules and systems in place to prevent unfairness.
conclusion: This is a complex and controversial question that does not have a simple answer. Different people may have different opinions on what constitutes fair elections and what regulations are necessary or desirable to achieve them. \n\n
argumentOpponent: The bedrock of any thriving democracy is fair and transparent elections. Therefore, it's crucial for the US to enact more regulations not just to ensure such fairness but also to increase accessibility, prevent voter suppression and restore public trust in the electoral system.\n
rebuttalOpponent: While respecting the existing systems, we can't overlook the systemic issues they fail to address including voter suppression and unequal access to voting. More tailored regulations can enhance voter participation, not discourage it, by making the electoral process more accessible, transparent and equitable.
conclusionOpponent: The aim here isn't to undermine existing systems but to refine them, acknowledging that there's room for improvement to increase accessibility and equality. With more robust regulations, we can address current loopholes, restore faith in our democracy and ensure every citizen's vote truly counts.

argument: The US should abolish the electoral college, as it is an outdated system that gives rural counties way too much power. I believe that it should definitely be abolished and replaced with popular vote or another more accurate system.
rebuttal: This is an outdated and factually incorrect statement. The electoral college has been proven to give an extremely unfair advantage to rural counties, and not urban areas, making it disproportionately difficult for a vote to matter in a state that does not align with typical politics in that state to matter.
conclusion: This is false, opposition against shifting to popular vote is unfounded and not rooted in fact. Popular vote is clearly the better option and has been proven time and time again.
argumentOpponent: The Electoral College ensures that all states, regardless of population size, hold a vital stake in the nation's overall decision-making process, thus preserving balance and fairness in our democratic system. It prevents candidates from winning purely based on populous urban areas, compelling them to address diverse regional concerns.
rebuttalOpponent: While it may seem as though the Electoral College gives undue weight to rural areas, it actually ensures that all regions of the U.S. have a meaningful voice, preventing urban majorities from dictating national policies. A shift to popular vote risks excluding the unique needs and livelihoods of lesser-populated regions from consideration.
conclusionOpponent: Maintaining the Electoral College necessitates candidates to consider not only large urban concentrations but also smaller rural populations, thereby ensuring national policies reflect the diverse interests of the entire country. While the system indeed has its challenges, they can be addressed via reforms without radical dismantlement, reinforcing our American principle - E Pluribus Unum (Out of Many, One).

topic: Should There Be Limits on Freedom of Speech to Prevent Hate Speech?

conclusion: That is true, but there are times when it's required because the cons outweigh the benefits. We need to tread carefully with allowing any type of speech, because we can control it when it gets out of hand.

topic: Is Online Learning a Suitable Replacement for Traditional In-Person Education?
argument: In the modern age, online learning can be a suitable replacement for in-person education. Technology has advanced to where online learning can suit many different learning styles with different uses of text, audio, and interactive learning. Online learning is also an important accommodation for those who may not be able to leave their homes, such as disabled or immunity compromised individuals. With the ability for teachers to be on video calls or chats with their students, they are able to interact just as much as they would in an in-person setting, but from the convenience of home. Students may also feel more relaxed and attentive when they are in their own individual environments, free from distractions. With all the tools we have with technology today, online learning measures up to in-person learning.
rebuttal: Online learning can use video calls and chats as a means of social interaction, which, in a learning setting, will measure up just as well as in-person learning does. They can also implement interactive learning and assign things to print out to fulfill the hands-on aspect.
conclusion: Online learning fills a very important role in today's society for those who cannot attend traditional learning, such at those who are disabled or who have compromised immunity. With various tools such as text, video, and interactive learning, online learning can create an experience equal to that of in-person learning. Just as one might not have the tools for online education, they also may be unable to afford school supplies or commuting costs, in which case online education could be a more viable option.
argumentOpponent: While online learning provides flexibility and accessibility, it fails to replicate the nuanced social interaction and hands-on experience essential to holistic learning, which traditional in-person education offers.
rebuttalOpponent: Despite technological advancements, online learning cannot simulate the comprehensive classroom environment that builds essential interpersonal skills, nor can it provide the immediate, tailored feedback that in-person teachers offer. Moreover, not all students have equal access to the necessary tools for online education, exacerbating educational inequality.
conclusionOpponent: Video calls and chats don't fully replicate the spontaneous interpersonal dynamics of a physical classroom, while printing materials ignores the digital divide issue. More importantly, online learning lacks the accountability, motivation and structure that traditional settings inherently provide, making it a less suitable overall replacement.

topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: The U.S. should ban fossil fuels to combat climate change because it's those fuels that are having a negative impact on global warming and on the environment. If we can eliminated those fuels detrimental to the environment, then the downward spiral toward the most harmful effects of climate change may be slowed. Researchers should find more economical and cleaner ways for consumers to be able to fuel cars and access energy without the harmful and negative effects on the environment. Clean buy-in across the board would be challenging,
conclusion: Yes, damage has been done, but to choose to do nothing at this stage of the game, would be irresponsible, nit just for us, but for the generations that follow. The U.S. government may be slow, but eventually makes monumental decisions for the good of the people, usually at the insistence of the people. It's not too late to enact policies and pressures now.

topic: Should the Rich Pay More Taxes?
argument: Wealthy individuals in the United States should not have to pay more taxes than the already do. The economy relies on individuals spending their money; therefore, wealthy individuals spend more, and become a more critical contributor to society and our economy as it functions today. Taking away more of their money and giving it to the governments would keep the money out of the hands of small business owners and the rich's community, which would be detrimental for business owners and their employees. Examples of this trickle down economics theory have been proven to work, as seen in the 80s during Ronald Reagan's era of "trickle down economics:". S If we want the American economy to thrive, we should keep the money in the hands of the people, and that includes the rich.
rebuttal: The opposition claims that taxing the rich will fund crucial public services. We are currently in an era where the US government is trillions of dollars in debt; we as a government are spending more money than we ever have, yet we continue to see social programs suffer. The extra money from the rich has been proven to go anywhere but public services; instead, we have bloated police budgets and presidents that are taking longer vacations than the average American citizen. The government does not need more of any of our money, including the rich. Keeping money in the hands of the people gives them power over where it goes, and allows them to choose wh
conclusion: Taxing the rich additional money will not fund public services the way my opponent claims; we can see time and time again that the money goes to the military, government wages, and the police, not the public services we care so much about. If we want to fund these services, or make an actual difference in the community, keep the money in the hands of the people; mutual aid within one's own community has proven to be far more effective than trusting our government to do anything good with it ever has.
argumentOpponent: Taxing the rich at higher rates benefits society as a whole by promoting income equality and funding crucial public services that are often underfunded due to tax cuts for the wealthy. Progressive taxation aligns with democratic values, empowering all members of society.
rebuttalOpponent: While there's merit in the incentive to spend provided by wealth, trickle-down economics often disproportionately benefits the already wealthy without ensuring meaningful growth at lower income levels. Hiking taxes on the rich would not remove their ability to contribute to the economy, but instead allow redistribution of capital for underfunded public services and infrastructure, fostering a more balanced community growth.
conclusionOpponent: Though government spending and handful of misplaced fiscal priorities are concerning, they underscore the need for a more balanced wealth distribution, rather than arguing against it. A progressive tax system can help fund crucial services effectively, given the implementation of robust fiscal oversight and transparency, contributing to a more equitable, inclusive society.

argumentOpponent: While space exploration may seem fascinating and potentially lucrative, it diverts significant resources away from urgent terrestrial concerns such as poverty, infrastructure and education. rebuttalOpponent: While it's true that some innovation has followed space exploration, not all return on investment is equitable; the costly nature of space research could instead find more immediate, tangible impacts if allocated to pressing issues on Earth, like healthcare, education and environmental preservation. conclusionOpponent: While space exploration has led to some technological advancements, it's not the only or necessarily the most efficient method for fostering innovation; concentrating on terrestrial issues can likewise lead to significant technological progress, with the added benefit of immediate utilization towards improving life on Earth. argumentOpponent: Global climate change policies should be determined by individual nations based on their unique environmental realities and development needs, not enforced through international agreements that may prioritize uniformity over effectiveness and fairness. rebuttalOpponent: While global warming is indeed an urgent issue, the accountability of adhering to strict rules enforced by international agreements might not necessarily fit the unique environmental and economic context of each country. conclusionOpponent: International agreements, while well-intentioned, may overlook the unique challenges and resources of individual nations. topic: Should There Be Limits on Freedom of Speech to Prevent Hate Speech?
argument:
Hate speech harms everyone by fomenting violence. There should be limits to use of certain platforms, such as university campuses, for speech that incites or encourages violence against particular groups of people. 

So called "canceling" is what I'm suggesting, and it does not really limit anyone's freedom of speech. Freedom of speech isn't the same as the right to a platform.

However, it is important to safeguard freedom of speech, especially because limits on speech can be weaponized, as in anti-anti-Semitism.
rebuttal: This is an important point, and yet calling for violence against people should not be allowed. Certain kinds of speech, such as Holocaust denial or "Trump won in 2020," are not receptive to logical argumentation, so they don't actually promote dialogue or democracy.
conclusion: In a sense it's an impossible choice between free speech and human rights. If I have to err, I would rather err on the side of protecting vulnerable populations and a fragile civic peace.
argumentOpponent: Freedom of speech, however challenging it may be, allows for diverse thoughts and dialogue crucial for the progress of democratic society; placing limits to ward off hate speech risks attenuating the essence of democracy.
rebuttalOpponent: Defining 'hate speech' becomes problematic due to individual subjectivity; this scalable notion can create a slippery slope ending with undue censorship, hence eroding the democratic exchange of ideas. While I agree that there’s no absolute right to a platform, disallowing certain speeches might inadvertently stifle the development of critical thought and debate, and be utilized as a political weapon against unpopular perspectives.
conclusionOpponent: Indeed, calling for violence should not be condoned, but we must remember that any form of speech can impact diverse individuals differently; by forbidding even unpalatable expressions, we could inadvertently disempower marginalized voices. A democratic society requires its citizens to critically engage with all types of ideas, nurturing resilience and understanding even in the face of misinformation or offensive speech.

topic: Should There Be Limits on Freedom of Speech to Prevent Hate Speech?
argument: Reduction in Hate Crimes: Evidence suggests a correlation between hate speech and an increase in hate crimes. For example, countries like Germany have strict laws against hate speech, especially related to Holocaust denial, and have observed lower rates of hate crimes compared to nations with less regulation. By limiting hate speech, potential instigators are less likely to incite or encourage acts of violence against marginalized groups.\n\nSocial Harmony: Countries like Canada and Sweden, which enforce laws against hate speech, tend to have higher social cohesion and inclusivity. These laws discourage public expressions of bigotry, promoting a more respectful public discourse. This helps in creating an environment where all individuals, regardless of their background, feel safe and valued, contributing to overall societal stability and harmony.
rebuttal:
Your concern about unrestricted freedom of speech leading to censorship and a loss of personal liberty is valid and important in preserving democratic values. However, it's essential to differentiate between free speech and speech that can cause direct harm, such as inciting violence or discrimination. Historical examples, like the incitement of violence in Rwanda or Nazi Germany, show the dangerous potential of unchecked hate speech.

The aim isn't to police thoughts or general opinions but to prevent speech that actively promotes harm to others. It's not about limiting freedom of expression, but about ensuring it's not used to infringe on the safety and rights of others. This approach seeks a balance, where people are free to express their opinions, yet held accountable when their speech directly threatens the well-being of others.

In essence, it’s about harmonizing the right to speak freely with the responsibility to respect the rights and safety of others, ensuring a society where freedom of speech is valued but not exploited to cause harm
conclusion: Freedom of speech is indeed a cornerstone of democracy, but it's not absolute and must be balanced with the responsibility to not harm others. It's not just about sensitivity; hate speech can lead to real-life consequences like violence and discrimination, affecting entire communities. Seeing a therapist is not a solution to systemic issues perpetuated by harmful rhetoric. Instead, empowering individuals to speak responsibly contributes to a society that values both free expression and mutual respect.

topic: Should There Be Limits on Freedom of Speech to Prevent Hate Speech?
argument: There should be limits put into place on the freedom of speech in order to protect vulnerable populations from the negative and dangerous consequences of hate speech. Although the freedom of speech is protect in the U.S., this is meant to protect individuals from being censored by the government--that freedom is revoked when individuals use their speech to target, demean, and endanger others. Just as individuals have the right to own guns but are not exempt from the consequences of malicious actions they take with those guns (e.g. it is a crime to shoot someone), individuals are not exempt from the consequences of malicious statements they make. Hate speech can lead to malicious actions being taken, and therefore should be prevented, as a means of protecting vulnerable populations. It is the government's responsibility to ensure the protection of its citizens, and therefore it is the government's responsibility to ensure that its citizens are not targeted or discriminated against.
rebuttal: It is a slippery slope argument to say that limiting speech will lead to censorship. Freedom of speech is specifically to protect citizens from censorship by the government, yes, but hate speech is directed between citizens--not between citizens and the government. Citizens have the right to criticize their government--and this right ought to be protected--but they do not have the right to infringe on the safety of other citizens. Each individual has the right to be safe, and hate speech infringes on that safety. Therefore, limiting hate speech does not actually limit freedom of speech.
conclusion: Although speech itself does not harm individuals in the same way as physical violence, it can a) have lasting, negative emotional and/or mental impacts and b) can lead to physical violence. It is true that defining hate speech is extremely subjective--it may be difficult to purely prevent it, but as it is a factor in endangering individuals, it should still have consequences to discourage people from threatening and targeting others.
argumentOpponent: While hate speech can be deeply troubling, placing limits on freedom of speech sets a potentially dangerous precedent for the suppression of diverse ideas and can pave the way for censorship. Considering the foundational role of free speech in fostering societal progression and open dialogue, we must critically assess the ramifications of stifling this cornerstone of democracy.
rebuttalOpponent: While the intention to protect vulnerable individuals from harm is noble, criminalizing speech is slippery because who gets to define what constitutes hate speech is subjective, often dependent on the bias of those in power. Furthermore, equating speech with physical harm like gun violence oversimplifies the issue - unlike the latter, the impact of words often depend on interpretation, and creating subjective legal boundaries may inadvertently curb dialogues that challenge status quos for societal improvement.
conclusionOpponent: Limiting hate speech is indeed a limitation on freedom of speech as it curtails citizens' ability to express their thoughts, however harmful they may be to some; it's crucial to differentiate between emotional harm and actual infringement on individuals' safety. We can better address hate speech by promoting inclusive education and encouraging tolerant discourse, as the remedy to bad speech is not less speech, but more and better speech.

topic: Is Online Learning a Suitable Replacement for Traditional In-Person Education?
argument: There are many reasons that online learning is not a suitable replacement for traditional in-person education. The first and probably most important reason being socializing our children. In-person schooling is for much more than just learning basic skills like math and science, it is for learning how to interact with others. We learn to interact with our peers and make friends, we learn how to interact with authority figures in our teachers, and we learn to interact with students in different age groups than your own. As long as life requires us to have interactions in real life, and not just over the internet, in-person schooling will always be important because of the social factors. Another reason in-person school is better than online is because of the rise of cheating with tools like AI. Cheating is much more difficult to do in the classroom with a teacher right there with you than at your own home on your own computer. Obviously it can still happen, but it is certainly less likely to happen.
rebuttal: There are some strong points here, and I agree that more access to education for all is a pro of online learning. That being said there are still going to be financial constraints, as you need a device capable of accessing the internet to have access to online learning, and I think it could be debated that this is a higher financial constraint than going to in-person school. The idea of learning at your own pace sounds good, and it can be good, but for many children their own pace is just not learning at all. Many people need that slight push of being in school to learn things, if you are at home and your Xbox is sitting right beside you it is much more difficult for some people to motivate themselves to schooling, but in the classroom you have less distractions.
conclusion: Sure, digital citizenship is kind of important I guess, but I still don't believe hardly anyone would argue that being a digital citizen is a more important skill currently than have in-person social skills. You can be a digital citizen when you get home from school or on the weekends easily, but it is much harder to get many peers and a teacher in one place for classes and learning at those same times. As for academic integrity, I have taken online classes that require things like locked browsers and webcams on, and these are obviously decent measures against cheating, but still much easier to beat than an actual teacher in a classroom, and you can't possibly expect people to have all of these anti cheating measures enabled for every single assignment and learning session.
argumentOpponent: Online learning provides equal access to quality education for all, regardless of geographical or financial constraints, promoting the democratization of knowledge. It also empowers individuals to learn at their own pace, leading to more thorough comprehension and retention.
rebuttalOpponent: While in-person education fosters social interaction, online learning encourages digital citizenship, a crucial skill in today's interconnected world. As for academic integrity, technology can also be employed to monitor and prevent cheating, making online learning just as reliable.
conclusionOpponent: While access to the internet does require financial investments, many organizations offer affordable devices and connectivity options, and it's undoubtedly less burdensome than commuting or relocating for school. Although distractions exist, the onus is on us to harness technology's potential, cultivate discipline, and transform these distractions into learning opportunities - a skill that's valuable beyond the classroom.

topic: Should the US Have Mandatory National Service?
argument:
Mandatory National Service simply infringes on the freedom of the citizen to live life as they please. The United States was founded on the principles of individual liberty and choice, not forcing citizens into choices. Mandatory Service would do just that, violating our national values.

Plus, not everyone is even suited well for national service. Having a massive conscript army means little if the conscripts are ill-trained, non-motivated, or otherwise physically disabled. This actually weakens our army rather than strengthening it. Those who volunteer (have the drive to do service) and who pass physical exams are exemplars of our armies, and mandatory service would pollute their ranks. 

Finally, taking young potential workers out of the economy to do mandatory service will hurt our economic growth, especially given our aging population. We need as many young workers as we can get to contribute, not national servicepeople.
rebuttal: There are other ways to unite a country besides infringement on personal liberty. Indeed, the militaristic environment may foster the wrong sort of connections that we need for a civilian population. After all, in the military, it is 'us vs. them', not a great mindset for civilian life.\n\nVolunteering, community organizations, and education can address the needs to unite people around common causes. They are voluntary, so not infringing on personal liberty, and don't require young workers to be removed from the economy to do military service. So, there are better alternatives.
conclusion:
Personal liberty still is infringed by this program. People should decide for themselves how they can best contribute to society, not being forced into it by a government. Only when people have free choice can we have true unity. In a society that values individual freedom and diverse career paths, there are alternative ways to achieve the stated goals without resorting to mandatory national service.

Furthermore, the argument that national service contributes to economic health by furnishing diverse sectors with valuable human resources must be scrutinized. Voluntary initiatives and education can better prepare individuals for various fields without the need for coercion, allowing for a more organic and motivated contribution to national development.

In conclusion, the promotion of freedom, choice, and individual agency remains paramount in building a robust and flourishing society, NOT a mandatory national service.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory national service allows individuals to develop key personal skills and plays an instrumental role in uniting a diverse country like the United States around a common cause. This not only fosters a stronger society but also creates a sense of responsibility and a greater understanding of our nation’s needs, which is highly beneficial especially for young adults making their way into the world.
rebuttalOpponent: Mandatory national service does not infringe on freedom but widens perspective, promotes growth, and equips individuals with valuable life skills, crucial for young adults amidst today's challenges. Yes, not all may be physically able or motivated, but let's remember national service is not solely military - it encompasses a broad spectrum from teaching to environmental protection, and such a system will balance economic health by furnishing diverse sectors with valuable human resources eager to contribute to national development.
conclusionOpponent: Mandatory national service, far from infringing on liberty, broadens horizons, and cultivates a deeper understanding of civic duty. The intent here is to create a national fabric woven with threads of service, fostering camaraderie, empathy, and unity, making every citizen a vital part of a greater communal effort that transcends the battlefield and expands to every sector of society, enhancing both individual and national growth.

topic: Should Colleges Consider Race as a Factor in Admissions to Ensure Diversity?
argument: Colleges should consider race as a factor in admissions due to the history of racial bias in our country. Issues such as redlining have made it so that black Americans do not have the same advantages as their white peers. Considering race in admissions would assure that other races have an opportunity for education and success in life, which is something they otherwise may not have had.
rebuttal: This argument does not take reality into consideration. It would be best for candidates to be chosen on merit alone, but that it just not something that can happen. Decades of racial inequality in society has resulted in certain races having more access to resources an education, which is something that does not have anything to do with merit.
conclusion: Wouldn't ensuring racial diversity in universities be considered providing resources to disadvantaged communities? Minorities have been disadvantaged from the start, which makes it difficult to understand how merit-based admissions would be considered fair. Acknowledging biases does not mean perpetuating them.
argumentOpponent: College admissions should be based on merit alone, ensuring equal opportunities for all, regardless of race or ethnic background. The true mark of diversity lies in sharing different ideas and perspectives, not just different colors.
rebuttalOpponent: While addressing historical biases is important, college admission should not perpetuate new biases by favoring certain races. Instead, we should focus on providing resources and equal opportunities to disadvantaged communities without compromising on merit-based admissions.
conclusionOpponent: While the effects of historical inequalities are profound, considering race in admissions would not level the playing field but merely reproduce inequality in a different form. It is therefore crucial we address the root causes such as unequal access to quality education and resources, maintaining the integrity of merit-based admissions.

topic: Should Elected or Appointed Government Officials Be Paid the Minimum Wage?
argument: Elected or appointed government officials should not be paid the minimum wage because the quality and effort of work that they conduct far exceeds that of a minimum wage worker. For example, a minimum wage employee is one that, for the most part, lacks a degree. Think of a fast food employee. A fast food employee can be someone that is the minimum age of employment (15 or 16 for most states) and will most likely be washing dishes, a cashier, or a janitor of sorts. The effort and power they hold for a 15 or 16 year old is equivalent to their compensation. However, a government official has far more experience and weight in their job title. As such, their compensation should also match the significance of their responsibilities.
rebuttal: Although I understand your side of the argument, that government officials do need to empathize more with the population, it doesn't make sense to make monetary compensation the deciding factor. Instead, it would make more sense to appoint government officials that already display an ability empathize and make "fiscally responsible decisions." As you mentioned, we are part of a democratic government, so it's the people that vote and elect these officials. If we want more people in government to have more empathy, we vote those people in based on their personal experiences. Minimum wage should not be the factor that makes these people more likable and responsible.
conclusion: Demonstration of solidarity with citizens should have already been a factor that was taken into account when electing/appointing the government in the first place. We can't expect people to change their entire perspective by paying them less, as if that will teach someone who is already set in their opinions a "lesson."
argumentOpponent: Though not without challenges, paying elected or appointed government officials the minimum wage could help them empathize more with the population, and make fiscally responsible decisions based on personal experience, fostering a more democratic and socially responsible government.
rebuttalOpponent: While it’s true that government officials carry additional responsibility, compensation should not only reflect job complexity but also demonstrate solidarity with citizens. By accepting the minimum wage, officials would be more motivated to improve those very same wages they are earning, benefiting a broader society.
conclusionOpponent: Empathy might indeed be a trait to look for when voting, yet socioeconomic privilege often disconnects our elected officials from such realities; therefore, experiencing minimum wage may bridge this gap. Furthermore, this could motivate officials to work for an economy where minimum wage ensures a dignified living, reflecting a truly democratic ethos.

topic: Should the US Expand (“pack”) the Supreme Court?
argument: "Packing the court" leads to a much more balanced court. It presents an opportunity for more fairness. With the court packed, it is less likely to be imbalanced. It is also a constitutionally protected activity to pack the court.
rebuttal: Packing the court is constitutionally protected. It doesn't undermine checks and balances because it is already allowed. If it is a protected activity, then it should be used however it can be.
conclusion: It doesn't have to be beneficial or ethical. It's protected. It offers more balance. It would still be an independent body. The law is the law, thus packing is protected by it.
argumentOpponent: Packing the Supreme Court jeopardizes judicial independence and undermines the system of checks and balances, which sets a dangerous precedent for future administrations to manipulate the court for political gain. Altering the Court's structure for partisan advantage undermines its credibility and stature.
rebuttalOpponent: Though 'packing' may seem to offer balance, it bears the risk of turning the Supreme Court into a political tool, dictated by whoever is in power, rather than an independent body focused on upholding constitutional law. Constitutionally allowed does not necessarily mean it's beneficial or ethical.
conclusionOpponent: While constitutionally there may be no prohibition against court packing, it remains a grave threat to the integrity and independence of the judiciary, potentially turning it into a political football. Rather than resort to court packing, we should focus on measures that improve the transparency and rigor of the judicial nomination process to ensure the Supreme Court's role as an unbiased interpreter of the Constitution.

topic: Should the US Have Mandatory National Service?
argument: The United States should not have mandatory national service for three main reasons. One of the main reasons that the United States should not have this is because it is not fair to people with disabilities or unique needs. Another main reason is that this gives the United States too much power over people and it is against national freedom. Finally, this is inefficient and will prevent people from working at jobs or tasks that they are more skilled at. \n\nI will explain each of these points in more detail in the future. These points will explain why the United States should not have mandatory national service. After reading these points in full, it will be clear why my side is correct.
rebuttal: The points that you state are not correct. I will explain why. First, the points about unity and patriotism are not right because people will not like a country that forces them to serve. Making people do service will push them apart and make them dislike the United States. Also, people should be able to choose the type of work that they are good at. They will not develop more skills if the United States forces them to serve. \n\nFinally, your point about shared understanding is not right because people can volunteer or do other activities in order to help democracy. Forcing people to serve is the opposite of a free democracy and thus it cannot teach people about democracy.
conclusion: I don't think that you really understand the points that I made. Even if we make accommodations, there will not be certainty that these accommodations will truly fit the unique needs of all people. Look at the government's track record in really honoring the needs of all Americans in the past. Does this make you think that they can really accommodate all in forced service?\n\nAnd yes, forced service does overrule freedom. Forcing a person to do work for a certain amount of time (years? days? months? how long?) is one of the most controlling ways that the state can interfere in a person's life and day-to-day situation.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory national service can foster unity, responsibility, and patriotism among citizens, while also providing valuable skills and experiences that benefit both the individual and society as a whole. Additionally, it would create a shared understanding of the sacrifices required for a functioning democracy.
rebuttalOpponent: Mandatory national service does not imply a one-size-fits-all approach; accommodations can be made for those with unique needs ensuring inclusivity. Furthermore, such a service is not a reflection of state power overruling freedom, but rather an obligation to promote civic responsibility and collective growth, while variations in tasks within the service can cater to individual's skills to maintain efficiency.
conclusionOpponent: Contrary to fostering resentment, shared national service facilitates understanding and cooperation among diverse citizens; compelled service may initially seem imposing, but it provides an equitable platform for personal growth. Moreover, democracy thrives not just on freedoms, but on the responsibilities individuals shoulder for its collective good, and national service aims at instilling this sense of duty.

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument: Global warming isn't called "regional", "local", or "national" warming - it's global because it is an international issue that affects everyone on the planet. Because of this, irregularities among laws where some countries may be contributing significantly to global warming while others are doing their best to combat it, creates a bit of a "one step forward, two steps back" stalemate that leads to regression. We should work together to solve problems that impact us together. This isn't to say that countries who might not be able to abide by certain guidelines should face struggles, but rather, that other countries should ensure they can and provide aid where necessary. As a whole, the world is a community, and the ideas of nations and borders is outdated, impractical, and just overall quite silly.
rebuttal: The start of your argument is based on an assumption, but it holds no guaranteed truth and isn't supported by any facts. Why would international policies be surface level, but other policies wouldn't? What if, instead of assuming the worst, you assume the best, and we say "Any policies agreed upon on an international level will be highly effective"? Such a statement could be just as easily said. The idea isn't to compare country A to country B and think who benefits more, it's to prevent global catastrophe that will impact everyone on this planet. The individual technology, economics, and conditions should be accounted for only in regards to ensuring everyone can implement equally, even if that means other countries helping, because it all works towards the same goal.
conclusion: The question of if the US and China are colluding to contribute to global warming is irrelevant because it doesn't matter if they are: both countries are contributing to global warming. And, yes, in part by trading with each other and creating producer and consumer relations, they are in effect colluding because corporations internationally prioritize profit over environmental safety. The idea that everyone is looking out for themselves only is exactly the problem and can be applied to any statement, but things would never get better at all then, we'd just be extremist anarchists with no regard for anyone or anything else. We are a society and always have been and that's what makes humanity flourish.
argumentOpponent: Any policies agreed upon on an international level will be surface level and thus be highly ineffective. While it is nice in theory, the fact is that countries will use this as a means to get advantage of others economically, technologically, and others. To what benefit do you believe international policy will affect us? Will a shared policy between the United States and South Africa benefit both countries equally? It is better to establish policies on a country by country basis, taking into account individual technology, economics, and conditions. Specific measures lead to specific benefits. The need to address climate change is real and necessary and we must take effective action quickly. That can NOT be done on an international level. That MUST be done on a domestic level.
rebuttalOpponent: Global warming is an international issue, but are countries affecting global warming in an international effort? Is the United States colluding with China to contribute to global warming? NO. Real regression is trying to implement an international policy for many countries because that will take an incredible amount of time to reach an agreement and in the end it will probably be ineffective as it pertains to so many different environments. Do you really believe adding more people will make an agreement easier to reach? The idea that 'the world is a community' is quite silly considering every actor is looking out for the betterment of themselves. It is naive to believe everyone will sacrifice their own money for global climate change policy.
conclusionOpponent: Assuming the best case scenario is EXACTLY why we're in this situation in the first place. Policies are in place to deal with the WORST case scenario. And that is exactly what will happen in international agreements, every country doing the minimum to abide to those policies while pursuing whatever action gives them the most economic gain. Do you really believe China, one of the largest contributors to adverse climate change, will partake in an international agreement that will lower their GDP?

Most of the things we learn in school aren't needed anyway, most people never hear these concepts after school anyway. That is my conclusion.
rebuttal: I think that the measurements are not accurate to what a person knows since there are many ways to measure knowledge and many types of knowledge. I think that most people don't even take these tests seriously so there is no way to know if these are true results or people just trying to get the tests over with.  I think school smarts, financial smarts, and street smarts require different measurements thus one test will not be accurate.

A lot of people don't take these tests seriously which will make the measurements inaccurate. I think that these tests need to be more tailored to the individual more than a generalized audience.
argumentOpponent: Standardized tests are integral as they offer an unbiased measurement of students' understanding and proficiency, and provide essential data for enhancing educational curricula and policies. topic: Should the US Keep Using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections?
argument: The electoral college should be continued in use for presidential elections, as is written in our constitution as a democratic republic. This means that we should have a group of individuals that vote as a representation of each person in the country. The electoral college is made of people that were elected by those that they represent, so it is therefore a fair and accurate representation. Furthermore, they also help to make sure that states with lower populations, such as those in the Midwest, have a fair say against states with larger population, such as those on the east and west coasts.
rebuttal: This is not how federal elections in the United States work, however. The constitution states that we are a democratic republic, and therefore have to listen to these representatives. If the popular vote were to determine the presidency each time, states with lower populations, like Montana and Wyoming, may be overlooked in the election and their considerations unheard.
conclusion: But that is because there is vastly more people in Wyoming versus California. They people of Wyoming have valuable resources and land to protect, and if electing a candidate that was from California, per se, their interests for their state may not even get acknowledged. This creates a balance.
argumentOpponent: The electoral college undermines the principle of "one person, one vote", giving uneven voting power among states, and potentially enabling a candidate who lost the popular vote to seize the presidency.\n
rebuttalOpponent: While the electoral college does ensure representation for lower populated states, it disproportionately affects the weight of a single vote - a vote in Wyoming, for instance, weighs more than a vote in California. Further, numerous elections have resulted in a president who did not secure the popular vote, questioning the legitimacy of the “representative” aspect of this system.
conclusionOpponent: Protecting the voices of smaller states should not result in the disillusionment of the majority; we can instead reform our electoral system to proportionally distribute electors, ensuring every vote matters equally. Democratic representation must reflect the will of the people, which an overhaul of the Electoral College can achieve while ensuring inclusivity and far-reaching representation.

topic: Is Space Exploration a Worthwhile Investment for Humanity?
argument: I think space exploration is a worthwhile investment for humanity because it is a common goal that can be shared by the entire world. This increases cooperation with many countries that would otherwise be enemies. I think it also creates a way to experiment with new types of energy production and output machinery which can benefit all of society as new types of energy generation becomes a growing concern in the future.
rebuttal: While space exploration is expensive in theory, it is really not costing the taxpayers much at all compared to some other government programs. Hunger and poverty aren't being neglected financially, they are just much harder problems to solve logistically. Spending on space exploration can help produce cheaper ways to use energy which may actually help farms produce food cheaper.
conclusion: In conclusion I believe that space exploration is something that needs to continue in order to maintain our ability to progress as a united species that is continually trying to evolve and become better and more efficient than we were in the past.\n
argumentOpponent: Despite the allure of space exploration, its astronomical costs and continuous neglect towards prominent earth-bound problems such as hunger, poverty, climate change, and healthcare, make it a non-viable investment for mankind at this point.
rebuttalOpponent: While space exploration may facilitate temporary global cooperation, the commonality of existential Earth-centric issues which we are yet to solve, unite us more urgently and realistically. The experimentation with new energy sources could be more effectively pursued within our existing, familiar environments without the colossal expenditure space programs require.
conclusionOpponent: Regardless of the comparative budget allocations, even a fraction of space exploration funding redirected to earth-bound issues could significantly alleviate them. Imagining that space programs will indirectly solve hunger and poverty, when direct, hands-on solutions still lack adequate investment, seems needlessly convoluted and detached from the urgent realities of life on Earth.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
argument:
Artificial Intelligence offers many benefits for society. With its creation, we can overcome many obstacles, It can be used to help doctors, nurses, and other hospital staff. We can use it to supplement the current education platforms. Once it is regulated for ethical uses, it can be used to help us become more eco-friendly. 

Artificial Intelligence is already in use in many fields- we don't notice it because its incorporation is seamless. We can use AI to lessen some of the burdensome work we currently have to do.
rebuttal: ANy perceived job losses caused by the implementation of ai can be mitigated by making sure the human counterparts are trained as overseers for the ai.  It's up to the employers to make sure those millions of workers receive alternative jobs with equal pay.\n\n
conclusion: Again, ai is not meant to replace humans- it is to help us become more efficient. It is important to remember that humans are creating and improving every element of AI- any bias or lack of empathy would come from humans.  We already know how that turns out.  With AI, we have a possibility of making sure everything is done
argumentOpponent:
AI's rapid rise brings both immense potential and critical risks:

Job losses: Automation through AI could displace millions, particularly in repetitive jobs. Think: of self-driving trucks displacing drivers.

Biased algorithms: AI trained on biased data can perpetuate discrimination in areas like law enforcement and hiring.

Black box AI: Many AI systems lack transparency, making it difficult to understand how they make decisions and raising concerns about fairness and accountability.

Privacy threats: The widespread use of AI for surveillance and data collection raises concerns about individual freedoms and potential misuse.

Existential risk: While speculative, some experts warn about the possibility of AI surpassing human control and posing a threat to humanity.

These risks are not inherent to AI, but potential pitfalls we must address through responsible development and regulation. By openly discussing and mitigating these concerns, we can ensure AI benefits all, without jeopardizing our values or well-being.
rebuttalOpponent:
While AI does offer potential benefits, your argument overlooks significant concerns that require cautious optimism, not sweeping enthusiasm. Let's address your points:

Overcoming Obstacles: True, AI can assist in various fields, but relying solely on it can overlook crucial human elements. In medicine, empathy and human judgment remain vital. AI tools should complement, not replace, healthcare professionals. Similarly, in education, AI-powered platforms risk homogenizing learning and neglecting individual student needs. Human educators remain essential for fostering critical thinking and social-emotional skills.

Ethical Concerns: Regulation for "ethical uses" sounds ideal, but how do we define and enforce that? Biased data can lead to discriminatory outcomes even with good intentions. Algorithmic bias in policing or hiring can have severe consequences.
Seamless Integration:

You say we don't notice AI because it's "seamless." This raises concerns about transparency and accountability. We need to understand how AI algorithms work and who controls them. Blindly trusting black-box systems can have unintended negative consequences.

Burdensome Work: Reducing workload is attractive, but automation can also lead to mass job displacement. We need to consider the economic and social implications of replacing human labor with AI before celebrating it as a solution to "burdensome work."
Conclusion:

AI holds promise, but not without significant risks. We must move forward with caution, prioritizing ethical development, and human oversight, and addressing potential downsides like job losses and algorithmic bias. Unbridled optimism without acknowledging these concerns can lead to unforeseen consequences and exacerbate existing inequalities. Let's focus on harnessing AI responsibly, ensuring it benefits all of humanity, not just the privileged few.

Remember, technology is a tool, and we need to be the responsible wielders, ensuring it serves our values and well-being, not the other way around.
conclusionOpponent:
Training "AI overseers" won't solve the problem. Skills mismatch, demotivation, and astronomical costs make it unrealistic. We need solutions beyond retraining, like targeted support and income assistance. Remember, the bigger picture includes:

Lingering bias: Oversight can't fix biased data or algorithms. We need ethical development from the source.
Opaque black boxes: Human oversight needs transparent systems with clear accountability.
Existential questions: AI's future impact demands proactive, human-centered development.

AI's potential shouldn't blind us to its risks. Let's prioritize responsible development, mitigating harm, and ensuring AI serves humanity, not replaces it. We hold the reins, let's steer towards a future where humans and AI thrive together.

topic: Should Students Have to Wear School Uniforms?

conclusion: As I have stated schools should not mandate uniforms for 3 reasons, they limit self expression, they can be a pain to keep available and they are reminiscent of the military. conclusionOpponent: Uniforms don't rob individuals of their unique identities, they simply create an environment conducive to focus on studies rather than appearances; being able to respect diversity while conforming to shared standards augments real-world preparedness. topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: There should be mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions in certain circumstances. For example, if there is a committee relating to issues where gender may be important - such as sexual harassment or domestic violence, issues disproportionately effect women and women would be needed to give their input in these committees. This would provide a safer environment for all and would increase the trust in these committees by women, who would likely be their primary audience. I do not think this would be necessary in all committees, but may be helpful in some specific circumstances.
rebuttal: I disagree. It would be better to have a woman in a position of power and have other's question their merits than to not be in a position of power at all. While it could be a side effect of the quotas in some small way, the benefits far outweigh the potential harms. In addition, the opportunity to serve in these positions would allow women to show their skills and abilities. This would improve their reputation overall. If you don't allow someone to try, nothing will change. Also people will judge anyways.
conclusion: Tokenism is the act of a symbolic effort, whereas putting women in leadership roles is not symbolic effort but a real catalyst for change. Women are more likely to promote other women to leadership roles. A change such as this could improve generations. Your argument is based on the women not being qualified, however we are talking about equally qualified applicants to leadership roles. No one said anything about promoting an unqualified applicant.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions, while well-intentioned, can inadvertently perpetuate the harmful stereotype that women need special assistance to succeed and may undermine the principle of meritocracy which should ideally guide professional advancement.
rebuttalOpponent: While women's perspectives are indeed crucial in gender-sensitive issues, mandatory quotas could risk tokenism and compromise the quality of decision-making, if not all members are qualified; instead, fostering an inclusive culture that encourages diverse participation can lead to the same goal without compromising meritocracy.
conclusionOpponent: Placing women in leadership positions solely based on quotas rather than their qualifications could backfire, undermining the actual skills and capabilities they possess; it is crucial to promote a culture that values diverse talent and fosters opportunities for all, ensuring that the most qualified individuals ascend to leadership roles, irrespective of gender.

topic: Should There Be Standardized Testing in Schools?
argument: There are many ways to check your students progress in school. Standardized testing is probably the worst out of all of them. Because of the tie between school funding and standardized test scores, struggling schools in cities may see decreased in funding whereas schools in wealthier areas will see increased funding. This creates a bias, therefore making it unfair. Not only that, standardized testing really only proves students can memorize materials rather than them actually learning the stuff.
rebuttal: In a non biased world, yes it would ensure all students are held to the same educational expectations. However this world is full of bias. ow would it provide equity when schools in wealthier areas will inevitably see an increase in funding where it is not needed meanwhile students in poorer areas or rural areas, who actually need more resources will see less resources leading overall to less equity, less student comprehension and less school effectiveness.
conclusion: This tests only can test what students memorize rather than retain. If you have students unable to memorize information they are taught, they will inevitably do worse on standardized tests. This puts stress on teachers to change their curriculums so their students MEMORIZE information rather than actually learn it. while it may provide an insight, this insight is inaccurate. The same student memorizing and doing well on standardized testing may also forget the information they learned
argumentOpponent: Standardized testing is beneficial in schools as it ensures all students are held to the same educational expectations, thereby promoting equity, while also providing a reliable measure for evaluating student comprehension and school effectiveness.
rebuttalOpponent: While funding disparities are a concern, standardized testing offers a universally recognized measure to highlight these inequalities and fight for reform; and while memorization is often involved, these tests primarily assess mastery of core academic skills and provide insights into which areas need improvement.
conclusionOpponent: The problem of educational funding is a systemic issue that needs to be addressed separately; standardized testing helps identify these gaps and work towards bridging them, hence promoting equity by showing the areas in dire need of improvement and attention, while consistently tracking the proficiency levels in essential academic domains across the socio-economic spectrum.

topic: Should Students Have to Wear School Uniforms?
argument:
School Uniforms are mandatory requirements for some schools to create uniformity and to allow students to be in a state to learn. Despite school efforts to push legislation to enforce mandatory wear of school uniforms, there have been voices that shared various concerns regarding limitation of expression, lack of evidence to show the benefits of uniforms, and the additional costs of uniforms.

In an age of individual expression, the way a students decides to wear is a form of self expression and an opportunity for students to make their own decision in what they wish to wear. Without a uniform assigned to them, students can decide on what they want to wear and when they want to wear it.

There are lack of evidence to prove that having mandatory uniforms increase students' performance.

The additional cost of uniforms can be d
rebuttal: Though there are claims that school uniforms foster inclusivity, there are many instances where students and parents voice concerns on the limited options students have when choosing the type of uniform. As an example, the length and width of uniforms may accommodate more for a certain size than others. As an example, a student with wider hips may not fit into a uniform well. This may cause great discomfort and feel more insecure when learning. This will distract their focus on education.
conclusion: Though uniforms may have a symbolic role, students may not value the importance of symbolic role when their uniforms do not fit them well or the length of certain uniforms make them feel uncomfortable. argumentOpponent: School uniforms foster equality and inclusivity, minimizing social class disparities and making students focus more on education than fashion. Drawing from a multi-cultural perspective, they can even instill a sense of pride and unity, encapsulating the academic mindset.

topic: Is Government Surveillance Necessary for National Security?
argument: Government surveillance is often necessary to maintain national security. Though it is not without risk and drawbacks, it's intent is to enhance the overall safety of a nation from it's enemies, both internal and foreign. \nAn example of government surveillance being necessary for upholding national security can be found with Islamists, radical terrorists, and their relation to the U.K. Some of these groups are known to inhabit the U.K., and actively support violence or propaganda against the U.K.
rebuttal: Government surveillance needn't be heavy-handed, and laws can be enforced to ensure that the surveillance does not impede upon civil liberties such as the right to a fair and speedy trial, and so on. Many nations have needed to keep an eye on bad actors for a long time, and some have done so with a general respect towards personal freedoms. It is imperfect, but no surveillance at all would be a worse .
conclusion: It is not a matter of labeling, it is being focused on people who are part of specific violent groups, e.g. gangs, religious fanatics, supremacists, etc. who have shown in the past and and currently that they pose a real and data-backed threat to national security. Surveillance can be used in conjunction with more surgical methods.
argumentOpponent: While the intent to maintain national security is indeed a noble cause, heavy government surveillance infringes upon civil liberties and fosters an environment of fear rather than safety. It is crucial we consider alternative, more respectful ways of ensuring security without violating personal privacy rights.
rebuttalOpponent: Labeling groups or communities as threats based on isolated incidents fosters division and hinders social cohesion, a crucial element to national security. Additionally, surveillance should not be used as a blanket solution, as it can often misdirect resources from more effective security measures, such as community-building and fostering mutual respect.
conclusionOpponent: While surveillance laws could potentially respect civil liberties, such ideal enforcement has proven to be challenging in practice, often resulting in abuse. The solution isn't a surveillance-less society, it's steering our methods towards intelligence-led policing and open-source intelligence, which have proven to be less invasive but just as effective in ensuring national security.

topic: Should There Be Limits on Freedom of Speech to Prevent Hate Speech?
argument: Every human being has the right to exist and to feel safe in the world. Part of feeling safe is that you are not subject to hateful speech, which can threaten your existence by leading to violence, cause emotional strife and prolonged stress, and leads to the general public feeling a sense of disunity. Because of these net negatives, free speech should be limited to prevent people from saying things that are untrue or things that are calls to violence against a specific group of people. Some people may be concerned with who gets to delineate the bounds of what is "good" speech, but these can be well defined in an un-biased manner. Any speech that is an explicit message promoting violence should be disallowed. Similarly, any speech that is untrue and said by a person who knows it to be untrue should not be considered as protected speech. These limits enable people to have genuine and robust conversations.
rebuttal: First, I believe you mean that free speech is protected under the first amendment - the second amendment deals with firearms. And hate speech, and the stereotypes it promotes, have been shown to have measurable effects on human health and wellbeing. People who have a negative self-image or who think that their world is unfriendly are going to be more stressed, which increases cortisol and leads to numerous health issues. By saying "as long as hate doesn't affect people," you have ceded the argument. The fact is that hate does affect people in real and quantifiable ways, especially when the speech is intended to cause harm.
conclusion: Speech is action. Words do not exist on their own, but lead people to think and behave differently. Of course people can have hateful thoughts, and they can even say hateful things, but there are some things that ought not be allowed. You are allowed to say bigoted things, or make off-color jokes, but if you give speeches calling for an entire ethnic group to be eliminated, or say that someone who is qualified for a job should not be hired because of their sexual orientation, these types of speech break other laws that are in place to promote an equitable society. Having limits on free speech is not the same as instituting an Orwellian "thought police," and it is already in place with many of the laws we currently practice.
argumentOpponent: I think freedom of speech should be protected by the Second Amendment and can't be removed or revoked in any case as long as hate doesn't affect people to the point where it's very personal and health-affecting whether it's mental or physical.
