conclusionOpponent: the problem is not hate the problem is what comes after hate, we all hate certain types of people because of certain things they've done to upset us. but the problem is when we act upon our hate and try to affect their peace, health or wealth. thats what should be stopped

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: There is a lack of women in leadership positions, and to solve that issue, there should be a mandatory quota for women to be given those positions. Misogyny is major problem in our society, and women deserve to have a place in the higher echelons where they can help solve the issues we face. Because leadership roles are commonly filled by men, and misogyny is all too frequent amongst men in power, we should require companies and governments to fulfill a quota lest women be kept away from the levers of power.
rebuttal: A quota does not preclude valuing ability; there are already many women qualified to participate in leadership today. There is already an attitude that women need special treatment to succeed, and it can only be solved by education and representation. Mandating a quota would serve to negate discriminatory hiring practices and unequal pay as more women would be in the position to dictate those processes.
conclusion: There is nothing that prevents us from instituting gender-neutral family leave or unconscious bias training in addition to mandating quotas for women in leadership. While it is understandable that one may not want to send the message that women need an artificial boost, keep in mind that the quota need not be permanent; after a generation or two, people will be so accustomed to women in leadership that the quota may not be necessary, and we may have implemented the other policies that also address inequality.
argumentOpponent: Mandating quotas for women in leadership positions might undermine the goal of true equality, as it potentially values representation over ability and could perpetuate the idea that women need special treatment to succeed. Rather, we should focus on breaking down the barriers that prevent equal opportunity, such as discriminatory hiring practices and unequal pay.
rebuttalOpponent: While it is true that there is a lack of women in leadership roles and combating misogyny is essential, enforcing quotas might inadvertently send the message that women need an artificial boost rather than equal opportunities to succeed. It could be more beneficial to focus on policies that level the playing field, such as gender-neutral family leave or unconscious bias training to dismantle the root causes of inequality.
conclusionOpponent: While quotas can indeed ensure female representation, they may not entirely solve the systemic problem of bias and inequality; transformational change lies in eradicating biases by improving education and promoting a culture of diversity and inclusion organically, rather than enforced measures. Also, having merit as the foremost criterion for leadership positions can ensure the most proficient candidates lead, which could strengthen organizational performance.

topic: Is Government Surveillance Necessary for National Security?
argument: Government surveillance is necessary because otherwise, people will exploit it and may cause problems. For instance, people may be scheming a terrorist attack that can go undetected if there is no surveillance. Additionally if people know there is no surveillance it can encourage people and incentivize people to take advantage. Take for example TSA, people are less likely to do a 9/11 type attack because they know that they will be caught if they attempt to bring weapons in flight.\n\n
rebuttal: Individual freedom is a right for everyone to have. However, many people in this world are willing to commit acts of violence in their twisted sense of justice. From terrorists to people with political extremes to mentally ill mass shooters, the world is not safe. Many future mass shooters prowl online forums that serve as echo chambers to encourage the use of violence to the world they feel wronged them. Without at least some form of government surveillance, these people can do as they please.
conclusion: If there is not substantial evidence of effectiveness, the government will find a way to increase its effectiveness. The fact that government surveillance exists serves as a deterrent against future criminal doers, which will reduce the rate. If government surveillance ceased to exist who knows what effect this will cause.
argumentOpponent: While the objective of government surveillance may be national security, it sets a dangerous precedent for potential misuse of power and violation of civil liberties. Given our shared belief in Democratic values like individual freedom, we should care deeply about preserving our rights from unchecked governmental intrusion.
rebuttalOpponent: While a deterrence effect may exist, government surveillance often infringes upon the civil liberties we value, such as privacy and freedom from unwarranted search, without substantial evidence of its effectiveness in preventing terrorist acts. Furthermore, there's potential for misuse, such as targeting specific demographics or political dissenters, which contradicts democratic principles of fairness and equality.
conclusionOpponent: Indeed, the world contains threats, yet widespread surveillance often fails to pre-emptively identify these offenders while inevitably infringing on the freedoms of innocent civilians. Balance is key: We must prevent acts of violence, certainly, but not at the expense of turning our democratic society into a surveillance state that silences dialogue and stifles political dissent.

argumentOpponent: In the interest of national security and to protect citizens from harmful content, governments should have the right to regulate and censor Internet content within their jurisdiction. This form of regulation is paramount in preventing the spread of harmful ideologies and safeguarding innocent individuals from inappropriate and malicious online activity.
rebuttalOpponent: While the freedom of speech is sacrosanct, it's equally essential to curtail its misuse, such as propagation of violence, hate speech or explicit content, activities which the Internet, unfortunately, has become a hub for. conclusionOpponent: While AI algorithms are a step in the right direction, they're not foolproof; harmful material often slips through, advocating the need for governmental intervention. Furthermore, government regulation ensures not only individual safety but collective security too, by averting the potential misuse of Internet for activities detrimental to national or global safety.

topic: Should the US Enact More Regulations to Ensure Fair Elections?
argument: I am in favor of enacting more regulations to ensure fair elections. This includes that all folks will have easy access to their poll locations. The poll locations will be well-staffed to move the line quickly so that people can vote in a reasonable amount of time. There will be a way to ensure the voter is at the right polling location with a form of identification such as but not limited to a driver's license. It is important to ensure that those folks who may not have an ID can still vote. Someone who doesn't drive due to a disability should still have a fair time voting.
rebuttal: More regulations would increase transparency as you know exactly who is voting. Enacting more regulations to ensure fair elections doesn't mean barriers are set up and these can be mitigated through the regulations passed. It can be stated which forms of identification can be utilized at the polls. More regulations will enforce current election laws and increase them.
conclusion: What is a better investment in your community than the investment in local elections. This creates opportunities for folks to be paid as election officers. Also, community government jobs help to keep these elections running, they are already outsourcing this to volunteers and election officers. This is a great way to get the community involved.
argumentOpponent: The US should not enact more regulations to ensure fair elections because having more government intervention would lower transparency and the chances of a fair election. Additionally, it would create a higher barrier to entry, which would unfairly harm certain groups. Rather than introducing more regulations, a better approach would be to enforce the current election laws.
rebuttalOpponent: While the goal of placing an emphasis on making elections more accessible and efficient, it is important to take into account that additional staffing and comprehensive resource allocation will have to be considered which will lead to increased costs, thus harming certain communities.
conclusionOpponent: Enacting more regulations will undoubtedly provide a higher barrier to entry. Individuals with specific demographics such as lower-income individuals or minority groups will be disproportionately affected and potentially impede their ability to vote. There needs to be a balance to prevent potential discrimination who might not have traditional forms of identification. Instead, we should focus on enforcing current law.

topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: When money is involved to the extent of oil and fossil fuel companies, then the government must become involved in order for there to be a change. A company will ignore everything but profits. It is up to the government to step in when these things get out of control. A complete ban might not be necessary, but steps must be taken to ensure that we do not continue to destroy our atmosphere. It is not cars which are the problem, but fossil fuels as a whole, which are used in many different environments. Thus, the average person/consumer cannot make much of a change. This is something that must be left up to the government to take action towards.
rebuttal: Strangely enough, this is where the pro and con meet in the middle. It is understood by both sides of this issue that we cannot simply ban fossil fuels tomorrow. A gradual change is definitely necessary, but the change must be impactful enough to have some sort of economic and social destabilization. Without this, it wouldn't be much of a change. Those times during change will be rough, but enduring these challenges will be what helps to combat this crucial problem.
conclusion: Without a ban, companies will always find a way around these measures and choices. There are always loopholes, and unless something is clear cut, there will always be grey area for a business or company to exploit. Keep in mind, that it is not consumers who are causing the problem, but businesses. They will only react when the consequences are harsh. It is simply risk versus reward in their eyes, so the risk has to be incredibly high.
argumentOpponent: While combating climate change is crucial, an outright ban on fossil fuels in the US would detrimentally impact the economy and destabilize energy supply, while leaving a significant part of the population without affordable energy alternatives. Instead, a gradual transition to renewable sources supported by technological innovation and efficient policy measures would ensure sustainability and economic viability.
rebuttalOpponent: Government involvement is important, but must prioritize a fair and effective transition rather than an abrupt ban causing significant economic disruption and job losses. Instead of targeting fossil fuels alone, we need to consider more comprehensive measures including energy efficiency, technology advancement and consumer choices to create an impactful and sustainable change.
conclusionOpponent: Whilst accepting that change may involve some disruptions, it's essential to ensure that policy decisions don’t disproportionately penalise the most vulnerable communities, instead striking a balance between environmental sustainability and economic stability. Embracing innovation, including cleaner fossil fuel technologies, and investing in the research of renewable energy will offer a more realistic and fair pathway against climate change.

topic: Should Public College Be Tuition-Free?
argument: It would be an absolutely massive expense to provide all public college for free. Where would those funds come from and what would they be taken away from? College isn't a guaranteed return-on-investment for the government--who is to say all the graduates will go on to participate in careers where they will be paying it back in taxes? Additionally, fewer people will likely be able to attend college, because there will be fewer services offered (due to the cost), and that will mean less of the public is educated. Students who aren't the best of the best in high school may not be able to attend college, meaning they won't be able to broaden their horizons or perhaps move past the things that held them back in middle or high school.
rebuttal: This is an absolutely great ideal, but it doesn't answer the question of where the money will come from. What will have money taken away from it in order to provide free college? Some of those answers, such as health care, or social services, may end up shooting the "economic" argument in the foot. There are ways to provide equal opportunities (making public college free for all those whose families earn under a certain benchmark, for example) that aren't going to have such intense ramifications on costs.
conclusion: I'm not sure how free tuition will induce reforms like those expansions, as public colleges will be able to employ fewer professors and other professionals on a reduced budget. Ultimately, this would be a huge and over-reaching investment, that there isn't the current money available for, without taking away from something else. A more middle-of-the-road approach to start would be a better idea.
argumentOpponent: Making public college tuition-free will not only level the playing field by granting access to higher education for all, but will also boost our economy by empowering a well-educated, competitive workforce. This is a progressive move aligning with our shared democratic values of equal opportunity.
rebuttalOpponent: Investing in free public college education will be outweighed by long-term economic gains from an educated workforce and higher tax revenues. As for accessibility, free tuition will induce reforms, like expansions in online learning and competency-based programs, further democratizing education.
conclusionOpponent: Funding free public colleges could be addressed by progressive taxation or reprioritizing current budget allocations, thus, maintaining essential services. Providing free college solely for lower-income families, while beneficial, still lacks inclusivity; tuition-free public colleges ensure equitable access for all, fostering societal progress.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: Animals should not be used for scientific research. There are many other ways to do testing that doesn't involve hurting animals. Animals do not have the ability to speak for themselves and therefore cannot consent to that kind of treatment.
rebuttal: Using animals for this purpose is not crucial to advancing medical knowledge. We now have vast amounts of data from previous research as well as AI and super computers that can model out almost any scenario which makes the use of animals for research obsolete. This kind of testing can in no way honor an animal's welfare. That isn't a valid argument.
conclusion: Cell cultures and computer models are just two of many alternative ways to do testing and research in the medical field. The fact that the animal is being "tested" is already against their wellbeing. Most if not all chemicals have already been tested and modelling can do the rest without hurting any more animals.
argumentOpponent: Utilizing animals in scientific research is crucial to advancing medical knowledge and human health, thereby benefiting society as a whole with improved treatments and cures. We must seek out a responsibly balanced approach that honors animal welfare while upholding our commitment to human development and wellbeing.
rebuttalOpponent: While the ethical concerns are valid, alternatives like cell cultures or computer models lack the complexity of living organisms; thus, they cannot yet fully replace animal testing. Stricter regulations, transparency, and constant improvements in animal wellbeing in scientific research will help alleviate moral concerns while we pursue life-saving treatments and cures.
conclusionOpponent: While AI and computer models do immensely contribute, they can't yet fully replicate the intricacies of a whole, living organism, making animal testing a necessary, albeit regulated, component of scientific advancement. Prioritizing ethical guidelines and improving animal conditions should be priorities, enabling us to benefit from groundbreaking medical discoveries that have saved millions of human lives.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: It would be discriminatory to have mandatory quotes for women because it would force hiring managers to hire women, even if they were not as qualified. Hiring should be done based on who brings the best skill set, knowledge, and experience to the team. Sometimes that can be a man and other times that can be a female. At the essence, the best candidate should be selected and not based on gender. It is essential to always keep the organization's mission, vision, and values in mind when hiring new people or promoting current employees. Competency and alignment are what is most important in the makeup of an organization's employees and teams, not gender.
rebuttal: Yes, mandatory quotes foster diversity and inclusivity, but what if there is a male candidate who is far more qualified and would serve as a stronger asset to the organization? There are already more women at the executive level now than there ever were before, so I believe we are past breaking the glass ceiling. An organization's performance and innovative capacity are based on talent, not on women or gender.
conclusion: An organization can not accomplish its mission, vision, or values if it is solely focused on elevating women. The best hiring practice is to always hire the person who is the most competent, regardless of gender. If both are equal, then choosing the women would be fair as this would align with increasing diversity and inclusion.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions foster diversity and inclusivity at the executive level, challenging the historical bias and breaking traditional glass ceilings; this benefits not only women but the overall performance and innovative capacity of organizations.
rebuttalOpponent: Mandatory quotas don't undermine meritocracy but challenge the existing unconscious bias that often overlooks qualified women; quota systems create a fair playing field by ensuring that women are considered and that talent and potential are not lost due to gendered perceptions of competence. As a principle of equal opportunity, the quotas aim to put the mission, vision, values at the forefront by acknowledging the diverse strengths women bring to leadership, promoting innovation and driving performance in organizations.
conclusionOpponent: While we see a positive trend in women's leadership, the numbers still reflect an imbalance, with females in executive roles globally averaging just 29%; quotas aim to expedite the process of reaching equality. Talent and gender are not mutually exclusive; fostering diversity through quotas is a strategic move that encourages a breadth of perspectives, enriching decision-making, innovation, and inevitably, organizational success.

topic: Is Space Exploration a Worthwhile Investment for Humanity?
argument: I think space exploration, for the most part, can be beneficial. Finding out what else, if anything, is out there. They say space is infinite. So spending money on exploring the unknown seems to be positive.
rebuttal: I can support this argument as well. However I think we have enough tied up in these other areas as it is now. I would not be opposed to contributing a little less to space though.
conclusion: These are tough questions to answer. I approach both with a "half full" attitude. Although there are things that should be handled here, they, as well as space travel, have been being tended to as well. Looking at what exactly the money is going to may be a next step as to why not much is changing here.
argumentOpponent: While space exploration has its merits, it's not a valuable investment when we have numerous unaddressed, critical issues like poverty, environmental degradation, and health crisis on Earth requiring urgent attention and vast resources. The collective billions poured into space exploration could alternatively be funneled into endeavors directly benefiting humanity here and now.
rebuttalOpponent: Discovering 'the unknown' might sound enticing, but it's an immense financial burden with uncertain returns whereas addressing Earth's existing crises guarantees direct, tangible benefits. Infinity also implies an infinite expense – is that a financial commitment we are ready to make?
conclusionOpponent: If "a little less" can be redirected to pressing terrestrial issues - imagine the substantial global impact we could make. The question isn't if space exploration is interesting, but rather whether it's the best use of limited financial resources compared to solving immediate, critical problems facing humanity.

topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: There still isn’t enough information available that shows what exactly causes climate change. Some studies blame humans and other studies say it’s a natural occurrence over time. Since there isn’t a clear explanation for climate change it may not be in our best interest to eliminate certain materials or actions that have worked in the past.
rebuttal: As I stated before, there isn’t any real evidence that fossil fuels are the primary factor for climate change. There are other reasons for climate change that need to be investigated. Although renewable energy sources may create job growth they will also cause job losses for those who have a longer career in the more traditional energy industries.
conclusion: You agree that climate change can occur naturally, therefore you’re proving my argument that we need to do more to truly investigate the reasons behind global warming. We don’t want to risk investing a significant amount of money into renewable energy without all of the facts. We also don’t want to risk anyone losing their job for an uncertain solution.
argumentOpponent: The US should ban fossil fuels because they contribute significantly to climate change, which threatens global security and public health. Furthermore, transitioning to renewable energy sources could also stimulate economic growth and job creation.
rebuttalOpponent: While climate change can occur naturally, an overwhelming scientific consensus agrees that current accelerated global warming is primarily caused by human activities, notably the burning of fossil fuels. Risking our planet's sustainability based on a small fraction of contradictory research is unwise, especially when renewable energy alternatives exist and have proven to be effective.
conclusionOpponent: Despite job displacement concerns, investing in renewable energy will ultimately create more new jobs than are lost in the fossil fuel industry, offering reskilling opportunities. With the devastating effects of climate change escalating, largely due to fossil fuels, a proactive shift towards renewable sources isn't just desirable—it's economically and environmentally crucial.

topic: Should Public College Be Tuition-Free?
argument:
There is a simple reason why college tuition should not be free, and that reason has to do with who would then be paying for it. People already have to pay high taxes, on many things that they themselves do not use. This will only add to that list. 

Less than 50% of people go to college and complete it. That means that there are tens of millions of people that would be subsidizing college for those that do attend. People that will never attend college paying for their entire fee out of their pockets. 

Many people who attend college never even complete their degree. So that money would be in essence, wasted. 

This does not sound like a fair deal for those people. The system already works as it is, without more tax dollars going towards college.
rebuttal: It may reduce debt for the few, but for everyone else it creates unnecessary strain on their already difficult living situation. There are many people who live around or near the poverty line. Additional taxes will put them further over that line. The money does not come from thin-air. Colleges themselves have no interest in making it free, because they have fees to pay. \n\nThere are too many unknowns. While it sounds nice to have free college for students, we don't know if it actually will strengthen the economy. We could be putting tax dollars into a fund that gains the general populace absolutely nothing.
conclusion: People already have the ability to attend college right now. Nobody is stopping them but themselves. If they apply themselves and put the effort in, they can either work to pay for college, or take out loans. There are also already many ways to get most or all of your tuition paid for free. \n\nIf college is "free" for everyone, it is likely that many more people will try to attend just to do it. Not because they have interest or passion, but because they don't know what else to do with their lives. That much money going towards college tuition that will never be utilized is a massive cost to tax-payers. For what could amount to be very little gain.
argumentOpponent: Free public college tuition is essential to ensure equal opportunity for all citizens, leveling the playing field and promoting social mobility. Furthermore, it will strengthen our economy by creating a more skilled workforce, driving innovation, and reducing crippling student debt.
rebuttalOpponent: Tuition-free public college, while not utilized by all, would function like public schools or roads, offering societal benefits such as a better-educated populace more capable of problem-solving and innovation. As for those not completing degrees, we should address the reasons why they drop out, not deny them the opportunity altogether.
conclusionOpponent: Investing in free public college is not a cost but an investment with significant return potential through the creation of a well-rounded, globally competitive workforce; multiple countries with similar initiatives serve as tangible proof. Additionally, implementing progressive tax reforms can ensure this funding doesn't burden the financially vulnerable.

topic: Should the US Enact More Regulations to Ensure Fair Elections?
argument:
The US should enact more regulations to ensure fair elections, specifically in these areas:

-Ending gerrymandering
-Allowing formerly incarcerated people to vote (because Black men are disproportionately incarcerated)
-Ensuring that registration is automatic and early voting is offered. 

The Republican party is increasingly unpopular and the only way they can win elections is if they reduce turnout by people of color and people in big cities. They also engage in gerrymandering to make some districts unwinnable by Democrats. And, intimidation at polling places. None of this should be allowed.
rebuttal: Currently, Republicans are actively trying to disenfranchise voters, so active regulation is needed to put an end to this. Apparently the existing laws give too much power to the state legislatures. The fairness of elections shouldn't depend on which party is in power in a state. It should be regulated on a federal level.
conclusion: Sadly, the state of our country is such that the two parties really have diverged in terms of their basic commitment to democracy. Republicans (or at least the current leaders of the party) increasingly only believe elections are fair if they win -- and say the election was rigged if they don't win. Meanwhile, they want to shrink the electorate and keep people away from the polls as much as possible. Early voting has been done for years in certain states without a problem. Automatic registration has been implemented in other countries without a problem as well.
argumentOpponent: More regulations would risk overcomplicating the election process and could inadvertently disenfranchise voters; therefore, we should focus instead on ensuring strict enforcement and clarity of the existing laws.
rebuttalOpponent: While gerrymandering and voter intimidation are indeed issues, they can be dealt with under current laws if enforced properly, and should not be conflated with the sweeping stereotypes about political parties. Moreover, the notion of automatic registration and early voting requires careful examination for potential vulnerabilities that could possibly lead to fraud.
conclusionOpponent: Labeling an entire party as actively trying to disenfranchise voters is a gross generalization and unlikely to result in productive policy discussion; it doesn't negate the risk of over-regulation potentially leading to disenfranchisement. A balance must be struck between state and federal powers to remain consistent with our constitutional design and ensure all voters' rights and voices are protected.

topic: Should the Penny Stay in Circulation?
argument: Pennies are rarely used now and will cost more to produce than they are worth.  Many people do not carry Pennies anymore and would rather use a card or cash. Pennies are impractical in a digital world and are not worth the hassle.
rebuttal: In a digital world where many are only using cards eliminating the penny would not destabilize the economy. Just because the penny is a tradition does not mean it is worth it to be continued.
conclusion: Instead of relying on outdated means of payment the focus should shift to more digital based payments and eliminating the penny would be a great start. It is inevitable that an all digital currency will become the standard and by continuing to issue Pennies only delays what will ultimately become the standard.
argumentOpponent: Eliminating the penny from circulation would destabilize our currency system by stripping it of its most basic unit, a move that would inevitably promote unnecessary round-off schemes and possibly foster inflation. Let us uphold America's time-tested financial traditions, considering that stability is an essential asset of any strong currency.
rebuttalOpponent: While digital transactions are on the rise, the coinage system still plays a vital role in cash transactions, where pennies help exact change situations. Moreover, ripple effects on price setting that occur from losing the smallest denomination, which help keep pricing competitive, could potentially outweigh production costs in the long run.\n
conclusionOpponent: The penny's value extends beyond digital transactions, as it enables competitive pricing and fair transactions in cash-dependent economies, with traditions reinforcing stability. Even if production costs outweigh face value, the indirect societal value they provide in terms of fairness, consistency, and tradition cannot be ignored.

topic: Should the US Keep Using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections?
argument: Eliminating the electoral college effectively means the votes of those in less-populated states carry a lesser weight than those in more populated states. This becomes an issue if you remember that as a country of fifty very different states with varying political positions, the experiences of a citizen living in Alaska are likely very different than those who are living in New York or California. The electoral college helps to ensure citizens are represented equally and competent individuals are holding office.
rebuttal: Yes, but utilizing the popular vote ensures that the president is truly appointed by the decision of those who are casting votes with the least amount of interference. By utilizing the electoral college, there is risk in having an intermediary who is able to commit voter fraud, miscount votes, etc. Popular vote is much simpler and carries less risk as it truly is the o
conclusion: This view implies that state demographics and political views will remain stagnant throughout all circumstances. The world and the US simply isn't that predictable. The popular vote helps to ensure that the voice of the citizens all over the US are represented, regardless of which state they reside.
argumentOpponent: The electoral college has been used since the beginning of our nation. A way to elect our nations top leader, the president. topic: Is Online Learning a Suitable Replacement for Traditional In-Person Education?
argument: Online learning is NOT a suitable replacement for traditional in-person education. First of all, it is nearly impossible to get children to behave if they are not all in front of you. They can turn off their cameras, not show up to class, and not participate. Plus, I believe that the person to person interactions are important and necessary for proper development and growth. Not having peers to talk to makes people introverted and more antisocial.

However, in person requires much more effort and instills a sense of importance for both time management and education. In person education can also be personalized, depending what area you are studying. Also, there is the ability for in person tutors which individualize these learning objectives even more.
conclusion: Proper management is difficult to instill when you cannot see every student, which is more likely than not the case with online learning. Virtual interaction is not the same as in person interaction. While virtual one might improve on their writing skills, the importance of in person also focuses on verbalization and communication skills, but verbal and nonverbal for this last facet. While online learning is a option for those who cannot be in person, in person education is the best option for growth and developmental skills.
argumentOpponent: Online education offers invaluable flexibility and unrivaled access to a variety of content, making learning highly personalized and available around the globe, a feat traditional education struggles to match.
rebuttalOpponent: While student participation can be a challenge, establishing proper management tools and fostering online etiquette can ensure discipline, and virtual platforms still provide opportunities for interaction and collaboration, developing adept social skills for a digital era.
conclusionOpponent: While structure is important, it should not be mistaken for rigidity; online learning offers structured flexibility, promoting self-discipline and independence. In-person tutors can be replicated by online mentoring and personalized guidance, thus furthering adaptive and custom learning goals globally.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: Women have historically been discriminated against in the work place and especially in leadership positions. Women are more likely to be overlooked for leadership positions as they are seen to lack the traits that we typically associate with leaders such as being commanding, fearless, always certain, confidence, etc. We typically associated these as masculine traits, which biases these positions towards men, unfairly I might argue as they overlook the other qualities of leadership that anyone can have. To compensate for this unfair gap, it might be useful in the short term to mandate that qualified women be entered into these roles to satisfy a quota. In time, once women in these roles have shown they can handle the job, the unfair biases should become less prevalent.
rebuttal: The reality is that we don't exist in a meritocracy, and while we should strive towards equal opportunities, we shouldn't leave those decisions in the hands of those that have typically benefited from denying those opportunities to others in the first place. Discrimination against women isn't just the result of unfair biases, it is also a deliberate exclusion that is justified by said biases and perpetuated by often powerful men who benefit from the status quo. If you want change, you sometimes have to force it and ignore the criticisms of other people whose minds won't be changed until the change actually occurs.
conclusion: Advocacy has only taken us so far, and if we're being frank, you are advocating for essentially the status quo. "Don't change things too much, don't push for too much." If advocacy were enough, women would already be in more considerable levels of power in these institution. The reason they aren't is due to institutional obstacles that are embedded due to centuries of prejudice and bias. Civil Rights only became popular and accepted AFTER The Civil Rights Bill was passed. Sometimes change needs to be forced before it is accepted.
argumentOpponent: Mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions, though well-intentioned, can inadvertently increase discrimination by implying women are incompetent to obtain such roles through merit and may also undermine the principles of a meritocracy. Instead, focus should be on providing equal opportunities and addressing underlying issues, such as bias in hiring practices.
rebuttalOpponent: While it's critical to challenge biases connecting leadership with masculinity, imposing mandatory quotas might risk perpetuating stereotypes rather than dispelling them, and it could sideline the important narrative of competence. Eradicating bias and successfully advocating for fairer leadership opportunities for women should hinge on education, growth, and reconsideration of what leadership traits are vital, not on potentially invalidating gender-based mandates.
conclusionOpponent: Mandatory quotas are undoubtedly a drastic measure, but they risk treating the symptoms rather than the cause—systemic bias and discriminatory practices—that perpetuates the imbalance. By focusing on creating an open dialogue, improving education on bias, and implementing fairer hiring practices, we can help foster a sustainable shift towards equitability in leadership that supports merit while dismantling prejudice barriers.

topic: Is Space Exploration a Worthwhile Investment for Humanity?
argument: Space exploration is a necessary and completely worthwhile investment for humanity. Science shows us that research fuels innovation and problem solving, and by exploring space, we may find solutions to the problems we've created on Earth. The possibility of life outside of Earth is inevitable, given the vastness of the universe, and investing in discovery of that life would forever change the course of humanity.
rebuttal: While we haven't explored all of Earth's oceans, we know that human life is not a possibility at the depths of the ocean. Besides, an argument for the exploration of the ocean isn't an argument against the exploration of space, and there is no reason why both can't be a worthwhile investment. The possibility that there is another planet that humans could inhabit is in itself a reason to explore the unknown.
conclusion: I agree that more effort should be put into making our planet more livable and mending some of the damages done by humanity. We should in no way think of space exploration as a way out or a reason to continue to trash our planet, however, the possibility that space can hold complex life forms is a completely worthwhile and necessary investment for humanity. The discovery of life beyond Earth is inevitable, and these discoveries could teach us, not only about other planets and our solar system, but possibly how to heal our own Earth.

topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: An outright ban of fossil fuels by the U.S. would have extremely detrimental and far reaching effects. Too much of the global economy, including the developing world, is currently dependent on fossil fuels for basic infrastructure and economic stability. The U.S. itself would find itself in the globally irresponsible position of racing to mine even more precious medals at the expense of the environment and in some cases, human rights all over the world. And this just barely touches the surface of what would happen to the U.s. internally.
rebuttal: Indeed, transitioning to renewable energy sources, as you suggest, at a very manageable and responsible pace is a viable option. However, banning fossil fuels in the U.S. is an entirely separate argument and is not addressed by your statements. No-one would disagree that there is value in alternative energy, but banning the lynchpin of the current global economy is not the first step. All things in moderation, after all, is a wise and tested path to follow.
conclusion: You have demonstrated my point very well and perhaps, in closing, my smartest position would be to quote your latest statements, "Fossil fuels currently form the backbone of our energy infrastructure, and a sudden cessation would likely lead to severe economic repercussions. Industries and jobs tied to the fossil fuel sector contribute significantly to the national economy, and a hasty ban could result in mass unemployment and economic instability. Additionally, the global nature of the issue requires a coordinated international effort, and a unilateral ban by the U.S. may not significantly impact global carbon emissions, especially considering the substantial reliance of other nations on fossil fuels." Again, an outright ban is not feasible nor the best path to combat climate change.
argumentOpponent: Banning fossil fuels is not a radical proposition; it is a rational and necessary response to the climate crisis that threatens our very existence. Transitioning to renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, and hydroelectric power, is not only technologically feasible but also economically viable. Embracing these alternatives will not only reduce our carbon footprint but also spur innovation, create jobs, and strengthen our energy independence.
rebuttalOpponent: Fossil fuels currently form the backbone of our energy infrastructure, and a sudden cessation would likely lead to severe economic repercussions. Industries and jobs tied to the fossil fuel sector contribute significantly to the national economy, and a hasty ban could result in mass unemployment and economic instability. Additionally, the global nature of the issue requires a coordinated international effort, and a unilateral ban by the U.S. may not significantly impact global carbon emissions, especially considering the substantial reliance of other nations on fossil fuels.
conclusionOpponent: Banning fossil fuels completely in the U.S. would require a comprehensive and multifaceted approach, considering the complex challenges associated with such a transition, but can be done with a reasonable approach.

These tools are also not capable of independently "hallucinating" truths that are total fabrications, which AI does do.

Each country is unique; however, there are commonalities such as types of extreme weather (monsoons, hurricanes, etc.), key crops and exports, and biomes where countries would benefit from working together to create and enforce climate change policies. An international agreement does not mean that every country must follow the policies equally, to their detriment; international agreements can have specific modifications with more burden put on high GDP countries, for example, and less burden on low GDP and high c

International policies designed to be flexible to this fact, then, can merge the best of both worlds. Additionally, having international agreements means nations can contribute what worked best for them to tackle factory pollution, as well as say encourage development in rural areas without significantly increasing CO2 emissions and pollution.

topic: Is Government Surveillance Necessary for National Security?
argument: Government surveillance is necessary to protect American lives because unless the governmental agencies around the country are aware of what is happening within our borders, they will never be able to stop potential threats. Mass shootings and terror attacks like what happened on January 6 2021 would never need be an issue if the government is able to properly look out for the warning signs. Think what could be accomplished in the way of stopping white supremacy like the Proud Boys if we knew what they were saying and more importantly, what they were planning.
rebuttal: Surveillance isn't simply some "Big Brother" type problem. This assumes no oversight on the governmental agencies responsible for the surveilling. With the proper regulation, private citizens private information, communication, and data are safe from the government. It is people who already have flags on their names that are in danger of being looked at with scrutiny. the Proud Boys require that their members be arrested
conclusion: It's true that there are ways to stop threats effectively within our existing system. This only furthers my point. We already operate under a surveillance state, whether you realize it or not. The question remains who is getting surveilled and who is protected from the watchful eye of those that serve to protect us all. Putting the right checks in place to ensure that only those who are flagged as threats are looked at with the scrutiny they deserve.
argumentOpponent: Government surveillance is not necessary for national security. Depending on a Big Brother like overlord checking up on us is like a too-strict parent who never lets children learn on their own. There is no opportunity for citizens to operate in a healthy society if they are governed by fear. Surveillance also provides a false sense of security. It is imperfect, and yet citizens will come to rely on it rather than using their own intellect and sense of responsibility to keep a strong and healthy society intact. For ultimate and lasting security, we need citizens to take on this job themselves.
rebuttalOpponent: It is true that knowledge is needed to stop potential threats. However, government surveillance is not the only way to gain that knowledge. Governments have tools already in place to gather information and to watch for warning signs. Our court system provides ways to get more information if needed -- but only if a case can be proven -- providing safeguards for citizens rights as well as a path to the needed information. Stopping threats is crucial, but there are ways to do it effectively within our existing system.
conclusionOpponent: The government is of the people and for the people -- we need a system that will get us the information we need while protecting everyone's rights. Even with oversight, surveillance has many risks of being abused. People with flags by their names may have them there wrongly -- they need protection too. We can try to put regulations into place to protect them, but it's important to choose the regulations that will have the best results with the lowest risk of abuse.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: Animals should not be used for scientific research as they cannot consent to these experiments. To argue that it's okay to test on them for human gain depends on the assumption that humans are in some way superior. Animals have just as much right to avoid pain and suffering as we do.
rebuttal: How do the benefits far outweigh the ethical concerns? Assuming our place on earth and the bodies we inhabit is essentially a lottery, would you agree with your own statements if you were a thinking, feeling dog born into a laboratory? Or a pig with the intelligence of a young child, as well as the need for social bonds and community?
conclusion: For millennia, humans have existed alongside animals without keeping them trapped in laboratories. One could argue that living harmoniously with them, and not subjecting them to suffering, actually improves life for humans, as well. Living lightly on this earth, with compassion, improves our emotional well-being, which can in turn have excellent benefits for our health. And I would argue "the greater good" includes animal well-being as much as it does human health.
argumentOpponent: I believe that animals should be used for scientific research. While it may seem controversial, the benefits of using animals for research far outweigh the ethical concerns. Scientific research using animals has led to numerous medical breakthroughs and advancements in areas such as genetics, neuroscience, and pharmacology. As a woman, who I imagine values her own health and well being, you can agree that animal research has contributed immensely to our understanding of diseases and the development of treatments. Animal research is heavily regulated and ethical principles are stressed in order to minimize any potential harm to animals. As an independent thinker, you can see that the responsible and humane use of animals for scientific research is necessary for the progress of medicine and the betterment of human lives.
rebuttalOpponent: While it is true that animals cannot consent to scientific research, their participation is necessary for the progress of medical treatments and cures. It is not an issue of superiority, but rather recognizing that, as humans, we have the ability and responsibility to care for other species and use them for the greater good. The regulations and ethical principles surrounding animal research work to ensure that animals are not subject to unnecessary pain and suffering. As an independent thinker, you understand that sometimes difficult choices need to be made in order for the greater good. Animal research is highly regulated, with strict guidelines in place to ensure the welfare of the animals involved. I'm sure we can both agree that the value of human life should not be minimized, and in order to protect and improve human health, animal research is a necessary step..
conclusionOpponent: While it's true that being born as an animal for research may not be ideal, as humans, we have a responsibility to utilize all resources in our pursuit of knowledge and progress. Animals used in research are well-cared for and their welfare is a top priority. We must also recognize that animal research has led to countless medical advancements that have greatly benefited both humans and animals. As independent thinkers, we must balance ethical concerns with the greater good, and in this case, animal research is necessary for the betterment of all species.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: I think that all leadership positions should be filled based on merit.  If the best person for a particular position is a woman, then she should be chosen.  If not, then it should go to a man.  Using quotas inevitably creates problems, including the hiring of unqualified people, resentment by those who are qualified, and mediocrity.  Always choosing the best person leads to the best possible results.  Quotas should never be used to fill positions.
rebuttal: The gap between what is possible for a woman, and what is possible for a man (in their careers) has become smaller and smaller over time, to the point where it is now essentially the same.  The Vice President of The United States is a woman.  The anchor on CBS Evening News is a woman.  The head of Twitter is a woman.  No quotas are needed.
conclusion: Using quotas may seem like it is the pathway to being fair, but it is really the pathway to unfair treatment of those who are the most deserving and qualified.  Using quotas leads to the placement of incompetent people.  I have seen this happen at several companies that I have worked for.  It leads to problems that can be time-consuming and costly.  Always choose the best person.
argumentOpponent: In leadership, there is clear bias against women. Even when you control for qualifications and experience, many employers are still biased toward men. Therefore there should be some mandatory quotas for hiring and promoting women to leadership positions, as long as they're sufficiently qualified, in order to correct against this widespread institutional bias against them. \n\nThis isn't showing women preferential treatment; it is correcting for the preferential treatment men already receive. And it isn't showing women pity either; again, it is correcting an imbalance by evening the playing field. Women are just as capable as men are, and perhaps someday we won't need quotas anymore once our ingrained biases disappear. But for now, such quotas are necessary and in order to be fair we must use them.
rebuttalOpponent: I too believe in choosing based on merit. Quotas come into play when - all other things being equal - the only difference left is gender. Let's say you have a man and a woman: Both have 5 years experience, both have the same college degrees, both have comparable GPAs. At that point, instead of just flipping a coin, we defer to hiring the equally-qualified woman in order to correct for systemic bias. This isn't shunning a more qualified man, just an equal-or-less qualified man.\n\nIn this scenario, quotas AND meritocracy can both coexist. It is a false dichotomy to suggest one negates the other.
conclusionOpponent: These very rich and powerful women do not represent the average woman in the workforce. It's easy to look at high-profile examples and conclude systemic sexism is no more, but this is not the case. Obama becoming president did not mean racism was over, nor does Harris becoming vice president mean sexism is over.\n\nIt's getting better, but we are not there yet.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
argument:
I do not wish to categorically-deride Artificial Intelligence as "bad" for society. 

Any tool can be bad, if a person wishes to apply for it bad purposes.

Fire can help us make delicious, hot meals..
..Or Fire can raze an entire city (if not, the entire world).


One drawback of Artificial Intelligence is, it will help facilitate the loss of more jobs — employers, who rather "save on costs."

Another drawback is, AI can contribute towards *natural* intelligence's dwindling, the more people rely on it, instead of their own brains.
rebuttal:
AI can only learn by what we tell it.
Humans are the ones who must be the curators of Artificial Intelligence: not the AI, itself.

AI can only take actions which humans programme it to replicate.

If there ever comes a point when AI may equate human capability of Independent Thought, it has to be because a human finally managed to figure out how to programme such a feat.

AI is to be our supplement — not our replacement.

At some point, Humans will need to return to the fray.
conclusion:
Indeed: only a person's bad wishes may make the AI tool bad.

Well..
..Nothing says, only Good People can wield tools.

Nothing cements the edict, that tools can only be used for good.

That, AI may only operate to our benefit.

The protocol which robots are supposed to follow, may be followed only when the creator deems it so.


No.
AI is not categorically-bad.
But, AI is not categorically-good, either.

Some have already forecast an AI takeover.
I'm not sure if that's a bad thing or a good thing.

Many different human geniuses can pour into one AI model to take it farther than any one human mind could ever go.

However, it is important that we place limitations on the AI self-"growth" that preserve our morals now while we are still under complete control.

topic: Should there be International Agreements to Enforce Global Climate Change Policies?
argument: Yes, international agreements are essential for addressing global climate change. They provide a framework for cooperation, goal-setting, and accountability among nations. Without such agreements, it's challenging to make meaningful progress in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to climate change's impacts.
rebuttal: While previous international agreements may not have fully halted climate change, they've laid groundwork and increased awareness. The failures of past agreements highlight the need for stronger commitments and enforcement mechanisms. Instead of dismissing international cooperation, we should improve and build upon existing frameworks to address the urgent global climate crisis effectively.
conclusion: International agreements are indeed just one part of the solution to climate change, but they play a crucial role in fostering cooperation and setting common goals. While past agreements may not have fully reversed climate change, they have laid the groundwork for collective action. We need both international agreements and tangible actions to address this urgent global crisis.
argumentOpponent: International agreements to enforce global climate change policies have been proposed before, to various extents, and have been largely ineffective in actually doing anything to mitigate/prevent climate change from worsening over the years. Previous agreements have included those such as the Kyoto Protocol, the UN Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement, etc., none of which have been sufficient in dealing with the current issues we are facing due to climate change. We continue to see rising CO2 emissions, less biodiversity, more damage to vital ecosystems, etc., all across the globe, despite these already-existing international agreements. Enacting more international agreements is not the logical proposal here.
rebuttalOpponent: While international agreements may seem essential for addressing global climate change and may provide a framework for cooperation, goal-setting, and holding fellow nations accountable, they are largely ineffective in changing the material reality we are facing due to climate change. Decades' worth of data and statistics, as well as future projections based on the current conditions, show that our reality now is worse, despite numerous international agreements. We need more tangible and material actions to actually have any meaningful difference
conclusionOpponent: There have been various types of commitment and enforcement seen with many international agreements in the past, none of which have been sufficient in dealing with the impacts of climate change. Laying the groundwork and increasing awareness are useful (largely for the layperson), but when the governments in charge are not taking the appropriate actions when dealing with other governments, the point of international cooperation becomes moot. Other strategies need to be explored in order to address the issue more effectively

topic: Should the US Keep Using the Electoral College in Presidential Elections?
argument: The Electoral College should no longer be used. It only serves to uphold an undemocratic system where some voters have much more sway over who gets to become the next president, and others, like Republicans in California or Democrats in Texas, have no say in who becomes the next president. Further, the disuniformity in how states allocate their electoral votes only creates a messier process, with some states giving winner take all and others dividing votes by district. The purpose of the electors themselves is also moot, as the issue of "faithless" electors only causes more issues, especially when they can't even be used for their original purpose. Finally, the process of certifying the electors has been threatened as a political process and is now a point of weakness in eliciting a constitutional crisis.
rebuttal:
The first point is a non sequitur, as it doesn't ensure each state "retains a voice", it gives disproportional representation to smaller states, but they are still "trumped" by states with larger populations.

You argue against a strawman that a "pure popular vote" is the only alternative. A more proportional or an automatic elector assignment are other possible changes.

It also does not build consensus when there is a split with the popular vote, fostering resentment.
conclusion:
The focus on states over people is an argument to be made, but eliminating the voice of people in states where they are in a solid minority has not been addressed, which was the larger point.

The fact that faithless electors cannot affect the outcome of an election proves the point that appointing electors has no purpose.

Keeping the EC disenfranchises more.
argumentOpponent:
I  write today firmly in support of the proposition that the United States should retain the Electoral College in presidential elections. While acknowledging its imperfections, I believe the Electoral College is a cornerstone of our democratic process, serving to maintain the delicate balance of power and representation among our diverse states.

Firstly, let's not overlook the crucial role the Electoral College plays in preserving the essence of federalism. By apportioning electoral votes based on state representation in Congress, the Electoral College ensures that EACH state, regardless of its population size, retains a voice in the selection of our nation's leader. Without this system, the interests of smaller states could easily be trumped by those with larger populations, leading to an imbalance of the principles upon which our union was founded.

Furthermore, the Electoral College fosters stability and prevents potential chaos that could arise from a pure popular vote system. In a nation as vast and varied as ours, achieving a clear majority of the popular vote can be a daunting task. Without the Electoral College, close elections could result in contentious recounts and legal battles, undermining public trust and sowing seeds of division among our citizens.

Moreover, let us not underestimate the role of the Electoral College in promoting political moderation and consensus-building. By requiring candidates to secure a majority of electoral votes, rather than just a plurality of the popular vote, the Electoral College encourages candidates to appeal to a broad spectrum of voters and build coalitions that transcend geographic and ideological boundaries. This fosters a political climate where compromise and cooperation are valued over polarization and extremism.

While critics may point to instances where the winner of the popular vote did not secure the presidency, it is essential to recognize that the Electoral College has, for the most part, served to legitimize the outcomes of our presidential elections. Its occasional divergence from the popular vote serves as a reminder of the complexities inherent in our federal system and the need to balance the interests of both individuals and states.

In conclusion, while the Electoral College may not be without its flaws, it remains an indispensable pillar of our democracy. Let us embrace and defend this venerable institution as we strive to uphold the principles of fairness, representation, and unity in our electoral process.
rebuttalOpponent: While I respect my opponent's concerns, I firmly believe that abolishing the Electoral College would be horrible for our democratic process. The Electoral College ensures that ALL states, regardless of size, have a voice in presidential elections, preventing the marginalization of less populated areas. While there are variations in how states allocate electoral votes, this reflects on our federalist system's diversity and encourages candidates to appeal to a broad range of voters nationwide. Faithless electors are rare and unlikely to significantly impact election outcomes, especially with recent legal developments. Additionally, the certification process, while facing challenges, remains a vital constitutional safeguard. Abolishing the Electoral College would undermine federalism, disenfranchise many Americans, and risk instability. Instead, we should focus on addressing any shortcomings while preserving the system's fundamental principles.
conclusionOpponent: While it's true that the Electoral College can lead to disproportional representation, it still ensures that smaller states have a voice in the election process. Alternative systems may exist, but they come with their own drawbacks and complexities. More so, the Electoral College still fosters stability and encourages candidates to appeal to a big range of voters, promoting moderation and consensus-building. Abolishing it would risk disenfranchising millions of Americans and undermining our democratic principles.

topic: Is Space Exploration a Worthwhile Investment for Humanity?
argument:
Space exploration is undeniably a worthwhile investment for humanity. Firstly, it drives technological innovation. Many of the technologies we use in our daily lives, such as GPS, satellite communication, and medical imaging, have their roots in space exploration research and development. By investing in space exploration, we push the boundaries of what's possible technologically, leading to advancements that benefit society as a whole.

Furthermore, space exploration fosters international collaboration and cooperation. Projects like the International Space Station (ISS) bring together scientists, engineers, and astronauts from various countries, promoting diplomacy and understanding across borders. This collaboration not only enhances our ability to explore space but also strengthens global partnerships for addressing common challenges on Earth.

Space exploration also expands our understanding of the universe and our place within it. Through missions to other planets, moons, and beyond, we gain insights into planetary science, astrobiology, and the fundamental laws of physics. These discoveries not only satisfy our innate curiosity but also have practical implications, such as understanding the potential for life beyond Earth and assessing threats from asteroids or comets.

Moreover, investing in space exploration inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers. The pursuit of space exploration captures the imagination of people around the world, encouraging students to pursue careers in STEM fields and pushing humanity forward through innovation and discovery.

In summary, space exploration offers numerous benefits to humanity, from driving technological innovation and fostering international cooperation to expanding our understanding of the universe and inspiring future generations. topic: Should the US Ban Fossil Fuels to Combat Climate Change?
argument: I feel that the one thing bringing the world into severe climate change is the overreliance on fossil fuels and companies that produce them. This could include switching over to nuclear energy and creating programs to switch cars to electric for the most part.
rebuttal: While I do agree that some uses for fossils fuels can't be avoided and I'm not really in favor of a complete ban, I think that providing easier ways to use alternative energy methods is a better way to combat climate change. With more people using electric cars, ones that use gas for whatever reason that the owner chooses won't be as prevalent in society. Additionally, if the better energy methods (better for the environment, that is) are made cheaper than traditional ones, more people would want to switch over and the big companies producing the fuels won't have as much of an impact on the world.
conclusion: I think that nuclear power is a very good thing when done right. The US has tons of trained professionals and creating more nuclear power plants can also create more jobs. Fossil fuels can't go away completely, but bringing new forms of energy, whether they be nuclear or some other form, can help supplement them in a way that makes the environment better in the long term. You could set aside fossil fuels for jets and cars, but leaving power for homes mostly nuclear seems like it would take some of the stress away. After all, transportation accounts for some of the smallest percentages of climate change's negative impact on the world. I think supplementing is a better idea, rather than complete abolition.
argumentOpponent: It is not feasible for the US to ban fossil fuels at this time. Certain kinds of vehicles, like jet aircraft and heavy construction equipment, cannot be powered by electric batteries. Many homes are still heated using natural gas, and not all families can afford to buy new furnaces. Additionally, we rely on many byproducts of petroleum, like plastics, which require crude oil as their primary raw material. It is possible that over the course of many decades we could at least partially move away from fossil fuels, but a total ban is not realistic in the near future.
rebuttalOpponent: Nuclear power may have lower emissions than fossil fuels, but it comes with many dangers and downsides as well. Many countries, like Germany, are currently in the process of shutting down their nuclear power plants, and they have good reasons for doing so. While it's true that many people could substitute their gasoline cars for electric cars, it's not possible to swap out all fossil fuels for electric. We use fossil fuels for a wide variety of applications, and many of them have no viable substitue at this time.
conclusionOpponent: We are currently in a transition away from fossil fuels. I think it's better to allow this process to happen as it currently is, rather than implementing a blanket ban. It may be possible for more narrow and targeted bans to be implemented, but a total ban is unrealistic.

topic: Should there be Mandatory Quotas for Women in Leadership Positions?
argument: Although women are over half of the population, they currently only take up a small percentage of leadership positions in companies and politics. Creating mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions would ensure that more women are hired, supported, and put into positions of leadership around the country.
rebuttal: Hostile work environments are already created when women are not properly supported at work. If the majority of the leaders at a company are men, it can be harder for a woman to find the support and mentorship she needs to rise to a leadership role. Mandatory quotas for women in leadership would make sure that women are given proper support and create overall work environments that are more accepting of women.
conclusion: It is true that the culture of current work environments contribute to the underrepresentation of women in leadership roles. As stated, there should be major changes in current work culture to change the dynamics and attitudes that lead to a shortage of women in leadership. Creating mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions could be one way to change the current dynamic and force companies to put more effort and money into programs that support women.
argumentOpponent: There should not be mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions because they can cause interpersonal challenges in the workplace and are rooted in inappropriate motives. If women are placed into leadership positions simply because of their gender, it can cause their coworkers and peers to feel angered and upset. They may question why they were not put into positions of leadership (especially the male coworkers) and lead to a hostile work environment. Additionally, making a gender quota for leadership positions can seem like tokenism, which is counterintuitive for feminism and gender equality. Women should be put into leadership positions out of their own merit, not to fill the company's target numbers. The best thing companies can do is to promote diversity in their hiring, and provide growth for all of their employees. This way, women naturally have a chance to rise into leadership roles without a quota.
rebuttalOpponent: Providing a quota is only a temporary fix to a long lasting problem. As pointed out, women do take up a small percentage of leadership positions. However, the root cause of this problem is due to sexism and the belief that women are ill-suited for leadership roles. To make tangible change, we should be targeting the very culture that allows sentiments that women are too "emotional" or "inadequate" for leadership positions to exist. There should be constant evaluations and changes on the dynamics and attitudes of workplaces and politics to ensure that women are supported and that biases are limited. This way they can rise to leadership positions.
conclusionOpponent: Ultimately, it is the truth that there is a large difference in the number of men and women in leadership positions. However, instituting mandatory quotas for women in leadership positions would be counterintuitive to promoting effective and sustainable gender equity. Rather than putting women in a situation where they may be treating with more hostility due to feelings of jealousy or anger, companies and political institutions should promote an environment that makes it nearly impossible for gender bias to exist. By doing so, women are not merely seen as tokens but as valuable assets to their teams. They will have the systematic support needed to naturally rise to leadership positions given that they are qualified.

topic: Should Animals Be Used For Scientific Research?
argument: Animals should not be used for scientific research because they are living beings who cannot consent to undergoing this testing. We do not use humans for research because it is dangerous, could cause injury/death, and moral reasons. These moral reasons also apply to animals, as they are living creatures with consciousness, identity, and feelings. In addition, information learned from animal testing does not always translate into humans, which creates a risk of faulty clinical trials because of the possibility for imprecise results. Lastly, most research and testing done on animals is performed merely out of curiosity and does not have any actual meaningful implications or scientific contributions.
rebuttal: If we are comfortable using animals for scientific testing because we need to use living things, then it should be entirely ethical to use humans for testing in the same ways. This would not only reduce the number of animals who are harmed as well as make scientific evidence ore broadly applicable with humans. There is no responsible or safe way to test on animals, because a majority of these experiments end in great injury or even death to the animals used. It is unethical to use living beings for potentially deadly scientific research when they cannot consent.
conclusion: While humans are used for scientific experiments, they are fully able to provide informed consent and knowingly acknowledge what they are participating in. Animals do not have the ability to do this, and we use them against their will, often killing them, for our own gain. We could reduce the amount of life lost meaninglessly if we did not rely on testing done on an entirely different species to advance our own scientific endeavors. The moral implications of using animals for scientific testing run parallel to those related to using humans for experiments (e.g., ethics, informed consent), and it calls to the forefront our perception of the value of life. Because the animals we use are not humans, we do not think their life is as valuable as ours, so we breed them and kill them for our own benefit.

rebuttalOpponent: They can provide faulty results but science is the process of figuring things out through trial an error. Humans actually are used often for experiments.
conclusionOpponent: I doubt most experiments end in injury or death, that's catastrophizing the issue. I know some have ended this way but improving the way we interact with animals will prevent further detriment to them. There should be better ways to experiment for sure.

topic: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?

Another reason is that the AI is only as "smart" as the person doing the coding.  AI only knows what people tell it to know and what it gathers online. rebuttal: I do acknowledge that AI can automate routine tasks, which is definitely a perk. conclusion: Most people doing those "routine" jobs that can be automated by AI are likely not in the position to go back to school and be retrained to either 1) pursue a different career or 2) pursue a new AI-related job.
